policies.title: Wage and Hour, Paid Sick Leave, Meal and Rest Periods
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME], especially hourly direct care, night, kitchen, housekeeping and maintenance staff, and those who work live-in or 24-hour shifts.
policies.purpose: To make sure employees are paid correctly, receive paid sick leave, and are given meal and rest periods as California law requires, while ensuring residents are always supervised.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] complies with California and federal wage and hour law. This policy covers minimum wage, overtime, paid sick leave and meal and rest periods.

1. Minimum wage. California's minimum wage is $16.90 per hour from January 1, 2026. Where a city or county minimum wage is higher at the facility's location, [AGENCY NAME] pays the higher rate. Examples are the City of Los Angeles ($18.42 from July 1, 2026) and San Francisco ($19.61 from July 1, 2026). The administrator checks local rates each year before January 1 and July 1.

2. Federal law. [AGENCY NAME] follows the Fair Labor Standards Act as it applies to home care and domestic service workers (29 CFR 552). It does not rely on any live-in or companionship exemption without a written review by employment counsel.

3. Paid sick leave (Labor Code §246). Every eligible employee receives at least 40 hours or 5 days of paid sick leave per year. The accrual or front-loading method is set out in the employee handbook. Leave may not be denied, and no one is disciplined or retaliated against for using it.

4. Meal and rest periods. Meal and rest periods are provided as required by IWC Wage Order 5. Wage Order 5 has special rules for a sole caregiver in 24-hour residential care of the elderly. [AGENCY NAME] will not use an on-duty meal or rest arrangement for a sole caregiver unless the arrangement was reviewed by employment counsel and the employee's agreement is in writing.

5. Live-in and 24-hour shifts. [AGENCY NAME] does not schedule live-in or 24-hour shifts until employment counsel has reviewed the arrangement.

6. Health care minimum wage. The SB 525 health-care minimum wage applies only if an RCFE is affiliated with or controlled by an acute-care hospital. The licensee confirms and documents annually whether this applies to [AGENCY NAME].

7. Coverage. Required staffing is maintained during meal and rest periods (see PP-01). Residents are never used to cover for staff on a break.

definitions.definition: Paid time off for the employee's or a family member's health needs under Labor Code §246, at least 40 hours or 5 days per year.
The only staff person on duty with residents in a 24-hour residential care facility for the elderly. Special meal and rest rules apply under Wage Order 5.
A work arrangement in which the employee resides at, or works a continuous shift of up to 24 hours in, the facility. It requires employment counsel review.
A city or county minimum wage that is higher than the state rate.

procedures: At hire, the administrator gives each employee a written notice of the pay rate, pay day, overtime rate and paid sick leave policy, and the employee signs for it.

Each year before January 1 and July 1, the administrator checks the state minimum wage and the local minimum wage for the facility's city or county, and documents the check. Any pay rate below the applicable minimum is raised the day the new rate takes effect.
Employees record actual start and stop times, including meal periods, on the time record or timekeeping system. Time is recorded at the time worked, not estimated afterward.
The administrator reviews time records each pay period and corrects errors in the employee's favor. Overtime is paid at the rates required by law.
The administrator determines which employees are exempt or non-exempt before hire and documents the basis. Live-in and companionship exemption claims are made only after counsel review.

The administrator schedules meal and rest periods on the shift schedule and assigns another staff member to cover residents during each period. Where only one caregiver is on duty, the administrator follows the counsel-approved procedure for a sole caregiver under Wage Order 5.
If an employee cannot take a required meal or rest period, the employee notes it on the time record and the administrator pays any premium that is owed.
The administrator tracks paid sick leave balances for each employee and shows the balance on each pay statement or in writing each pay period.

When an employee requests sick leave, the administrator approves it on request. The employee gives notice when practicable, and no doctor's note is required unless counsel advises that one is allowed in the circumstance.
The administrator arranges replacement staff using the on-call list so that required staffing is maintained when an employee uses sick leave.
The administrator does not take adverse action against any employee for using sick leave, asking about wages, or raising a pay concern.
Before the licensee approves any live-in or 24-hour shift, the administrator obtains written advice from employment counsel and files it in the administrative file.
Once a year, the administrator documents whether [AGENCY NAME] is affiliated with or controlled by an acute-care hospital and, if so, applies the SB 525 health-care minimum wage.

Employees who believe they were underpaid or denied a break report this to the administrator, or to [LICENSEE / OWNER NAME] if the concern involves the administrator. The concern is investigated and answered in writing within 14 days.
Payroll and time records are kept for at least [PAYROLL RETENTION PERIOD - confirm with payroll provider or counsel] and are available for inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Funds compliant wages, approves counsel review of any live-in or 24-hour arrangement, and receives employee wage concerns about the administrator.
Checks wage rates, approves timecards and sick leave, schedules breaks with resident coverage, and keeps wage and hour records.
Records time accurately, takes assigned meal and rest periods, and reports missed breaks or pay problems.
Advises on sole caregiver, live-in and 24-hour arrangements and on payroll compliance.

Time records and payroll records
Semiannual minimum wage check log
Paid sick leave balance records
Missed meal or rest period records and premium pay

Annual determination on hospital affiliation (SB 525)

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, consultants and contractors who are in the facility or who work with residents.
policies.purpose: To set clear standards for how staff treat residents, protect residents' personal rights, and keep relationships with residents professional so that no resident is harmed, exploited or discriminated against.
policies.policy:
All staff at [AGENCY NAME] treat every resident with dignity and respect and uphold the personal rights listed in 22 CCR §87468.1. Staff are trained on resident personal rights (see TR-01 and RD-01).

1. Prohibited treatment. Staff may not punish, humiliate, intimidate or abuse any resident, physically, verbally, emotionally or sexually. No resident is locked in or kept from leaving.

2. Discrimination. Staff may not discriminate against, or deny or treat residents differently in admission, transfer, discharge, room sharing, room or restroom assignment, use of preferred name or pronouns, or association, based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)). The Department cannot waive these protections.

3. Money and valuables. Staff may not accept, borrow, hold or manage resident money, valuables or property except as allowed by the resident cash and theft-and-loss procedures (TL-01 and TL-02). Staff may not accept gifts of value, tips, bequests, loans or powers of attorney from residents.

4. Boundaries. Staff may not have romantic or sexual relationships with residents, may not use resident property or services for personal benefit, and may not take or post photographs or recordings of residents without written consent. Staff may not engage with residents or families on personal social media about resident matters.

5. Staffing. Residents may not substitute for required staff. Volunteers are supervised and not counted in the staffing plan (22 CCR §87411).

6. Reporting. Any staff member who sees or suspects a violation of this policy reports it right away (see SAF-01 and PP-02). Retaliation against a person who reports is prohibited.

7. Discipline. Violations lead to discipline up to and including termination and, where required by law, a report to the appropriate agencies.

definitions.definition: The limit between a caregiving relationship and a personal, financial or romantic one.
Taking or using a resident's money, property or services for the benefit of someone other than the resident.
The name and pronouns a resident asks staff to use. Staff must use them.
The rights of residents listed in 22 CCR §87468.1, including dignity and freedom from punishment, humiliation, intimidation or abuse.

procedures: At hire, each employee receives this policy and signs an acknowledgment that is filed in the personnel file.
During orientation, before working alone, the administrator or trainer reviews resident personal rights and this policy, with examples, and documents the session on a sign-in sheet (see TR-01).
The administrator posts the resident personal rights where residents and visitors can read them, and staff are shown where they are posted.
Staff use each resident's preferred name and pronouns. The preferred name and pronouns are recorded in the resident's file and on the care plan if the resident wishes.

Staff assign rooms, roommates and restrooms without regard to actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status. Questions go to the administrator, not to other residents or families.

Staff who are offered a gift, money, a loan, a bequest or a request for personal help from a resident tell the administrator the same day. Gifts of nominal value, such as handmade cards, may be accepted and are noted in the log kept by the administrator.
Staff never hold resident cash or valuables. If a resident asks for safekeeping, staff refer the request to the administrator, who follows TL-02.

Staff who see or suspect abuse, humiliation, intimidation, exploitation or a boundary violation stop it if it is safe to do so, make sure the resident is safe, and report right away to the administrator. If the administrator is involved, staff report to [LICENSEE / OWNER NAME] or directly to Community Care Licensing or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (CRISISline 1-800-231-4024). Mandated reporting follows SAF-01.

The administrator records reports on an incident form, investigates within 24 hours, separates the staff person from the resident while the matter is reviewed, and takes the actions required by SAF-01 and SAF-02.
Staff are told that no one will be retaliated against for reporting in good faith.
Staff do not take photographs or recordings of residents unless the resident or the resident's representative has given written consent, kept in the resident file.
The administrator directly supervises volunteers, tells them this policy before they begin, and does not count them in the staffing plan.
At least once a year, the administrator reviews this policy with all staff, documents attendance and records it in the training file (see TR-02).
The administrator imposes discipline for violations according to the severity and documents it in the personnel file.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and addresses any report involving the administrator.
Trains staff, supervises volunteers, investigates reports, enforces the policy and protects reporters from retaliation.
Treat residents with dignity, keep boundaries, never accept resident funds or valuables, and report violations immediately.
Follow this policy and work only under supervision.

Orientation and annual training sign-in sheets
Gift or offer log kept by the administrator
Incident reports and investigation notes

policies.title: New Employee Orientation and Initial Training
policies.applies_to: All new employees who provide direct care or supervise residents, including night staff, and all staff who assist with medications.
policies.purpose: To make sure every new employee is trained and competent before working alone with residents, and to describe how initial training is delivered, by whom, and how it is documented.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 item B6.0 — In-service training for staff: a plan for in-service training, submitted to Licensing at the time of application as part of the plan of operation. It also meets LIC 281 item B6.1 — New employee training: a description of the training, stating who will conduct it. [AGENCY NAME] submits this plan, together with TR-02, with the plan of operation.

1. Who trains. Initial training is conducted by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the administrator, and by qualified outside trainers or approved training vendors: [TRAINER NAMES / VENDORS]. Each trainer's qualifications are documented and filed in the personnel records (22 CCR §87411).

2. Direct care staff: 40 hours of initial training (HSC §1569.625). The first 20 hours must be completed before the employee works alone with residents and include 6 hours of dementia care and 4 hours covering postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice. The remaining 20 hours are completed within 4 weeks of hire and include 6 further hours of dementia care. Together this meets the 12 hours of initial dementia training required by HSC §1569.626.

3. Medication assistance (HSC §1569.69). Staff who assist with self-administered medications complete initial training and pass an exam. For a home of 15 or fewer residents, this is 10 hours: 6 hands-on hours before the employee assists with any medication, and 4 more hours within 2 weeks. For a home of 16 or more, it is 24 hours: 16 hands-on hours before assisting, and 8 more within 4 weeks. [AGENCY NAME]'s licensed capacity is [LICENSED CAPACITY].

4. First aid. Staff who assist with personal activities of daily living receive first aid training from a qualified provider. Night staff are first aid trained.

5. Bloodborne pathogens. All staff with exposure risk receive training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 at orientation.

6. Supervision. Until the first 20 hours are done, the new employee does not work alone and works only alongside a trained staff member. Training hours count only when documented.

definitions.definition: Employees who assist residents with personal activities of daily living.
Devices used to support a resident's body position. They are used only as allowed by regulation (see RD-02).
Health conditions that may be accepted or retained in an RCFE only under specific rules (see AD-06).
Practical, supervised instruction, including medication assistance practice.

procedures: On or before the first day, the administrator checks that the new employee's clearance and health screening are on file (see PP-04). If either is missing, the person does not start.

On day one, the administrator gives the new employee this policy, the job description, the facility's policies on resident rights, abuse reporting and emergency procedures, and a training record sheet.
The administrator schedules the first 20 hours of training before the employee works alone, and schedules the second 20 hours to be completed within 4 weeks of hire.

The first 20 hours include at least 6 hours of dementia care and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice. Training also covers resident personal rights, abuse reporting, emergency and fire procedures and the employee's job duties.
The administrator assigns a trained staff member to supervise the new employee and records the name of the supervising staff member on the training record sheet.
Within the 4 weeks, the new employee completes the second 20 hours, including 6 additional dementia hours, so that 12 hours of dementia training are completed (see PD-09).

Staff who will assist with medications complete the medication assistance training. In a home of 15 or fewer residents, the 6 hands-on hours must be finished before the employee assists with any medication and the other 4 hours within 2 weeks. The employee then passes the exam. The employee does not assist with medications until the 6 hands-on hours are complete (see PD-05).
The employee gets first aid training from a qualified provider. The administrator files the provider's certificate. Night staff are verified as first aid trained before they work a night shift.
The administrator gives bloodborne pathogen training at orientation (infection control, exposure incident procedures and hepatitis B vaccine offer) and records it.
The trainer signs the sign-in sheet for each session showing date, topic, hours, trainer name and qualifications; the employee signs it too.
Within 5 working days of each session, the administrator files the sign-in sheet, trainer qualifications, certificates and exam results in the employee's personnel file (see PP-04).

The administrator reviews the training record at the end of week 2 and week 4 and confirms in writing that all required hours are complete. If hours are short, the employee's schedule is limited to supervised work until completed.
The administrator evaluates competency before the employee works alone, by observing the employee perform personal care tasks and emergency procedures, and records the result.

responsibilities.duty: Funds training and approves the training plan submitted with the plan of operation.
Schedules and verifies training hours, assigns supervision, evaluates competency and keeps training records.
Deliver training on approved topics, hold the qualifications documented in the file, and sign the sign-in sheets.
Attend and complete all training, and do not work alone or assist with medications until the required hours are complete.

Training record sheet for each employee

policies.title: Ongoing In-Service Training, Administrator Continuing Education and Documentation
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, staff who assist with medications, and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To keep staff and the administrator current through regular training, to state the topics and frequency of that training, and to ensure it is documented for Licensing.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 item B6.2 — Ongoing training: the topics to be covered (including administrator continuing education units), how often training will be given, how it will be documented, and inclusion of the topics specified in regulation sections 80065 (General) and 87565 (Residential Care Facilities for the Elderly). The topic list in this policy is confirmed against the text of sections 80065 and 87565 by the administrator before the plan is submitted.

1. Direct care staff. Each direct care employee completes 20 hours of training every year (HSC §1569.625). At least 8 of those hours cover dementia care (HSC §1569.625 and §1569.626), and 4 cover postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice.

2. Medication assistance. Each staff member who assists with self-administered medications completes 8 hours of training every year (HSC §1569.69).

3. Administrator continuing education. The administrator completes 40 hours of continuing education every 2 years, including 8 hours on dementia (HSC §1569.616). The administrator's CE topics and hours are listed in the plan: [ADMINISTRATOR CE TOPICS AND VENDOR].

4. Topics. Annual topics include: resident personal rights; abuse and neglect recognition and reporting; dementia care and behavioral expression; postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice; assistance with self-administered medications; personal care and activities of daily living; infection control and bloodborne pathogens; fall prevention and skin integrity; nutrition and special diets; first aid and medical emergencies; and emergency, fire and disaster procedures.

5. Frequency. Training is scheduled at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly] so that each employee finishes the annual hours by the employee's hire anniversary date.

6. Documentation. For every session, [AGENCY NAME] keeps a sign-in sheet, the topic and hours, and the trainer's qualifications in the employee's personnel file (22 CCR §87411).

definitions.definition: Ongoing training given to employees after initial training.
Hours the administrator must complete to keep an RCFE administrator certificate.
The 12-month period starting on the employee's hire date.
The record of session date, topic, hours, attendees and trainer signature.

procedures: By December 1 each year, the administrator prepares an annual training calendar covering all required topics and hours for direct care staff and medication assistance staff, and shares it with staff.
The administrator tracks each employee's hours on an individual training log, by anniversary year, showing total hours, dementia hours, and postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice hours.
Training is delivered by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or by a qualified outside trainer or vendor. The administrator verifies the trainer's qualifications before the session and files them.
Each session starts with a sign-in sheet listing date, topic, hours, trainer and attendees. Attendees and the trainer sign it.
The administrator schedules each employee to finish 20 hours each anniversary year, including at least 8 hours of dementia care and 4 hours of postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice.
The administrator schedules the 8 hours of annual medication assistance training for each staff member who assists with medications and documents it on the training log.
Sessions are held at various times so that night and part-time staff can attend. Make-up sessions are held for anyone who misses one.
Within 5 working days after each session, the administrator files the sign-in sheet, trainer qualifications and any certificate in each attendee's personnel file.

At 90 days before an employee's anniversary date, the administrator checks hours and arranges the remaining training. An employee who is short on hours at the anniversary date is placed on a written plan, with a completion date within 30 days.

The administrator tracks the 2-year CE cycle for the administrator's certificate, schedules 40 hours of CE including 8 hours on dementia with an approved vendor, and files the CE certificates in the administrator's file and in the administrative file.
The administrator confirms the administrator's certificate renewal with the CDSS Administrator Certification Bureau, 916-653-9300, before the renewal date.
Quarterly, as part of the mock inspection of personnel files (see PP-04), the administrator checks that training logs are current.
The administrator reviews the training plan once a year with the licensee, updates topics based on resident needs, incident reports and regulation changes, and records the review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves and funds the annual training plan and reviews it yearly.
Schedules training, verifies trainers, tracks hours, completes the administrator's own CE, and keeps records.
Attend training and complete annual hours by the anniversary date.
Provide qualified instruction and sign sign-in sheets.

policies.title: Program Description, Philosophy and Hours of Operation
policies.applies_to: The licensee, administrator, all staff, residents, families and prospective residents.
policies.purpose: To give residents, families and Licensing a clear overview of [AGENCY NAME]'s philosophy, services, activities and hours of operation, consistent with the plan of operation.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.0 — RCFE Program Description (a general overview of program philosophies, services provided and activities in the facility). It meets LIC 281 item B7.1 — Brief statement of the purpose, goals and program methods (program philosophy). It meets LIC 281 item B7.2 — Days and hours of operation. This text also appears in the admission policies (AD-01).

1. Overview. [AGENCY NAME], located at [ADDRESS], is a Residential Care Facility for the Elderly licensed by the California Department of Social Services, Community Care Licensing Division, with a licensed capacity of [LICENSED CAPACITY]. The facility provides room, board, supervision, assistance with activities of daily living, assistance with self-administered medications, and social activities for older adults who need this level of care (see PD-02 and PD-03).

2. Purpose and goals (B7.1). The purpose of [AGENCY NAME] is to provide a safe, dignified, home-like place for older adults. Goals: (a) protect each resident's personal rights, dignity and privacy; (b) provide care and supervision that match each resident's needs and services plan; (c) promote independence and choice; (d) offer meaningful activity and social connection; (e) keep residents safe and respond quickly to changes in condition; and (f) work with families, physicians, hospice and home health agencies and the Ombudsman.

3. Program methods (B7.1). Goals are met through: pre-admission appraisal and a written needs and services plan with reappraisal (AD-02, AD-04); trained staff supervised by the administrator (TR-01, TR-02); person-centered care that respects choice and preferred name and pronouns; assistance with self-administered medications (PD-05); planned activities (PD-03); a nutritious menu (FD-01); and prompt incident, complaint and grievance response (PD-08, RR-01).

4. Days and hours of operation (B7.2). [AGENCY NAME] operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, every day of the year. Staff are on duty at all times as set out in PP-01.

5. Consistency. This program description is consistent with the plan of operation (22 CCR §87208). If a brochure is used instead, it must contain every element B7.1 through B7.11 of the LIC 281 form. Any change to the program is reviewed by the licensee and, where required, reported to Licensing before it is made.

definitions.definition: The overview of philosophy, services and activities required as part of the plan of operation.
The written plan required by 22 CCR §87208 describing how the facility will operate.
The facility's stated purpose, goals and methods.
The facility is open and staffed with care and supervision every day and night of the year.

procedures: The licensee and administrator write the program description using this policy and keep it in the plan of operation binder.

Before the license application is submitted, the administrator reads the program description against the other plan of operation sections (admission policies, staffing and training plan, transportation and others) to check that the philosophy, services, activities and hours match.

If a brochure is used in place of this text, the administrator checks it against every element B7.1 through B7.11 on LIC 281 and records the check on a signed checklist. Any missing element is added before the brochure is used.
The administrator gives a copy of the program description to each prospective resident and family at the first inquiry or tour.
At admission, the administrator reviews the program description and hours with the resident or representative and records that it was provided on the admission checklist (see AD-07).
The administrator posts the hours of operation and the license in the manner required by GOV-02, and uses them in any advertising.
The administrator trains staff on the program philosophy during orientation (TR-01) so they can explain it.
The licensee confirms 24-hour coverage by checking the staffing schedule each month against PP-01.
The administrator reviews the program description annually and whenever services, activities or the population served change, updates it, notes the revision date and distributes it to staff.
When a change would alter the plan of operation, the administrator informs the licensee and contacts Community Care Licensing before the change takes effect.
The administrator keeps prior versions of the program description in the document control file for [RETENTION PERIOD] (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the philosophy, goals and program methods, and ensures the program matches the plan of operation.
Maintains the program description, gives it to prospective residents, trains staff and reviews it annually.
Understand and carry out the program philosophy in daily care.

documentation: Program description in the plan of operation
Brochure checklist (B7.1 through B7.11), if a brochure is used
Record that the program description was provided to resident or representative
Annual review record and revision dates
Staffing schedules showing 24-hour coverage

policies.title: Basic and Optional Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, direct care staff, billing staff
policies.purpose: To state clearly which services every resident receives as part of the basic rate, which services are optional and priced separately, and how rates and services are put in writing and changed, so residents, families and licensing staff can see what [AGENCY NAME] provides.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.5 — Description of the basic services provided by the facility, and LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.6 — Description of the optional services provided in the facility, as listed in the admission agreement. Both descriptions also appear in the Admission Policies section of this manual (AD-07).

BASIC SERVICES (item B7.5). [AGENCY NAME] provides the following basic services to every resident for the basic monthly rate. The list follows the basic services listed in Admission Guideline LIC 604/604A and is repeated word for word in each resident's admission agreement:
1. Safe, healthful and sanitary living accommodations, including a furnished or resident-furnished room, utilities, and housekeeping of common areas and the resident's room.
2. Meals and snacks: three nutritious meals a day plus snacks, including modified or therapeutic diets ordered by a physician (FD-01).
3. Personal care and supervision: help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, eating, walking, transferring and other activities of daily living, and observation of the resident's general well-being.
4. Assistance with self-administered medications by trained staff (PD-05).
5. Planned activities and social programming (PD-03).
6. Arranging for medical and dental appointments and for transportation to them (PD-06).
7. A plan for incidental medical care, including first aid, calling 9-1-1 or the physician, and coordinating with home health and hospice (PD-04, PD-07).
8. Linen and towel service and laundry service as stated in the admission agreement.
9. Emergency and disaster preparedness, and 24-hour staff supervision as described in PP-01.

Before this manual is finalized and each time LIC 604/604A is revised, the Administrator compares this list line by line with the current LIC 604/604A and with the admission agreement form. Any difference is corrected before the document is issued.

OPTIONAL SERVICES (item B7.6). Optional services are services a resident or the resident's representative chooses and that cost more than the basic rate. They are listed in the admission agreement exactly as follows, each with its rate, and the policy and the agreement must always match:
- [OPTIONAL SERVICE 1 — e.g., incontinence supplies or extra laundry] — [RATE AND BILLING UNIT]
- [OPTIONAL SERVICE 2 — e.g., escort to appointments] — [RATE AND BILLING UNIT]
- [OPTIONAL SERVICE 3 — e.g., additional personal care hours] — [RATE AND BILLING UNIT]
- [OPTIONAL SERVICE 4 — e.g., guest meals] — [RATE AND BILLING UNIT]
A service not listed in the admission agreement is not charged. No optional service may be a condition of admission or of retaining basic services.

RATES AND NOTICE. Under 22 CCR §87507, the admission agreement is a written, plain-language document in at least 12-point type. It must specify basic services, additional (optional) services, rates and payment terms. Any increase in the basic rate or in the cost of optional services requires at least 60 days' written notice to the resident and the resident's representative before it takes effect. The agreement contains no waiver of the facility's liability.

definitions.definition: The services included in the basic monthly rate for every resident, as listed in Admission Guideline LIC 604/604A and the admission agreement.
Services beyond the basic services that a resident elects, listed in the admission agreement with a stated rate.
The individual written contract signed by the resident or the resident's representative and the facility under 22 CCR §87507.
The person legally authorized to act for a resident or designated by the resident as the person responsible for the resident.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the current Admission Guideline LIC 604/604A on file and, at least annually and whenever it is revised, compares the basic services list in this policy and in the admission agreement against it. The review is dated and initialed.
The Administrator maintains one master list of optional services with rates. Only that master list is used to prepare admission agreements, rate sheets and the Program Description.
During the pre-admission visit, the Administrator or designee reviews the basic services list and the optional services list with the prospective resident and representative and answers questions.
The Administrator or designee gives the prospective resident the written list of basic and optional services and rates before the admission agreement is signed.
The admission agreement is prepared in at least 12-point type, in plain language, with titled sections, listing basic services, additional services, rates and payment terms (see AD-07).
The resident or representative and the Administrator sign and date the agreement no later than 7 days after admission. A copy is given to the resident immediately.

When the Needs and Services Plan shows the resident needs an optional service, the Administrator or designee explains the service and its rate. The resident or representative must accept the service in writing before it is provided or billed.
Direct care staff provide only the services in the resident's agreement and Needs and Services Plan. Staff do not offer or sell optional services directly or accept payment for them.

The Administrator reviews each resident's list of optional services at each reappraisal (AD-04) and when the resident's condition changes. Services that are no longer needed are removed and billing stops from the date of change.
Before any increase in a basic or optional rate, the Administrator prepares a written notice stating the old rate, the new rate and the effective date, which is at least 60 days after delivery.
The notice is hand-delivered or mailed to the resident and representative. The date and method of delivery are recorded in the resident's file, and a signed acknowledgement is requested.
If a resident disputes a charge or says a service was not provided, the Administrator reviews it within 5 business days. Disputes go through the grievance process in RR-01.
If a resident's needs exceed the basic and optional services the facility can provide, the Administrator follows AD-06 and AD-08, including notice rights.
The billing clerk checks monthly invoices against the signed admission agreement. The Administrator reviews discrepancies and corrects them within one billing cycle.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the master lists of basic and optional services and rates, checks them against LIC 604/604A, signs agreements, and issues 60-day rate notices.
Explains services and rates to prospective residents and provides written lists before signing.
Provide basic and agreed optional services per the Needs and Services Plan and report changes in need.
Bill only services listed in the signed agreement and reconcile invoices monthly.

documentation: Signed and dated admission agreement with the basic and optional services lists
Master list of basic and optional services with rates and review dates
Annual comparison to LIC 604/604A, dated and initialed
Written optional service elections and cancellations
60-day rate change notices and delivery record
Billing records and dispute log

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents of [AGENCY NAME], a Residential Care Facility for the Elderly licensed by CDSS Community Care Licensing, including residents in dementia/memory care. Applies to the Administrator, Activity Coordinator, direct care staff and volunteers.
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has daily opportunities for social, educational, recreational and spiritual activity that match their interests, abilities and Needs and Services Plan. This policy also sets out who plans, conducts and assists with activities, and it contains the daily schedule and the one-month activity calendar required for the license application.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] provides a planned activity program every day of the week. Activities are voluntary. Residents are invited, encouraged and helped to take part, and no resident is required to attend. Activities are planned around resident interests, cultural and language background, abilities and the preferences recorded in the pre-admission appraisal and the Needs and Services Plan. Activities are adapted for residents with cognitive impairment, hearing or vision loss, limited mobility or limited English proficiency.

This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.3 — Daily schedule of activities to be provided by the facility, stating who plans, conducts and assists clients in participating. It also meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.4 — A one-month schedule of planned social, educational and recreational activities, stating who plans, conducts and assists clients in participating. The daily schedule and the monthly calendar follow.

ITEM B7.3 — DAILY SCHEDULE OF ACTIVITIES (Monday through Sunday; times may shift for resident needs, weather or outings)
Roles: PLANS = Activity Coordinator [ACTIVITY COORDINATOR NAME] with Administrator approval. CONDUCTS = person named. ASSISTS = direct care staff on duty (help with mobility, hearing aids, glasses, toileting, seating and encouragement).
• 7:00–9:00 AM — Personal care, wake-up routine and breakfast (see FD-01). Gentle morning conversation and reading of the daily calendar and news. Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: caregiver on shift. Assists: caregivers.
• 9:30–10:15 AM — Seated exercise, stretching and balance (chair-based). Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: Activity Coordinator or trained caregiver. Assists: caregivers, who stand by for safety and encourage participation.
• 10:30–11:30 AM — Educational or cognitive activity (current events, trivia, word games, reminiscence, memory activities, gardening, crafts). Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: Activity Coordinator. Assists: caregivers.
• 11:30 AM–1:00 PM — Lunch and social dining (see FD-01). Caregivers sit with and assist residents who need help eating.
• 1:00–2:00 PM — Quiet time, rest, phone and video calls with family, or individual activities such as reading, puzzles, letters and music with headphones. Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: resident-directed. Assists: caregivers.
• 2:00–3:30 PM — Group social or recreational activity (music, games, movies, crafts, cooking, birthday celebrations, entertainers, volunteers or faith-based visitors). Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: Activity Coordinator, volunteer or outside presenter, supervised by staff. Assists: caregivers.
• 3:30–4:30 PM — Outdoor time, walking group or patio and garden activity, weather permitting. Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: caregiver on shift. Assists: caregivers.
• 5:00–6:30 PM — Dinner and social dining. Assists: caregivers.
• 6:30–8:00 PM — Evening activity (music, movie night, cards, bingo, family visiting, sing-along, spiritual or devotional time by resident choice). Plans: Activity Coordinator. Conducts: evening caregiver. Assists: caregivers.
• 8:00 PM onward — Evening routine, calming music or television, personal care and bedtime. Residents with sleep disturbance or sundowning receive one-to-one calming activity from the awake caregiver.
Weekend schedule: The same format applies. The Activity Coordinator leaves a written plan and supplies, and the caregiver on duty conducts the activities. Sunday morning offers a faith or reflection option based on resident preference.

ITEM B7.4 — ONE-MONTH SCHEDULE OF PLANNED SOCIAL, EDUCATIONAL AND RECREATIONAL ACTIVITIES (sample 4-week cycle, repeated and updated monthly)
The Activity Coordinator plans the month. Unless another person is named, the Activity Coordinator conducts and caregivers on duty assist.
WEEK 1
• Mon — Social: Morning coffee and conversation circle. Educational: Current events discussion.
• Tue — Recreational: Chair exercise; Bingo (Activity Coordinator conducts; caregivers assist with cards and hearing).
• Wed — Educational: Trivia and memory games. Social: Music hour with sing-along.
• Thu — Recreational: Gardening or plant care on the patio. Social: Hand massage and nail care (caregiver conducts).
• Fri — Social: Movie afternoon with popcorn. Spiritual: Resident-led reflection or devotional time.
• Sat — Recreational: Card and board games (caregiver conducts).
• Sun — Social: Family visiting hour and tea; faith service by visiting clergy or volunteer, by resident choice.
WEEK 2
• Mon — Educational: Reminiscence group on a theme such as hometowns or work.
• Tue — Recreational: Balloon volleyball and seated exercise.
• Wed — Social: Birthday celebration for the month's birthdays (Administrator and Activity Coordinator conduct).
• Thu — Educational: Guest speaker or health talk by outside presenter, arranged by the Activity Coordinator.
• Fri — Recreational: Arts and crafts (painting, card making).
• Sat — Social: Music appreciation with residents' favorite songs (caregiver conducts).
• Sun — Social: Family visiting hour; video calls for out-of-area family.
WEEK 3
• Mon — Educational: Word games and crossword group.
• Tue — Recreational: Walking group and outdoor time, weather permitting.
• Wed — Social: Baking or cooking activity with simple tasting, within resident diets (see FD-01).
• Thu — Recreational: Group exercise and balance.
• Fri — Social: Entertainer or volunteer musician, arranged by the Activity Coordinator.
• Sat — Recreational: Movie or documentary afternoon (caregiver conducts).
• Sun — Spiritual: Faith service or quiet reflection by resident choice.
WEEK 4
• Mon — Educational: Reading aloud and book discussion.
• Tue — Recreational: Bingo and card games.
• Wed — Social: Seasonal or holiday craft and decorating.
• Thu — Educational: Memory activities and sensory stimulation (see PD-09).
• Fri — Social: Resident meeting. Residents give feedback on meals, activities and the next month's calendar (Administrator and Activity Coordinator conduct).
• Sat — Recreational: Outdoor patio time, music and refreshments (caregiver conducts).
• Sun — Social: Family visiting hour and ice cream social.
Additional monthly items: one community outing or off-site event when resident health, staffing and transportation allow (see PD-06), and at least one intergenerational or community visitor program.

ADAPTATIONS FOR RESIDENTS WITH DEMENTIA
Residents with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia receive activities matched to their cognitive level and remaining abilities. These include short sessions of 15 to 30 minutes, simple one- or two-step tasks, music and familiar songs, sorting and folding tasks, picture books, sensory stimulation, reminiscence, walking with staff and structured one-to-one engagement. Staff watch for fatigue, agitation and sundowning, and redirect with calm, non-confrontational approaches. Activities for these residents are further described in PD-09.

The Administrator reviews the activity program at least quarterly and whenever resident needs change. Residents may suggest activities at any time and at resident meetings.

definitions.definition: The staff member designated by the Administrator to plan, schedule and lead resident activities. In a small facility this may be the Administrator or a trained caregiver.
A scheduled social, educational, recreational, spiritual or physical activity offered to residents on a regular basis and posted on the calendar.
The written plan for each resident that records their needs, preferences and services, including activity interests (see AD-04).
To provide hands-on or verbal help so a resident can take part, such as transport to the activity area, positioning, hearing or vision aids, prompting and supervision.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator or designee records each resident's life history, interests, hobbies, faith or cultural preferences, preferred language and past routines during the pre-admission appraisal, and the information is carried into the Needs and Services Plan (see AD-02 and AD-04).

The Activity Coordinator ([ACTIVITY COORDINATOR NAME]) writes the next month's calendar by the 20th of the preceding month. The calendar covers social, educational, recreational and, by preference, spiritual activities, and names who plans, conducts and assists for each.
The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) reviews and approves the calendar before it is posted and confirms that staffing and supplies are in place for each activity.

The calendar is posted by the 25th of the preceding month in the common area and at the dining area at a readable height and in large print. Copies are given to residents, and to family or representatives on request, in the resident's preferred language where possible.
The daily schedule is posted each day. Staff verbally remind residents of the day's activities each morning and personally invite each resident, including residents who stay in their rooms.
The Activity Coordinator or the caregiver on duty prepares the room, supplies and any equipment 15 minutes before each activity, and removes tripping hazards and checks seating and lighting.
Direct care staff assist residents to the activity area, position them safely, ensure hearing aids, glasses and walkers are available, and meet toileting needs before the activity begins.
Staff offer choices, never force participation, and respect a resident's right to decline. A resident who declines is offered an alternative in-room activity or one-to-one visit.

For residents who are bedbound, have limited mobility or prefer to stay in their rooms, a caregiver provides one-to-one activity (conversation, music, reading, hand care) at least three times per week and records it.

For residents with dementia, staff apply the adaptations in this policy and in PD-09: short sessions, simple tasks, a calm setting, redirection and one-to-one engagement. Staff keep an eye on residents who are at risk of wandering (see SAF-03).

Activities involving outings, outside entertainers, volunteers or pets follow related policies on transportation (PD-06), visitors and pets (SAF-05) and infection control (SAF-04). Volunteers are never left alone with residents unless they have met the screening requirements of PP-03.
The caregiver conducting an activity records attendance and level of participation on the daily activity log before the end of the shift.

The Activity Coordinator reviews the logs weekly and notes residents who are withdrawn, show a marked drop in participation or show behavioral changes. These are reported to the Administrator, and the Needs and Services Plan is reassessed if needed (see AD-04).
The Administrator holds a resident meeting at least monthly to gather feedback and suggestions for the next calendar. Suggestions are recorded and considered in planning.
Staff who conduct activities complete orientation and in-service training in activity programming and dementia engagement (see TR-01 and TR-02).

The Administrator reviews the activity program, logs and resident feedback at least quarterly and updates this policy and the schedules as needed (see GOV-03). Calendars are kept as a record for at least the current and prior 12 months.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the monthly calendar, ensures staffing and supplies, ensures activities are available daily and reviews the program quarterly.
Plans the daily schedule and monthly calendar, conducts or arranges activities, trains staff on engagement techniques, keeps activity logs and reports observed changes.
Conduct activities when assigned and assist residents to take part, including mobility, sensory aids, toileting and safety supervision, and record participation.
May choose, decline or suggest activities and give feedback at resident meetings.
Follow facility rules and screening requirements and work under the direction of staff.

documentation: Posted daily schedule of activities (B7.3)
Monthly activity calendar naming who plans, conducts and assists (B7.4)
Daily activity attendance and participation log
One-to-one activity notes for residents who stay in their rooms
Resident interest and activity preference information in the pre-admission appraisal and Needs and Services Plan
Resident meeting notes and suggestions
Quarterly program review notes by the Administrator

policies.title: Medical Emergencies, Change of Condition and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All staff
policies.purpose: To make sure a resident who becomes ill or injured receives immediate and appropriate help, that the physician, family and required agencies are notified on time, and that hospital transfers are orderly and documented.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.7 — Description of how the facility will handle medical emergencies if a client becomes ill or injured.

Under 22 CCR §87465, [AGENCY NAME] keeps a plan for incidental medical care. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to a resident's health. The only exception is where a resident's advance directive or resuscitative request calls for a different response, handled per HC-04. A stocked first aid kit is kept at [FIRST AID KIT LOCATION]. Emergency numbers, including the physician, ambulance, poison control, fire and police, are posted at [POSTING LOCATION]. The ambulance number is kept near each phone. Staff may perform first aid and CPR within their training and certification, but do not act beyond their scope.

When a resident's condition changes, staff promptly notify the Administrator, the resident's physician and the person responsible for the resident.

Under 22 CCR §87211, the facility reports to the licensing agency as follows: (1) a written report to licensing and the person responsible within 7 days of any death, any serious injury as determined by a physician, any use of an AED, or any incident threatening the welfare, safety or health of a resident, including unexplained absence; (2) outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported within 24 hours by phone or fax to licensing and the local health officer; (3) fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to licensing; and (4) suspected abuse is reported per SAF-01, including within 2 hours to the local ombudsman, licensing and law enforcement when it involves serious bodily injury, otherwise within 24 hours.

definitions.definition: A sudden illness or injury posing an imminent threat to a resident's life, health or safety, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe bleeding, choking, or a serious fall.
A noticeable change in a resident's physical, mental or functional status that differs from the resident's usual baseline.
The family member, representative, agency or other person identified in the resident's records as responsible for the resident.
Automated external defibrillator.

procedures: The Administrator ensures a first aid kit is stocked and checked monthly. The check is logged with date and initials, and used items are replaced right away.

The Administrator posts emergency numbers (9-1-1, ambulance, poison control, local fire, police, licensing office, ombudsman, Administrator [PHONE]) near the telephone and in staff areas, and verifies them every quarter.

Each resident's emergency information, medication list, physician, hospital preference, advance directive or resuscitative request, and responsible person contacts are kept in an easily accessed file (AD-05, HC-04).
The staff member who finds a resident in distress stays with the resident, gets help, and starts first aid or CPR if trained and consistent with the resident's advance directive.

If there is an imminent threat to health, the staff member (or another caregiver) calls 9-1-1 right away and states the address [ADDRESS], the resident's condition and the entrance to use. Staff check the resident's advance directive or resuscitative request as described in HC-04 without delaying emergency care.
Staff follow dispatcher instructions, keep the resident comfortable and safe, send a second staff member to meet and guide emergency responders, and keep other residents calm and supervised.
Staff gather the face sheet, medication list, advance directive or resuscitative request and recent vital sign notes to send with the resident to the hospital.

A staff member notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's physician and the person responsible as soon as the emergency is under control, and no later than the same day.

If the resident goes to the hospital, a staff member accompanies the resident or follows when staffing permits, without leaving the remaining residents unsupervised, and ensures medications, aids, glasses and dentures are sent as appropriate.

For a non-emergency change of condition (new confusion, decreased appetite, a new skin problem, a fall without apparent injury, new pain), the caregiver informs the Administrator and records the observation the same shift. The Administrator contacts the physician and the person responsible the same day.
Staff follow physician instructions, which are recorded in the resident's record, and step up observation as ordered.
The Administrator reviews the resident's Needs and Services Plan after any significant change or hospital return, and re-appraises as needed (AD-04, AD-06).

For a death, any serious injury as determined by a physician, AED use, or any incident threatening welfare, safety or health, the Administrator sends a written report to licensing and the person responsible within 7 days using the licensing agency's incident report form, and keeps a copy (SAF-02, REC-02).

For an outbreak, poisoning, catastrophe or major accident, the Administrator reports by phone or fax within 24 hours to licensing and to the local health officer at [COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT PHONE], and records the time, person contacted and what was said.
For a fire or explosion, staff call 9-1-1 and the Administrator reports immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to licensing (EDP-02).
For suspected abuse, staff follow SAF-01 and the time limits above.
After the event, the Administrator holds a debrief with staff within 3 days, identifies any preventive steps and records the follow-up.

responsibilities.duty: Respond immediately to emergencies, call 9-1-1 for imminent threats, report changes of condition the same shift.
Maintains the first aid kit and posted numbers, makes notifications and state reports, and reviews every emergency.
Sends emergency information with the resident and meets emergency responders.
Provides orders for the resident's care after a change of condition.

documentation: Incident report and emergency response notes
Resident's record entries for change of condition and physician orders
Record of calls made (9-1-1, physician, person responsible, licensing, health officer), with date and time
7-day written reports to licensing and person responsible
First aid kit check log
Posted emergency number verification log

policies.title: Assistance with Self-Administered Medications
policies.applies_to: Direct care staff authorized to assist with medications, Administrator
policies.purpose: To define how trained staff assist residents who take their own medications, to keep staff within the legal limits of assistance, and to protect residents from medication errors.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.8 — Procedure for handling and assisting clients/residents with self-administered medications.

Under 22 CCR §87465, staff of [AGENCY NAME] may only assist residents with the self-administration of their medications. Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law. Staff never force, hide or camouflage medications (for example, in food or drink without the resident's knowledge). A resident has the right to refuse a medication.

Only staff who have completed the required medication assistance training and exam under HSC §1569.69 may assist. For a facility of 15 or fewer residents, that is 10 hours of initial training (6 hours hands-on before assisting any resident and 4 more hours within 2 weeks) plus an exam, then 8 hours annually. For a facility of 16 or more residents, it is 24 hours of initial training (16 hours hands-on before assisting and 8 more within 4 weeks) plus an exam, then 8 hours annually. [AGENCY NAME]'s licensed capacity is [LICENSED CAPACITY], and the Administrator applies the matching requirement.

PRN (as-needed) medications may be assisted only with a signed, dated physician's order on a prescription blank stating the symptoms for use, the exact dose, the minimum hours between doses and the maximum number of doses in 24 hours. Medications are stored centrally in a locked place in the original containers, with a record kept for at least 1 year. Unused or discontinued medications are destroyed by the Administrator and one other non-resident adult, with a record kept for at least 3 years. Details are in HC-01.

definitions.definition: Helping a resident take medication that the resident is able to take, such as reminding, opening containers, steadying a hand, reading the label and observing that the resident takes it.
A medication ordered to be taken as needed, rather than on a fixed schedule.
Hiding medication in food, drink or other items without the resident's knowledge.
Any wrong resident, drug, dose, time, route or omission, or assistance not matching the label or order.

procedures: Before assisting any resident, a staff member must complete the hands-on training required for the facility's size (6 hours if 15 or fewer residents; 16 hours if 16 or more), as documented by the Administrator.

The staff member completes the remaining initial hours (4 hours within 2 weeks for 15 or fewer; 8 hours within 4 weeks for 16 or more) and passes the exam. The Administrator files the certificate and exam record in the personnel file.
Each year the Administrator verifies that each assisting staff member completes 8 hours of medication training and records the date and subject (TR-02).
The Administrator keeps a current list of staff authorized to assist with medications. No one else may assist.

Before accepting any medication, staff check that the original container is labeled with the resident's name, drug, dose, directions, prescriber and date. Staff report any missing or unclear label to the Administrator, who contacts the pharmacy or physician before assistance.
The Administrator or designee records each resident's medications on the medication record from the label or physician order, and updates it with every change of order.
At each scheduled time, staff wash hands, check the resident's identity, the label and the medication record, and confirm the right resident, drug, dose, time and route.

Staff bring the medication to the resident, remind and help the resident take it (open containers, hand the pill, steady a cup) and stay until it is taken. Staff do not hide, crush into food, or force a medication.
Staff immediately initial the medication record after the resident takes the medication. They do not pre-charting.

If a resident refuses, staff do not force or trick the resident. They respect the refusal, document it, and notify the Administrator. The Administrator notifies the physician and the person responsible when refusals continue or the medication is important.

For PRN medications, staff give assistance only if the resident's physician order is signed and dated on a prescription blank and states the symptoms, exact dose, minimum hours between doses and the maximum doses in 24 hours. Staff record the time, symptom, dose and effect on the medication record each time.
Staff do not give injections. A resident who self-injects or who is injected by a licensed professional or other person authorized by law follows HC-02, and staff do not take part.
Staff never share one resident's medication with another, and never keep a resident's medication after discontinuation, except per HC-01.

A staff member who makes or finds a medication error calls the physician or pharmacist for direction, notifies the Administrator immediately, observes the resident and records an incident report the same shift (SAF-02).
Medications are stored in a locked central place in original containers, as in HC-01. Records of medications are kept for at least 1 year, and destruction records for at least 3 years.
The Administrator, with another non-resident adult, destroys discontinued, expired or left-over medications and both sign the destruction record.
The Administrator reviews medication records at least monthly for missed doses, gaps and PRN use, and acts on any concern.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies training, keeps the authorized staff list, reviews medication records and conducts destruction with a second adult.
Assist with self-administered medications per the label and order, and document each assistance and refusal.
Provide written orders, including complete PRN orders, and clarify questions.
Advises on medication concerns per HC-02.

documentation: Medication records for each resident
Physician orders, including signed and dated PRN orders on prescription blanks
Training certificates and exam results for each authorized staff member, and annual 8-hour training records
Refusal notes and physician notifications
Medication error and incident reports
Medication destruction records (3 years)
Medication storage and disposition records (1 year)

policies.title: Transportation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, drivers, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To describe how residents are transported safely to medical appointments and outings, who provides the transport, and how drivers, vehicles and insurance are verified.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.9 — Transportation arrangements.

The Plan of Operation required by 22 CCR §87208 includes a description of transportation. [AGENCY NAME] arranges transportation for residents to medical and dental appointments and facility outings as part of its services (PD-02). Transportation is provided in one of these ways:
1. Facility vehicle driven by an authorized employee: [FACILITY VEHICLE DESCRIPTION, if any].
2. Contracted accessible transport or non-emergency medical transport provider: [TRANSPORT CONTRACTOR NAME AND PHONE].
3. Family or the resident's representative, by their own arrangement.
4. Public paratransit or a transport benefit through the resident's health plan, where the resident is eligible.
Wheelchair-accessible transport that meets ADA accessibility requirements is available for residents who use wheelchairs or mobility devices. Any person who transports residents must hold a valid driver's license of the correct class and carry current auto insurance, verified by the Administrator before first use and renewed on expiration. Transportation is included in the emergency disaster plan (EDP-01). Ambulances are used for emergencies and not for routine transport.

definitions.definition: A vehicle owned or leased by [AGENCY NAME] and used to transport residents.
An employee approved by the Administrator who holds a valid license and has met the driver requirements of this policy.
Transport using a vehicle with a lift or ramp and wheelchair securement that meets ADA accessibility requirements.

procedures: The Administrator decides which transport methods the facility uses and lists them in the Plan of Operation and the admission agreement.
At admission, the Administrator or designee asks about the resident's mobility, equipment, appointment needs and who normally provides transport, and records it in the Needs and Services Plan.

Before any employee drives residents, the Administrator checks a copy of the employee's valid driver's license and a driving record check, and confirms the employee is covered under the facility's auto insurance (INS-01). Copies are kept in the personnel file.
For any contractor, the Administrator obtains a written agreement and proof of current commercial auto liability insurance and licenses, and files them before first use.

For family or volunteers who transport a resident on the facility's behalf, the Administrator verifies license and personal auto insurance. Transport by a resident's own family for the family's own purposes is the family's responsibility.

Staff schedule appointments at least [NUMBER] business days ahead where possible, record the date, time, address, purpose and transport method on the appointment calendar, and tell the resident and the responsible person.

The day before the appointment, the Administrator or designee confirms transport, a staff escort or family member if needed, and gathers the resident's medication list, insurance cards, face sheet and advance directive or resuscitative request.
Before departure, staff check that the resident is dressed for the weather, has glasses, hearing aids, mobility devices, a toileting opportunity, and any needed water or snack.
Staff sign the resident out and in on the sign-out log (AD-05), noting the time, destination and expected return.
Drivers use seat belts for all passengers, secure wheelchairs with the vehicle's securement system, use the lift or ramp properly, and do not drive while using a phone or when impaired.
The number of staff on the vehicle and the number left at the facility must meet staffing needs, so residents left behind are still supervised (PP-01).
Staff stay with residents with dementia or high risk for the entire trip and prevent elopement (SAF-03, PD-09).
If a resident becomes ill or injured during transport, staff call 9-1-1 and follow PD-04.
If there is an accident, staff call 9-1-1, assist residents, notify the Administrator immediately, and the Administrator makes licensing reports as required (SAF-02, REC-02).
The Administrator inspects the facility vehicle, if any, at least monthly (tires, lights, brakes, lift, seat belts, first aid kit), and keeps maintenance and inspection records.
The Administrator reviews driver licenses and insurance annually and when they expire, and removes any driver whose license or coverage lapses.
The Emergency Disaster Plan lists the transport resources for evacuation and relocation and their phone numbers (EDP-01).

responsibilities.duty: Selects transport methods, verifies licenses and insurance, and maintains vehicle records.
Drive safely, follow securement and seat belt rules, and report incidents immediately.
Prepare residents, sign them out and in, and escort when required.
Provide accessible vehicles, licensed drivers and proof of insurance.

documentation: Driver license, driving record and insurance verification for each driver
Contractor agreements and certificates of insurance
Appointment calendar and transport log
Resident sign-out and sign-in log
Vehicle inspection and maintenance records
Incident reports for transport events

policies.title: Community Resources, Consultants, Hospice and Home Health
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, nursing consultants
federal: 42 CFR §441.301(c) (HCBS Settings Rule, only if the facility enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver)
policies.purpose: To identify the community resources and consultants [AGENCY NAME] uses to meet residents' needs, and to set rules for working with hospice and home health agencies, including the hospice care waiver.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 (9/04) p.16, item B7.10 — Description of community resources and consultants to be used by the facility.

COMMUNITY RESOURCES AND CONSULTANTS. [AGENCY NAME] uses the following, and the Administrator keeps current names and phone numbers in the Resource Directory:
- Physicians and nurse practitioners: the resident's own physician, plus [ON-CALL OR VISITING PHYSICIAN].
- Pharmacy: [PHARMACY NAME AND PHONE].
- Home health agency: [HOME HEALTH AGENCY NAME AND PHONE].
- Hospice agency: [HOSPICE AGENCY NAME AND PHONE].
- Dietitian or nutrition consultant: [NAME AND PHONE], as needed for therapeutic diets.
- Licensed nurse consultant: [NAME AND PHONE].
- Dentist, podiatrist, optometrist, audiologist, therapists: [NAMES AND PHONES].
- Local Long-Term Care Ombudsman program: [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE]; state CRISISline 1-800-231-4024.
- County Adult Protective Services: [COUNTY APS PHONE].
- CDSS Community Care Licensing, Adult and Senior Care Program: (916) 657-2592 and the regional office at [REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE].
- Local fire authority and county health department: [PHONES].
- Faith, volunteer and senior service organizations: [LIST].

HOSPICE. Hospice care in the facility is provided by a licensed hospice agency chosen by the resident. Where a resident's hospice needs call for a hospice care waiver under 22 CCR §87632, [AGENCY NAME] will submit a written request to CDSS stating the maximum number of hospice residents it will care for. CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request. The facility will not exceed the maximum number stated and approved. The facility coordinates the hospice plan of care with the Needs and Services Plan in writing.

HOME HEALTH. Home health services are provided by a licensed agency on the resident's physician's order, coordinated in writing with the facility.

ASSISTED LIVING WAIVER. This paragraph applies only if [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver through DHCS. In that case the facility lists its care coordination agencies and the licensed nurse resource for ALW residents (HC-02, GOV-04) and meets the HCBS Settings Rule (42 CFR §441.301(c)): residents have a lease or agreement, privacy, choice, and access to food and visitors.

definitions.definition: A professional outside the facility's staff who provides advice or services, such as a nurse, dietitian or pharmacist.
A licensed program that provides comfort-focused care for people with a terminal illness.
CDSS approval, requested in writing under 22 CCR §87632, for the facility to care for a stated maximum number of hospice residents.
An agency that coordinates services for residents enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver.

procedures: The Administrator develops the Resource Directory listing each community resource and consultant in this policy, with name, address, phone, services and the date last verified. A copy is kept in the office and at the staff desk.
The Administrator verifies and updates the directory at least every 6 months and whenever a provider changes.

Before relying on a home health agency, hospice, pharmacy or consultant, the Administrator confirms the provider's license, and files a written agreement or letter describing services and contact numbers.
At admission, the Administrator or designee asks each resident for physician, pharmacy, dentist and other provider information, and respects the resident's choice of providers.
When a resident needs a community service, staff help the resident or representative to arrange it, and record the referral and outcome in the resident's record.

If a resident or physician wants hospice care, the Administrator reviews the resident's needs against the facility's capabilities and retention requirements (AD-06) and confirms whether a hospice care waiver is needed.
If a waiver is needed, the Administrator prepares a written request to CDSS stating the maximum number of hospice residents, and keeps a copy and proof of delivery.
The Administrator marks a calendar to follow up with CDSS 30 days after the request is submitted, and does not accept or retain hospice residents beyond what is allowed until CDSS has acted.

When hospice or home health is in place, the Administrator and the agency nurse meet within 3 business days to write down who does what, including personal care, medications, equipment, emergency contacts, and who to call at night.

The written coordination is added to the Needs and Services Plan (AD-04). It states that facility staff assist only with self-administered medications and do not perform tasks outside their training (PD-05, HC-02).
Staff review the coordinated plan, the agency's phone numbers and the resident's advance directive or resuscitative request, so a change of condition or death is handled correctly (HC-04, PD-04).
Staff communicate with the hospice or home health agency after changes of condition, and record the contact, date and instructions.
The Administrator invites the local ombudsman to visit and posts the ombudsman and CDSS contact information where residents can see it (RR-01).

If the facility enrolls in the Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator keeps the DHCS enrollment documents, the contact list of care coordination agencies, and the licensed nurse resource, and reviews the HCBS Settings Rule requirements (lease or agreement, privacy, choice, access to food and visitors) with staff (GOV-04).
For ALW residents, the Administrator shares the Needs and Services Plan with the care coordinator as needed, and confirms that resident choices on privacy, food and visitors are respected.
The Administrator reviews the use of community resources and any gaps at the annual policy and quality review (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the Resource Directory, verifies provider licenses, submits any hospice waiver request, and coordinates with agencies.
Help residents use community services and follow coordinated plans of care.
Provide services within their license and coordinate care in writing.
Advises the Administrator on health care needs and, for ALW residents, provides nurse oversight (HC-02).

documentation: Resource Directory with verification dates
Provider agreements and license verifications
Hospice care waiver request, proof of submission, and CDSS decision
Written coordination plans with hospice and home health agencies
Referral and contact log in each resident's record
ALW enrollment, care coordination and licensed nurse resource records, if enrolled

policies.title: Immediate Response to Incidents and Complaints (Licensing-Approved Procedure)
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and the Licensee
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident and every complaint is answered right away, investigated, reported to the right agencies on time, and written down with its outcome. This procedure is part of the Plan of Operation (22 CCR §87208) and is submitted to Community Care Licensing for approval.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.11 — a procedure, approved by the licensing agency, for immediate response to incidents and complaints. [AGENCY NAME] responds to every incident or complaint immediately. The first priority is the safety and health of the resident. Any staff member who witnesses or learns of an incident or complaint takes immediate protective action and tells the person in charge at once. The Administrator, or the Administrator's designee when the Administrator is absent, takes the report, leads the investigation, and makes every required report to the state within the deadlines of 22 CCR §87211. Every incident and complaint is entered in the Incident and Complaint Log together with its resolution. This procedure will be submitted to Community Care Licensing for approval with the Plan of Operation, and any later change will be submitted to Licensing before it takes effect. No resident, family member, representative or employee will be retaliated against for making a complaint or reporting an incident.

definitions.definition: Any event that threatens or may threaten the welfare, safety or health of a resident. Examples are a death, a serious injury, a fall with injury, use of an AED, an unexplained absence, psychological abuse, a poisoning, an outbreak, a fire or explosion, or a major accident.

Any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction or concern about care, services, staff, other residents, the building or the facility's operations, made by a resident, family member, representative, visitor, employee or neighbor.
The Administrator, or the staff member designated to be in charge of the facility on that shift.
The CDSS Community Care Licensing Division, Adult and Senior Care Program, through the regional office serving [ADDRESS OF LOCAL LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE].

procedures: The staff member who witnesses or learns of an incident immediately makes the resident safe, gives first aid or calls 911 when needed (see PD-04), and stays with the resident until help arrives.
The staff member notifies the person in charge immediately, in person or by phone. The person in charge notifies the Administrator at [PHONE] right away if the Administrator is not on site.

For a complaint, the staff member who receives it listens, does not argue or dismiss it, writes down the complainant's name, date, time and what was said, and gives it to the person in charge by the end of the shift. Anyone may also complain directly to the Administrator. A complaint about the Administrator may go to the Licensee.

The Administrator takes the report. For an incident, the Administrator or designee records the facts: who, what, when, where, witnesses, resident condition, immediate actions taken, and who was notified. The Administrator opens an entry in the Incident and Complaint Log the same day.

The Administrator decides within 24 hours whether the event is reportable under 22 CCR §87211 and which agencies must be told. The Administrator makes the call or report personally or assigns a named designee.

Death, serious injury as determined by the physician, AED use, or any other incident threatening welfare, safety or health (including unexplained absence or psychological abuse): a written report goes to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days.

Outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents: a report is made by phone or fax within 24 hours to the licensing agency and to the local health officer. The phone call is confirmed in writing.
Fires and explosions: call 911 and report immediately to the local fire authority. Notify the licensing agency no later than the next working day.

Suspected physical abuse of an elder or dependent adult: report to the local long-term care ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if there is serious bodily injury, and otherwise within 24 hours. Follow SAF-01 for the full abuse-reporting procedure.
