Notice of foreclosure, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy, a rent default notice or a utility shut-off notice: the Licensee gives written notice to the licensing agency within 2 business days, and gives notice to applicants before they sign an admission agreement.
Change of Administrator: notify the licensing agency within 30 days. Change of chief corporate officer: notify within 15 working days.

The Administrator notifies the resident's representative, responsible person, physician and, where applicable, the case manager, as soon as possible after an incident, and no later than the same day for any injury, hospital transfer or death.

The Administrator starts the investigation within 24 hours of the report. The investigation includes interviewing the resident, the complainant and staff or witnesses, reviewing records, and inspecting the area. Statements are written and signed and dated by the person giving them.

The Administrator completes the investigation within 7 calendar days unless an outside agency has taken over. The Administrator decides whether the complaint or incident is substantiated, and records the corrective action, such as retraining, a change in the Needs and Services Plan, a repair, or discipline. Any staff member under investigation for abuse is removed from resident contact until the matter is resolved.

The Administrator gives the complainant a response, in writing if the complainant is a resident or representative, within 14 calendar days of the complaint (sooner if urgent). The response explains what was found and what was done. It also tells the person they may contact Licensing or the ombudsman (1-800-231-4024) if they remain dissatisfied.
The Administrator completes the written incident report to Licensing (the unusual incident/injury report form, LIC 624) and files a copy in the resident's record and in the incident file.

The Administrator updates the Incident and Complaint Log with the date, summary, reports made and when, investigation outcome, corrective action and the date of resolution. The log is kept in a locked file.

At least quarterly the Administrator reviews the log for patterns (repeat falls, repeat complaints about one staff member or area) and records changes made. The results are reported to the Licensee under GOV-03.
During any Licensing inspection or complaint investigation, the Administrator cooperates fully and gives the evaluator the log, reports and records requested.

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report every incident or complaint to the person in charge immediately, and write down what they saw.
Take the first report, make sure the resident is safe, notify the Administrator, and preserve the scene and the facts.
Take the report, investigate, make or delegate every required report within the 22 CCR §87211 deadlines, respond to complainants, and keep the log.
Receive reports on serious events and complaints about the Administrator, give written notices of foreclosure, bankruptcy and similar events, and make sure corrective action is carried out.

documentation: Incident and Complaint Log (date, nature, reports made, investigation outcome, resolution date)
Written incident reports to Licensing (LIC 624 or equivalent) and to the person responsible for the resident
Records of phone and fax reports with date, time, agency and person spoken to
Witness and staff statements and investigation notes
Written complaint responses and corrective action records
Quarterly log review notes

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, night staff and anyone involved in marketing and admissions
policies.purpose: To make sure residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementia receive safe, respectful care from trained staff, with the night supervision the regulations require, and to make sure that any dementia care [AGENCY NAME] advertises is backed by a written dementia program.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will accept and retain residents with dementia only when the pre-admission appraisal and reappraisals show that their needs can be met safely in this home. In a home with fewer than 16 beds, at least one night staff person will be awake and on duty whenever a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, as shown by appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705). Direct care staff will complete the dementia training required by HSC §1569.625 and HSC §1569.626. If [AGENCY NAME] advertises or promotes itself as providing dementia care or special care, it will first have a written dementia program that meets 22 CCR §87706 and will keep every advertisement for 3 years. Dementia care at [AGENCY NAME] is built around dignity, individual choice and the resident's personal rights; behavior is treated as a form of communication, and restraints are never used as a substitute for care (see RD-02).

definitions.definition: A condition, such as Alzheimer's disease, that causes progressive decline in memory, judgment, communication or the ability to carry out daily activities.
At least one night staff person who is awake, alert and on duty at all times during the night because a resident with dementia needs it.
The written program required before a facility advertises dementia care, covering philosophy, admission, training, activities, environment, changes in condition and success indicators.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator completes the pre-admission appraisal (AD-02) and records whether the applicant has dementia, the stage, wandering or exit-seeking, behavioral expressions, night-time needs and the level of supervision needed.

The Administrator admits a person with dementia only when the documented appraisal shows that current staffing, the building and the program can meet the person's needs safely, and the person has no prohibited health condition (see AD-06). The decision and reasons are written in the resident's record.

At admission and at every reappraisal (AD-04), the Administrator records whether the resident needs awake night supervision. The need is also reassessed whenever staff observe night-time wandering, exit-seeking, falls, agitation or sleeplessness.

If any resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, the Administrator schedules at least one awake night staff person every night, and records this on the schedule (see PP-01). Night staff may not sleep on duty.

If the home cannot provide awake night staff when a resident needs it, the Administrator notifies the resident's representative, makes a plan for the resident's safety, and begins relocation planning under AD-08.

The Administrator makes sure every direct care staff person has the training required by HSC §1569.625 and §1569.626: 40 hours of initial training, of which 20 hours are completed before working alone with residents and the remaining 20 within 4 weeks of hire.

The first 20 hours must include 6 hours of dementia training, and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. The second 20-hour block also includes 6 hours of dementia training, for a total of 12 hours of initial dementia training.

Each direct care staff person completes 20 hours of training every year, of which 8 hours are on dementia. The Administrator tracks hours for each employee and records dates, topics, hours and trainers (see TR-01 and TR-02).

Care staff use person-centered approaches: they learn each resident's life story, routines and preferences, use a calm and simple manner of speaking, offer choices, redirect rather than argue, and look for unmet needs (pain, hunger, toileting, fear) behind behavior.

The activity coordinator plans daily activities suited to each resident's abilities, such as music, reminiscence, movement, sensory activities and outdoor time, and offers them at times of day when residents are most restless (see PD-03).

The Administrator checks the environment for safety each month: lighting, clear walkways, secured hazards (chemicals, sharps, medications), door alarms or other exit protections allowed by the fire clearance and licensing rules, and a layout that is easy to follow.

Staff report any change in a resident's condition, such as new confusion, loss of skills, falls, weight loss or behavior change, to the Administrator on the same shift. The Administrator contacts the physician and representative and updates the Needs and Services Plan (see PD-04, AD-04).
Staff follow SAF-03 for any resident who may leave the building unsupervised. Residents are not locked in (see RD-01).

Before any advertisement, brochure, website text or sign refers to dementia, Alzheimer's, memory care or special care, the Administrator confirms that a written dementia program exists. The program states the philosophy of care, admission criteria and process, staff training, activities, the physical environment, how changes in condition are handled, and how success will be measured.
The Administrator keeps a copy of every advertisement, in every format and version, for 3 years from the last date it was used, in the Advertising File.

Success indicators are reviewed at least every 6 months, such as incidents, falls, weight, use of antipsychotic medication, resident and family satisfaction, and staff turnover. The Administrator records results and improvements in the quality assurance file (GOV-03).

If the home does not have the staff, training or program for dementia care, the Administrator does not advertise dementia care and does not admit residents whose needs exceed what the home can provide.

responsibilities.duty: Decide admission and retention of residents with dementia, arrange awake night staffing, maintain the written dementia program and the 3-year advertising file, and track staff dementia training.
Complete required dementia training, give person-centered care, report changes in condition and follow safety and elopement procedures.
Remain awake and on duty when awake night supervision is required, and complete a written night observation record.
Plan and document dementia-appropriate activities.
Make sure staffing and funding are sufficient to meet the night supervision and training requirements.

documentation: Pre-admission appraisal and reappraisals noting dementia and night supervision needs
Night staffing schedule showing awake night staff
Staff training records for each direct care employee (dates, hours, topics)
Written dementia program
Advertising File with every advertisement kept 3 years
Success indicator and quality assurance review notes

policies.category: B8 Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights
policies.title: Personal Rights of Residents
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, the Licensee, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To protect the dignity and personal rights of every resident and to make sure residents and their representatives are told about those rights and know how to complain if they are not respected.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B8 — Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights (personal rights apply to all facility categories, and the facility will not violate personal rights and will not use corporal or unusual punishment) and LIC 281 item B9.5 — Client's Rights/Personal Rights. Every resident at [AGENCY NAME] will be informed of his or her personal rights at admission, and the personal rights of residents will not be violated. Residents and their representatives receive a written list of rights at admission, and the list is posted in a place where residents and visitors can read it. Under 22 CCR §87468.1, residents have the right to: be treated with dignity; be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation or abuse; be told how to complain to Community Care Licensing and to the long-term care ombudsman; leave the facility at any time and not be locked in; receive private visits from ombudsmen and other advocates at reasonable hours without prior notice; keep and spend their own money; use the telephone, send and receive mail, and vote; refuse care; and move out. The full list of 18 rights is set out in the notice given to residents. No resident will be denied admission, transferred, discharged, or given a room, roommate or restroom assignment, or be denied a preferred name or pronouns or association, because of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status, and these protections cannot be waived. Staff are trained on residents' rights at hire and every year. [AGENCY NAME] will not retaliate against any resident or person who asserts a right or makes a complaint.

definitions.definition: The rights of every resident, set out in 22 CCR §87468.1, that the facility must honor at all times and cannot take away by rule, agreement or practice.
A person legally authorized or designated by the resident to act on the resident's behalf, such as a conservator, agent under a power of attorney or family member.
A representative of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, who advocates for residents and may visit privately and without prior notice.

procedures: At or before admission, the Administrator reviews the personal rights list with the resident and the representative in plain language and in the resident's preferred language, and answers questions (see RD-03).

The resident and representative receive a written copy of the rights, which includes the telephone numbers of Community Care Licensing at [PHONE OF LOCAL LICENSING OFFICE] and of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline, 1-800-231-4024. The resident or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment that this was done, and the acknowledgment is filed in the resident's record. A signature is not required for admission, and refusal is noted.

The Administrator posts the personal rights in a visible common area at a height and in a type size that residents can read, and replaces damaged or outdated postings immediately. A copy of the admission agreement or a notice that it is available is also posted (see AD-07).
Staff treat every resident with dignity: they knock before entering a room, use the name or pronouns the resident prefers, give personal care in private, and speak to residents as adults.

Residents may leave the facility at any time. No door, bed rail, device or practice may be used to lock a resident in. If staff are worried about a resident's safety when leaving, they follow SAF-03, tell the Administrator, and never physically stop the resident.

Residents may refuse care, medication assistance, meals or activities. Staff note the refusal, explain possible consequences, tell the Administrator and the physician if health is affected, and do not punish or pressure the resident.
Staff allow private visits by ombudsmen and other advocates at reasonable hours without prior notice, and provide a private place. Staff do not ask for advance notice or for the reason for the visit.
Residents keep and spend their own money. Staff handle resident funds only under TL-02 and only with written authorization.
Residents may use the telephone, send and receive mail unopened, and vote. Staff help with registration, ballots or transportation to vote when asked.
Residents may move out at any time, subject to the notice terms in the admission agreement. Staff support planning for the move and never discourage or punish a resident for choosing to leave.

The Administrator will not deny admission, transfer, discharge, assign rooms, roommates or restrooms, or restrict a preferred name, pronouns or association, because of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (see RD-03).

Any staff member who sees or suspects a violation of a resident's rights reports it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates under PD-08, takes corrective action, and reports abuse as required under SAF-01.
Residents and representatives may complain to the Administrator, the Licensee, Community Care Licensing or the ombudsman, with no retaliation. Complaints are handled under RR-01.

The Administrator trains all new employees on personal rights during orientation, before the employee works alone with residents, and again every year. Training dates are recorded in the personnel file (see TR-01 and TR-02).
The Administrator reviews this policy at least yearly and when the regulations change, and checks that the postings are current.

responsibilities.duty: Give and explain rights at admission, post them, train staff, investigate violations and correct practices.
Honor each resident's rights at all times and report suspected violations immediately.
Make sure no facility rule, practice or agreement violates personal rights.

documentation: Signed Personal Rights acknowledgment in each resident file
Posted copy of personal rights (date of posting noted in the compliance file)
Staff training records on residents' rights
Complaint and rights-violation investigation records (Incident and Complaint Log)

policies.category: B8 Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights
policies.title: Rules of Conduct, No Corporal or Unusual Punishment, and Restraints
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, residents and visitors
policies.purpose: To state the house rules residents and staff are expected to follow, and to make clear that [AGENCY NAME] will never use corporal or unusual punishment, humiliation, intimidation or any practice that violates a resident's personal rights.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B8 — Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights. The detailed discipline items in LIC 281 B8 (types of discipline, conferences with placement representatives, grounds for dismissal) are headed for Group Homes and Foster Family Agencies only and do not apply to this Residential Care Facility for the Elderly. For this RCFE, the rules of the home must not violate personal rights, and this clear statement applies: no corporal or unusual punishment will be used at [AGENCY NAME]. Residents are adults and are not disciplined. No resident will be punished, humiliated, intimidated or abused (22 CCR §87468.1). Staff will not strike, shake, restrain, isolate, threaten, shame, withhold food, water, care, visits, mail, phone use, medication or activities, or take away personal property or money as a consequence for behavior. House rules are limited to what is needed for safety and for respect for others, are explained at admission, and are never applied in a way that violates a personal right. Postural supports or restraints are never used for discipline or staff convenience.

definitions.definition: Any physical punishment, including hitting, slapping, pinching, shaking, rough handling, or forced physical positions or exercise.

Any punishment that is humiliating, frightening or deprives a resident of basic needs or rights, such as isolation, withholding meals, threats of eviction used to control behavior, or taking away mail or visits.
Any physical, mechanical or chemical means that limits a resident's freedom of movement or behavior and that the resident cannot easily remove.
A resident's behavior that communicates an unmet need, discomfort or distress, which staff respond to with understanding and not with punishment.

procedures: At admission the Administrator reviews the house rules (for example, quiet hours, respect for others' belongings, safe use of equipment, the smoking policy in SAF-05 and the visitor policy) with the resident and representative, and gives a written copy. The rules are limited to health, safety and consideration for others.

The Administrator reviews every house rule against the personal rights list (RD-01) before adopting it. Any rule that would limit a right, such as leaving the building, privacy, visitors, phone, mail, money or refusing care, is removed.

When a resident's behavior is disruptive or unsafe, staff first stay calm, make sure everyone is safe, look for the cause (pain, infection, hunger, noise, fear, medication effects, boredom, toileting needs), and respond with redirection, reassurance, a change in environment or activity.

Staff report any ongoing behavior concern to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator contacts the resident's physician and representative, and updates the Needs and Services Plan with approaches that work (AD-04).

Staff never use, threaten or imply corporal or unusual punishment, humiliation, intimidation or abuse. This includes yelling, name-calling, ridicule, withholding care or attention, isolating a resident in a room, or restricting meals, visits, phone or mail.

Staff never use physical force, locked doors, bed rails, belts, devices or medication to control a resident's behavior or for staff convenience. Medication is given only as ordered by a physician and for a medical reason, as in PD-05 and HC-01.

Postural supports or any device that restricts movement may be used only if allowed by licensing regulations, ordered in writing by the resident's physician, with consent of the resident or representative, and any approval Licensing requires. Before use the Administrator confirms the current requirements with Community Care Licensing, notes them in the Needs and Services Plan, and has staff trained on their use. No device is used without these steps.

In an emergency where a resident is in immediate danger of hurting self or others, staff move others away, use the least intervention needed such as verbal calming, call 911 or the physician, and notify the Administrator. Staff do not physically restrain.

Any staff member who sees or suspects corporal or unusual punishment, humiliation, intimidation or a restraint used without authorization reports it at once to the Administrator, or to the Licensee if the Administrator is involved. Suspected abuse is reported under SAF-01 within the required deadlines.

The Administrator removes any staff member suspected of such conduct from resident contact during the investigation (PD-08), and the employee is subject to discipline up to termination and to reporting to the licensing agency and law enforcement as required.

If a resident's behavior cannot be safely managed in the home despite documented efforts, the Administrator follows the retention and relocation procedures in AD-06 and AD-08, including the written notice and appeal rights. Eviction is never used as punishment.

Staff receive training on this policy at orientation (TR-01) and annually (TR-02). Each employee signs a statement acknowledging that corporal and unusual punishment is prohibited, and it is kept in the personnel file.

responsibilities.duty: Set rules that respect personal rights, make sure no punishment or unauthorized restraint is used, investigate reports, and confirm Licensing requirements before any postural support is used.
Never use punishment or restraint, respond to behavior with understanding, and report any violation immediately.
Support the removal and discipline of any staff member who violates this policy.

documentation: Written house rules signed or acknowledged at admission
Staff acknowledgment of the no corporal or unusual punishment statement
Physician orders, consents and any approvals if postural supports are used
Needs and Services Plan notes on behavior approaches
Incident and investigation records

policies.category: B8 Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights
policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and the Licensee
policies.purpose: To make sure every applicant and resident is treated fairly regardless of who they are, and that people with limited English or with a hearing or other disability can understand and use our services and know their rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, services, room assignment, transfer or discharge. Under 22 CCR §87468.1(b), [AGENCY NAME] will not deny admission to, transfer, discharge, require to share a room with, assign a room or restroom to, or restrict the preferred name or pronouns or association of, any person because of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status. The Department cannot waive these protections (22 CCR §87468.1(d)), and neither can [AGENCY NAME], the admission agreement or the house rules. [AGENCY NAME] also complies with the Americans with Disabilities Act and, where it receives federal financial assistance (including Medi-Cal), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d), and will not discriminate on the basis of race, color or national origin. Admission decisions are based on the person's care needs and the home's ability to meet them under the admission criteria (AD-01), never on a protected characteristic. When the pre-admission appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, [AGENCY NAME] completes form LIC 9158 as required by 22 CCR §87507. [AGENCY NAME] provides interpretation or translation at no cost to residents with limited English proficiency.

definitions.definition: A resident or applicant who does not speak English as a primary language and has limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.
How a person shows gender through name, pronouns, clothing, grooming or behavior.
A person trained and competent to interpret accurately between English and another language, who understands confidentiality and who is not chosen simply because they are available.
The Licensing form required when the pre-admission appraisal shows that a resident has a hearing or other disability, so the disability and the resident's communication needs are on record.

procedures: The Administrator uses the same written admission criteria (AD-01) for every applicant. Admission decisions are recorded with the specific care-related reasons, and the Administrator confirms that no protected characteristic played a role.

No staff member may ask an applicant about HIV status, sexual orientation or gender identity as a condition of admission. Medical information is requested only as required for the medical assessment (AD-03) and appraisal (AD-02).
Staff use the name and pronouns each resident prefers in speech, records, name tags, room signs and mail, and record the resident's preference in the record with the resident's permission.

Room, roommate and restroom assignments are made by the resident's expressed preference, consistent with the resident's gender identity, and safety and compatibility. A resident is never moved or refused a room because of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status.
Residents may associate with whom they choose, including partners, friends and visitors, and the visiting policy is applied the same way to all residents.

Staff use universal precautions with all residents (SAF-04). Staff do not tell others about, and do not treat residents differently because of, any person's HIV status, and this information is kept confidential (RR-02).

At the first contact the Administrator asks every applicant and representative what language they prefer for speaking and reading and any communication needs, and records the answer in the resident's record.

For a resident with limited English, the Administrator arranges a qualified interpreter, in person or by phone or video, for the admission interview, appraisal, admission agreement review, personal rights review, Needs and Services Plan, medical decisions and any grievance. The home does not charge the resident for interpretation.

The Administrator provides translated copies of key documents, including personal rights and the admission agreement, when available, or has the documents read aloud by a qualified interpreter and records that this was done. Family members or other residents are used as interpreters only if the resident asks, and the request is recorded. A minor is never used as an interpreter.

When the pre-admission appraisal shows that a resident has a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes form LIC 9158 and files it with the admission agreement. The Needs and Services Plan lists the aids and supports the resident needs, such as hearing amplification, written materials or large print, and staff are told.

The Administrator makes reasonable modifications for residents with disabilities, such as accessible rooms and bathrooms, assistive devices, extra time, and different formats, unless doing so would create an undue burden or a direct threat to safety, and the reasons for any refusal are documented.

Staff who see or suspect discrimination or harassment of a resident report it to the Administrator at once. The Administrator investigates under PD-08, stops the conduct, and takes corrective action up to discipline or termination.

Residents and applicants who believe they were discriminated against may complain to the Administrator, Community Care Licensing, the ombudsman (1-800-231-4024) or other agencies. [AGENCY NAME] will not retaliate. Complaints are handled under RR-01.

The Administrator trains staff on nondiscrimination, preferred names and pronouns, cultural respect, working with interpreters and disability access at orientation and every year, and records the training.

responsibilities.duty: Apply admission criteria fairly, arrange interpreters and translated materials, complete LIC 9158 when indicated, investigate complaints and train staff.
Treat residents respectfully, use preferred names and pronouns, protect confidentiality and report discrimination.
Make sure no facility policy, agreement or practice discriminates, and provide funds for interpreter services.

documentation: Admission decision notes with care-related reasons
Language preference and interpreter use records
Form LIC 9158 where applicable
Preferred name and pronoun records
Staff training records on nondiscrimination and language access
Complaint and investigation records

policies.title: Persons Accepted, Compatibility and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff and the Licensee
policies.purpose: To state who [AGENCY NAME] accepts for care, how it decides whether a person is compatible with current residents and appropriate for the home, and which persons it cannot accept.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.0 — Admission Policies, and item B9.1 — Persons accepted for care, including age range and compatibility determination process. [AGENCY NAME] is licensed as a Residential Care Facility for the Elderly for up to [LICENSED CAPACITY] residents and accepts adults age 60 and older. Persons under 60 are considered only where permitted by licensing law and where their needs and age are compatible with the other residents and are approved as the law requires. Admission is decided only after a pre-admission appraisal with a functional, mental and social evaluation and a determination of suitability against the admission criteria (22 CCR §87457), and never for a reason prohibited by RD-03. [AGENCY NAME] will not admit or retain a person who has, or needs health services for, a prohibited health condition under 22 CCR §87615, including stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all activities of daily living, and tracheostomies; the list is not exhaustive. Admission policies cover the items below, each in its own policy: pre-admission appraisal (AD-02); medical assessment (AD-03); Needs and Services Plan and reappraisal (AD-04); acceptance and retention limits (AD-06); and the admission agreement, rates, deposits and refund policies (AD-07).

definitions.definition: A documented determination that a prospective resident's needs, behavior, age and lifestyle are suitable for the current residents and the home, and that current residents are not placed at risk.
The Administrator's written decision, made on the pre-admission appraisal, that the home can meet the person's needs within the license and the admission criteria.

A condition listed in 22 CCR §87615 that bars admission and retention, including stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all ADLs, and tracheostomies.

procedures: The Administrator is the only person who may accept or refuse an applicant. Admission staff give information to the public but make no promise of admission.

At first inquiry, staff give the applicant a description of the home, the age range served, the services, the rates, and the refund policy, and tell the applicant that admission depends on a pre-admission appraisal. They explain the services and levels of care the home can and cannot provide.

The Administrator schedules a pre-admission interview with the applicant and, with consent, the representative and family, at the home or where the applicant lives, and completes the appraisal under AD-02. Consent for the appraisal and for contact with the physician is obtained in writing before it begins.

The Administrator reviews the appraisal findings against the admission criteria: age range, ability to evacuate with staff help (confirm against fire clearance), medical stability, mental and social functioning, behavior, level of assistance needed, and the home's current staffing and services.

The Administrator checks that the applicant has none of the prohibited health conditions in 22 CCR §87615 and does not need services for them. If there is doubt, the Administrator requests a written opinion from the applicant's physician, and where needed a consultation with Licensing, before deciding.

The home does not admit a nonambulatory or bedridden person unless the local fire authority's clearance allows it (see EDP-02). The Administrator confirms the fire clearance conditions before the decision.

The Administrator assesses compatibility with current residents: age, cognitive level, behavior, sleep patterns, noise, safety risks, and any known history of aggression, wandering or substance use. The Administrator also checks whether the new resident's needs would reduce care available to existing residents.
For an applicant with dementia, the Administrator applies the criteria in PD-09, including whether the home can provide awake night supervision when needed.

The decision is based on needs and the home's ability to meet them, and never on a basis prohibited by RD-03, such as sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, HIV status, race or national origin.

The Administrator writes the suitability determination, with the reasons for acceptance or refusal, signs and dates it, and files it with the appraisal. A copy is kept even when the applicant is not admitted.

If the applicant is not accepted, the Administrator tells the applicant and representative promptly and explains the reason in plain language, and, if possible, helps them find other options through community resources (PD-07).

If the applicant is accepted, the Administrator proceeds to the medical assessment and physical exam and TB test (AD-03), the emergency information (AD-05), and the admission agreement, which is signed and dated within 7 days of admission and a copy given immediately (AD-07). The Needs and Services Plan is developed under AD-04.

The Administrator reviews these admission criteria at least yearly and whenever the license, staffing, building, or regulations change, and records the review in the quality assurance file (GOV-03). Any change to the type of persons served is reported to Licensing before it is made.

responsibilities.duty: Conduct the appraisal, make the written suitability and compatibility decision, apply the prohibited health condition rules and the fire clearance limits, and keep admission records.
Give information, schedule appraisals, collect consents and forward documents to the Administrator, but not decide admission.
Approve the admission criteria and make sure the home has the staffing and building to match the persons it accepts.

documentation: Pre-admission appraisal and consent forms
Written suitability and compatibility determination for each applicant
Physician statement regarding prohibited health conditions, when requested
Fire clearance conditions on file for nonambulatory or bedridden residents
Annual admission criteria review notes

policies.title: Pre-Admission Appraisal and Placement Appropriateness
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designated intake staff, and any licensed professional consulted on a prospective resident's needs
policies.purpose: To make sure every person admitted to [AGENCY NAME] has had a documented pre-admission interview and a functional, mental and social evaluation, and that a written decision confirms we can safely meet the person's needs before the person moves in.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit any person until a pre-admission appraisal is complete and the Administrator has recorded a written suitability decision against the facility's admission criteria. The appraisal is done with the prospective resident's consent (or the consent of the legal representative) and includes a pre-admission interview and a functional, mental and social evaluation, as required by 22 CCR §87457. This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.7 (Pre-admission appraisal plan) and item B9.3 (Criteria for assessing appropriateness of placement, including the interviews and the procedures for obtaining and developing the necessary paperwork). LIC 281 item B9.2 (Intake procedures for placement in group homes) is written for the group home category and does not apply to an RCFE. The intake procedure in this policy replaces it, and it is described here so the reviewer can see how [AGENCY NAME] handles intake. The appraisal and the suitability decision are made without discrimination, as stated in RD-01 and RD-03. Placement is never denied because of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)).

definitions.definition: The interview and the functional, mental and social evaluation completed before admission to decide whether [AGENCY NAME] can meet the person's needs.
The Administrator's written, dated decision that a person does or does not meet admission criteria and can be appropriately served by this facility.
A person who has applied for admission and has not yet moved in.
A person legally authorized to act for the prospective resident, such as an agent under a power of attorney, a conservator or a responsible party named in writing.

procedures: Intake staff record each inquiry on the Inquiry Log with the date, caller, the person's age, care needs, payor source and desired move-in date, and give the caller the facility's information packet, including the services and rates summary.

The Administrator or designee screens the inquiry against the admission criteria in AD-01, the prohibited health conditions in AD-06, licensed capacity, and the current staffing and bed availability. If the person clearly cannot be served, staff tell the caller promptly, give the reason, and suggest other resources (RR-01 and PD-07).

The Administrator or designee schedules a pre-admission interview in person where possible, at the person's current residence, hospital or other setting, or at the facility. Interviews by video or phone are used only when an in-person interview is not practical, and the reason is noted.

At the start of the interview, staff explain the purpose of the appraisal and obtain the written consent of the prospective resident, or the authorized representative, to the interview, evaluation and collection of records. If the person cannot consent, staff document the basis for the representative's authority.
Staff interview the prospective resident directly, with family or the representative present if the person wishes, and note preferences, daily routines, language, culture and goals for care.

Functional evaluation: staff record the person's ability to bathe, dress, groom, toilet, transfer, walk, eat and manage continence, any assistive devices, fall history, and how much help the person needs with each activity.

Mental evaluation: staff record cognitive status, memory, orientation, mood, behaviors, wandering or exit-seeking, and any dementia diagnosis. Staff note whether the person may need awake night staff or the memory care practices in PD-09.

Social evaluation: staff record the person's history, family and support network, interests, social and religious preferences, and expectations about the move. Staff consider whether the person will be compatible with current residents, as set out in AD-01.

Staff request the physician's medical assessment and the information listed in AD-03, together with the current medication list, diet orders, hospice or home health records, and any hospital or skilled nursing discharge summary. Records are requested with a signed release that meets RR-02, and each request and receipt is dated in the file.

The Administrator reviews the paperwork against the prohibited health conditions in AD-06. Where a condition raises a question, the Administrator consults the person's physician, a home health agency, hospice or a licensed nurse before deciding (PD-07 and HC-02).

The Administrator decides whether [AGENCY NAME] has the staff, training, equipment, physical plant and bed to meet the person's needs, and whether any needed services must come from an outside provider.

The Administrator completes the written suitability determination, signs and dates it before the admission date, and states whether the person is accepted, accepted with conditions, or not accepted, with the reasons.

If the person is not accepted, the Administrator tells the person or representative the reason in writing within [NUMBER] business days and provides referral resources. Non-acceptance is never based on a protected characteristic.

If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator makes sure the admission agreement process in AD-07 includes the Department's required disability form, LIC 9158, and that the person's communication needs are met (RD-03).
If more than 30 days pass between the appraisal and the admission date, or the person's condition changes in that time, the Administrator updates the appraisal and the determination before admission.
The appraisal, consent, records received and determination are placed in the resident's record on admission, and the findings are used to build the needs and services plan under AD-04.
The Administrator reviews the intake log and a sample of appraisals quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Conducts or oversees the appraisal, makes and signs the suitability determination, and decides non-acceptance.
Log inquiries, schedule interviews, request and track records, and keep the appraisal file complete.

responsibilities.role: Licensed professional consultant (physician, nurse, hospice or home health)
responsibilities.duty: Advise on whether a medical condition can be safely managed in the facility when asked.
Take part in the interview, give consent and provide accurate information and records.

documentation: Inquiry Log
Signed consent to appraisal and records release
Pre-admission appraisal (functional, mental and social)
Records received with dates
Written suitability determination, signed and dated before admission
Non-acceptance notice with referral resources, when applicable

policies.title: Medical Assessment, Physical Examination, TB and Immunization Requirements
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designated admission staff and prospective residents
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a physician's medical assessment, a physical examination and a TB test on file at or before admission, and that immunization information is requested and recorded in a way that respects the resident's rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires a medical assessment by a physician and a physical examination that includes TB testing before or at admission. This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.6 (Medical assessment), item B9.11 (Physical examination requirements, including TB testing) and item B9.10 (Immunization requirements). The medical assessment gives the facility information on diagnoses, medications, diet, functional limits, contagious disease and any need for special care. Immunizations are requested and recorded. The facility does not force an immunization. A resident keeps the right to refuse care (22 CCR §87468.1), and a refusal is documented in the resident record. Medical records are obtained only with a valid release under HIPAA (45 CFR 164) and are kept in the resident record under RR-02 and REC-01. Staff health screening, which also requires a physician's screening and TB clearance under 22 CCR §87411, is covered separately in PP-04.

definitions.definition: A written report by a physician on the person's health, diagnoses, medications, special diet, functional capacity, and whether the person is free of contagious or infectious disease.
A tuberculosis screening, either a skin or blood test, with a chest x-ray and physician clearance when the result is positive.
Documentation of vaccines the resident has received, such as influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19 and tetanus.

procedures: During the pre-admission process (AD-02), the Administrator or designee gives the prospective resident or representative the physician's report form the Department requires and asks that a physician complete it.

Staff explain that the report must include a physical examination, diagnoses, current medications, allergies, special diet, ability to perform activities of daily living, and a TB test result, and that it must be completed before or at the time of admission.
The prospective resident or representative signs a records release that meets HIPAA requirements, so that [AGENCY NAME] may obtain records directly from the physician, hospital or other provider.

On receipt, the Administrator reviews the report for completeness and signature, and checks that it identifies no condition prohibited under AD-06 and no contagious condition that cannot be managed under SAF-04.
If the TB test is positive, the Administrator requires a chest x-ray result and the physician's written statement that the person is free of active TB before admission.
If the report is incomplete, unclear or inconsistent with the appraisal, the Administrator contacts the physician by phone or in writing for clarification and records the contact in the file.

If a person arrives in an emergency or the report is not available at the time of admission, the Administrator does not admit unless the missing information can be obtained and documented on the day of admission or as the Title 22 requirements allow, and records the reason and date received.

Staff ask for the immunization history and record it. [AGENCY NAME] offers or recommends annual influenza vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other vaccines according to current CDC and CDPH guidance, and helps arrange them through the resident's physician or a pharmacy.

If a resident declines an immunization, staff document the offer and the refusal, explain the risks, and notify the physician. A refusal alone is not a reason for denying admission or discharging a resident.
The Administrator places the medical assessment, TB result and immunization record in the resident record and keeps them confidential under RR-02.
The Administrator updates medical information after any change of condition, hospitalization or new diagnosis, and when the physician reviews the needs and services plan (AD-04).
The Administrator checks the resident files annually for an up-to-date medical assessment and TB information and requests updates as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews medical reports for completeness, applies the prohibited-condition and infection-control screens, and keeps files current.
Distribute forms, obtain releases, track receipt, and file records.
Completes the medical assessment, physical exam and TB test and returns them to the facility.
Arrange the exam, sign releases and make immunization decisions.

documentation: Physician's medical assessment and physical examination report
TB test and any chest x-ray or physician clearance
Signed records release (HIPAA)
Immunization record and documentation of offers and refusals
Log of calls and requests for clarification

policies.title: Needs and Services Plan and Reappraisal
policies.applies_to: Administrator, care staff, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a written needs and services plan built from the appraisal, that it is kept current through reappraisal, and that the resident and representative take part in decisions about care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prepares an individual written needs and services plan for every resident from the pre-admission appraisal and medical assessment. This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.4 (Needs and services plan). The plan states the resident's needs, the services [AGENCY NAME] will provide, who will provide them, and how often. The plan is reappraised whenever the resident's condition changes and at the intervals Title 22 requires, and in any case at least once a year. The resident and the representative take part in developing and changing the plan, and staff follow the resident's wishes and personal rights (RD-01). The reappraisal also decides whether the night supervision in place is still adequate, especially for residents with dementia.

definitions.definition: The written plan listing the resident's care needs, goals, preferences, the services to meet them, and who provides them.
An updated evaluation of the resident's functional, mental, social and health status that is used to revise the plan.
A noticeable change in the resident's health, function, cognition, behavior or ability to remain safely in the facility.

procedures: Within [NUMBER] days of admission, and no later than the time Title 22 requires, the Administrator or a qualified designee drafts the needs and services plan using the pre-admission appraisal, the physician's report and what the resident and family say.

The plan lists the resident's needs in each area: personal care, mobility and fall risk, continence, nutrition and special diet, medication assistance, skin, cognition and behavior, social and spiritual interests, and any outside services such as home health or hospice.
For each need, the plan states the service to be provided, who is responsible, how often, and any equipment or assistance needed.
The Administrator meets with the resident and representative, reviews the plan in plain language, records their choices and objections, and invites questions.
The resident or representative signs and dates the plan. If the resident declines a service, staff record the refusal and tell the physician if safety is affected.
The Administrator gives a copy of the plan to the resident or representative, files the original in the resident record, and makes the plan available to the staff who give care.
Care staff are trained on each resident's plan before they work with that resident (TR-01 and TR-02) and report changes to the Administrator or the person in charge.

A reappraisal is done when there is a change of condition, after any hospitalization or major incident, when the physician changes orders, when behavior or cognition changes, and on a regular schedule at least annually.
For each reappraisal, the Administrator reviews the plan with the resident and representative, updates it, and has it re-signed. Changes are made in the file with the date and the reason.
If the reappraisal shows that the resident's needs are beyond what [AGENCY NAME] can safely provide or that a prohibited condition has developed, the Administrator follows AD-06 and AD-08.

For residents with dementia, the reappraisal records whether the resident needs awake night staff, supervision for wandering or additional monitoring, and the Administrator adjusts night staffing under PP-01 and PD-09 on the same day the need is identified.
The Administrator reviews a sample of plans each quarter for completeness and for timely reappraisal after changes of condition (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every plan is prepared, reviewed with the resident and updated on time, and adjusts staffing to meet identified needs.
Follow the plan, observe the resident and report changes promptly.
Take part in developing the plan, state preferences and sign the plan.
Give orders and input on care needs when involved.

documentation: Signed needs and services plan
Reappraisals with dates and reasons
Notes on resident and representative participation
Refusals of service
Change of condition notes
Quarterly plan review results

policies.title: Emergency Information and Sign-In/Sign-Out
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff, residents and visitors
policies.purpose: To make sure staff can reach the right people and give the right medical information in an emergency, and to keep an accurate record of when residents leave and return, without limiting their right to come and go.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] collects emergency and medical contact information for every resident at admission and keeps it current and immediately available. This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.8 (Emergency information). Residents have the right to leave the facility at any time and may not be locked in (22 CCR §87468.1). The sign-in and sign-out procedure below is a safety record only, and it never restricts a resident's freedom. This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.9 (Sign-in and sign-out procedures). A resident who does not return when expected is handled under SAF-03.

definitions.definition: Contacts and medical data needed in an emergency: next of kin, representative, physician, hospice or home health agency, preferred hospital, medications, allergies, diagnoses, code status and insurance.
A record that a resident has left the facility, including time, destination, escort and expected return.
A resident who cannot be located and has not signed out or told staff of a departure, as defined in SAF-03.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator or designee records each resident's emergency information on the facility's identification and emergency information form, including the resident's name, date of birth, room, and preferred language.

Staff record at least two emergency contacts and the authorized representative with phone numbers, as well as the primary physician, any specialists, the hospice or home health agency, the pharmacy and the preferred hospital.

Staff record the current medications, allergies, diagnoses, special diet, mobility aids, hearing, vision or communication needs, and any advance directive or resuscitative request (HC-04), copied from the medical assessment.
The Administrator checks that the information is complete, and the resident or representative signs and dates it.

A current copy of each resident's emergency information is kept in a readily accessible place that staff can reach at all hours, and a copy goes with the resident to any emergency room or hospital (PD-04).
The Administrator reviews and updates the emergency information whenever it changes, after any hospitalization, and at least every [NUMBER] months. Staff date each update.

Each resident is told at admission that he or she may leave the facility at any time and that doors are not locked to keep residents in. The facility's delayed-egress or secured features, if any, are used only as permitted by the licensing rules and PD-09.

A sign-in/sign-out log is kept at [LOCATION, such as the front desk]. When a resident leaves for an outing, appointment or overnight stay, the resident, family member or staff enters the date, time out, destination, who accompanied the resident, a contact phone and the expected return time.

The resident or the escort enters the time of return. Staff on duty verify that the entry is complete and note any medications or equipment that went out with the resident or need to be reviewed on return.

If a resident has not returned within [NUMBER] minutes of the expected return, staff call the contact number on the log and the resident's family or representative. If the resident cannot be located, staff start the response in SAF-03 immediately.

Staff who see a resident leaving without signing out do not stop or lock the resident in. They offer the sign-out log, make sure the resident is safe to go, and tell the person in charge. If the resident has cognitive impairment and may be at risk, staff follow SAF-03 and PD-09.
Logs are kept in the facility with other resident records for the period set in REC-01, and the Administrator reviews them weekly for gaps or patterns.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures emergency information is complete and current and that the sign-out system is used and reviewed.
Use emergency information correctly, help residents and visitors with the log, and report late returns.
Give accurate information, update changes and sign out when leaving.

documentation: Identification and emergency information form for each resident
Dated updates
Sign-in/sign-out log
Late-return and missing resident notes (see SAF-03)

policies.title: Retention Limits and Prohibited Health Conditions
policies.applies_to: Administrator, licensed professionals consulted, care staff
policies.purpose: To state the health conditions that prohibit admission or retention, and the process [AGENCY NAME] follows when a prospective or current resident has or develops such a condition.
policies.policy: This policy, together with AD-01, AD-02, AD-03, AD-04 and AD-07, meets LIC 281 item B9.0 (Admission Policies), by stating the acceptance and retention limitations of [AGENCY NAME]. [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a person who needs health services for, or who has, any of the following conditions under 22 CCR §87615: stage 3 or stage 4 pressure injuries; a gastrostomy tube; a naso-gastric tube; staph or other serious infection; total dependence on others for all activities of daily living; or a tracheostomy. The list in the regulation is not exhaustive ("including, but not limited to"), so the Administrator treats any other condition that the Department prohibits, or that cannot be safely managed with the facility's staff, license and physical plant, as a limit on acceptance and retention. Hospice residents are retained only under the hospice waiver rules of Title 22, and certain other conditions are allowed only when Title 22's allowable-condition and exception requirements are met. When the Department issues a relocation order, [AGENCY NAME] follows it and the resident's review rights. Retention decisions are made without discrimination (RD-03).

definitions.definition: A condition for which Title 22 bars admission or retention in an RCFE, including those listed in 22 CCR §87615.
Continued residence of a person who has already been admitted.
The Department's approval process that allows a resident who is terminally ill to remain in the facility under a hospice plan, subject to Title 22 conditions.
A written Department order requiring a resident to be moved because the facility cannot meet the person's needs or the person has a prohibited condition.

procedures: At each pre-admission appraisal (AD-02), the Administrator checks the resident's records for stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, a gastrostomy or naso-gastric tube, a tracheostomy, staph or other serious infection, and total dependence on others for all ADLs, and records the result on the suitability determination.

If any prohibited condition is present, the Administrator does not admit the person, tells the person or representative the reason in writing, and gives referral options such as a skilled nursing facility or home health resources.

If a condition is not on the list but is unusual, complex or beyond staff training, the Administrator consults the physician, home health agency or a licensed nurse, and also contacts the Department's licensing analyst when there is doubt whether Title 22 allows the condition.

For conditions that Title 22 allows only with specific requirements or an exception (such as certain treatments given by home health or a nurse), the Administrator confirms the requirement in writing, gets any required physician's order and consent, and obtains approval from the Department before admission or continued stay where the rules require it.

Staff who see signs of a possible prohibited condition in a current resident, such as a worsening pressure injury, a new feeding tube order, infection, a tracheostomy, or increasing dependence in all ADLs, report to the Administrator the same day (PD-04).
The Administrator arranges a reappraisal under AD-04, consults the physician, and decides within [NUMBER] days whether the resident can stay with additional services or must be relocated.

A resident with a terminal illness may stay on hospice only if the hospice agency, the physician and the resident or representative agree in writing, the hospice waiver requirements of Title 22 are met, and the Department's approval is in place when required. The Administrator reviews the hospice plan, staff training and supports (PD-07 and HC-04).
If a resident can no longer be retained, the Administrator gives the written notice and follows the relocation procedures in AD-08, and helps the resident and family find a suitable placement.

If the Department issues a relocation order, the Administrator complies, informs the resident and representative of the order and review rights, and keeps a copy in the file. The facility cooperates with the review process and documents the steps taken.
The Administrator reports the situation to the Department when a report is required (REC-02) and documents the incident under SAF-02.
The Administrator reviews this list at least annually and whenever the regulation changes, and updates staff training accordingly (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Screens for prohibited conditions, decides on admission and retention, obtains required approvals, and carries out relocation.
Watch for changes that may signal a prohibited condition and report them the same day.

responsibilities.role: Physician, hospice, home health or licensed nurse
responsibilities.duty: Evaluate the resident's condition and advise on safe management.

documentation: Screening result on the suitability determination
Physician and consultant statements
Reappraisal records
Hospice agreements and Department approvals where required
Written notices to resident or representative
Relocation orders and responses

policies.title: Admission Agreement, Rates, Deposits and Refunds
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admission staff, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident or representative receives a clear, lawful written admission agreement, with rates, services, refund terms and rights explained before the resident moves in.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] signs an individual written admission agreement with every resident or authorized representative, as required by 22 CCR §87507. This policy, with AD-01 through AD-06, meets LIC 281 item B9.0 (Admission Policies), by providing rates and refund policies and the information a resident or representative needs before entering. The agreement is in 12-point type, in plain language, with titled sections. It is signed and dated within 7 days of admission, and a copy is given to the resident or representative immediately. A copy, or a notice that it is available, is posted in the facility. The agreement contains no provision that waives the facility's liability and no provision that limits the resident's personal rights (RD-01).

definitions.definition: The written contract between the facility and the resident or representative describing services, rates, payment terms and rights.
The services included in the base rate, as listed in PD-02.
Optional services and items for which an extra charge is made, listed in the agreement with the price (PD-02).
Any fee collected before admission, which is limited and refundable as the agreement and Title 22 specify.

procedures: Before the resident moves in, the Administrator gives the prospective resident or representative a blank copy of the admission agreement and the rate schedule, and invites them to take time to read it and ask questions or consult an attorney, family member or the Ombudsman.
The agreement is prepared in 12-point type or larger, in plain language, with titled sections, and uses the facility's approved template reviewed annually (GOV-03).

The agreement states the basic services included in the base rate and each additional service with its price, and the monthly rate and how and when payment is due, including payment by the resident, a representative, SSI/SSP or other payor.

If the resident is enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, the agreement states that the waiver does not pay room and board and describes the room and board charge and the waiver service arrangements as set out in GOV-04.
The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] will give at least 60 days' written notice of any rate change, and that the same notice applies to changes in services that carry a charge.

The agreement describes any preadmission fee or deposit, the limits Title 22 places on it, and the conditions and timing for refund, including refunds on death, discharge or if the resident does not move in. Amounts are stated as [DOLLAR AMOUNT] and no amount is collected that is not in the agreement.
The agreement states the refund conditions on departure, including how unused prepaid amounts are calculated and returned and the number of days within which the refund is made.

The agreement includes the facility's visiting policy (SAF-05), the firearms policy, the grievance procedure (RR-01), the grounds for eviction and the notice and appeal rights (AD-08), and the right to contact the Department of Social Services and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, with current phone numbers (1-800-231-4024 for the CRISISline).
The agreement lists the resident's personal rights or attaches them (RD-01). It does not contain any clause that waives the facility's liability or limits the resident's rights.

If the pre-admission appraisal shows that the resident has a hearing or other disability, the Administrator includes the Department's required form LIC 9158 with the admission papers and records how the agreement was explained in an accessible way (RD-03).

The Administrator or designee goes through the agreement with the resident or representative, explaining each section, and uses an interpreter or translated copy when the person's language is not English.

The resident or representative signs and dates the agreement and the Administrator signs on behalf of [AGENCY NAME], no later than 7 days after admission. The Administrator aims to have it signed before or on the day of admission.
A complete copy is given to the resident or representative immediately upon signing, and the receipt is noted in the file.
The facility posts a copy of the agreement, or a notice that copies are available on request, in a place visible to residents and visitors at [LOCATION].
The original signed agreement is kept in the resident record (REC-01). The Administrator checks every new file within 7 days of admission to make sure the agreement is signed and dated.

When rates or terms change, the Administrator sends the written notice at least 60 days before the effective date, gets an updated acknowledgment, and files both. The Administrator reviews the template at least annually and when the law changes.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement template, reviews it with each resident, signs it, gives notice of rate changes and makes sure refunds are paid on time.
Prepare the packet, give copies, post the notice and file signed documents.
Read, ask questions, sign and keep a copy.

documentation: Signed and dated admission agreement
Rate schedule and list of additional services
LIC 9158 when required
Receipt for copy given to the resident
60-day rate change notices and acknowledgments
Deposit and refund records
Posted agreement or notice of availability

policies.title: Discharge, Eviction and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Licensee, Resident Care Staff, Business Office, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that any move-out, discharge, eviction or relocation of a resident is lawful, respectful, based only on permitted grounds, preceded by the required written notice, and carried out with help to the resident and the resident's representative.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes that a resident may move out at any time. The facility will end a residency involuntarily only on the grounds listed in the Title 22 eviction regulation and restated in each resident's admission agreement, and only after giving the written notice that regulation requires. The facility will not change the regulatory wording of the eviction grounds or notice rights. The only addition allowed is a general house policy that the regulation permits and that is stated in the admission agreement. The facility will never discharge, transfer, evict or reassign a room, roommate or restroom based on a resident's actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)); the Department cannot waive these protections (22 CCR §87468.1(d)). The admission agreement must state the eviction grounds, the resident's notice rights, and the right to contact CDSS and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (22 CCR §87507). When the Department orders relocation of residents, the facility will cooperate fully and follow the Department's order. Notice periods and form wording are taken from the current text of the regulation each time a notice is prepared, and the Administrator verifies them before issuing it. This policy is part of the facility's Admission Policies (LIC 281 B9).

definitions.definition: A resident's decision, or the decision of the resident's legal representative, to leave the facility. The resident may leave at any time.
Involuntary termination of a residency by the facility on a ground permitted in the Title 22 eviction regulation, after written notice.
A relocation of residents required by CDSS Community Care Licensing, for example when the facility's license is revoked or suspended or health and safety are at risk.

The person identified in the admission agreement and emergency information who is authorized to act or receive notices for the resident, such as a conservator, agent under a power of attorney, or responsible person.
A written facility rule stated in the admission agreement that the eviction regulation allows to be enforced as a ground for eviction when the resident fails to comply.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator gives the resident and representative the admission agreement. It states the eviction grounds exactly as worded in the regulation, the resident's notice rights, the right to move out at any time, and the right to contact CDSS and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (22 CCR §87507).

When a resident or representative says they want to move out, the Administrator meets with them within 2 business days. The Administrator records the requested move-out date, helps plan the move, and calculates any refund owed under the admission agreement.
The facility does not retaliate against any resident for a complaint, a call to the Ombudsman or CDSS, or a request for services.
When staff think a resident may no longer be appropriate, or a ground for eviction may exist, they report it to the Administrator the same day, in writing.

The Administrator reviews the resident's record, including the Needs and Services Plan, the most recent reappraisal, incident reports and any physician or consultant input. The Administrator documents the facts supporting the possible ground and whether reasonable steps (added services, a care conference, a referral, a plan to correct behavior) could resolve the problem without eviction.

The Administrator holds a care conference with the resident and representative to discuss the concern. If the concern is a change in the resident's condition, the Administrator follows AD-06 (Retention Limits and Prohibited Health Conditions) and AD-04 (Needs and Services Plan and Reappraisal).

The Administrator confirms that the proposed reason is not based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status, or on any other prohibited basis (22 CCR §87468.1(b); RD-03). Any such reason is rejected and documented, and the decision is escalated to the Licensee.

If the ground is nonpayment, a rule violation or conduct, the Administrator checks that the facts match the ground as worded in the regulation and the admission agreement. For a house-policy ground, the Administrator confirms the rule is in the signed admission agreement.

Before issuing any notice, the Administrator reads the current regulation text, confirms the correct notice period and required content for the ground, and records the ground and notice period on the notice worksheet. The Licensee reviews and approves every eviction notice before it is given.

The Administrator prepares the written notice in plain language and in at least 12-point type. It states the specific ground and facts, the effective date, and the resident's rights, including the right to contact CDSS and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (1-800-231-4024) and any right to contest the eviction or request a hearing that the regulation provides.

The Administrator delivers the notice to the resident and the representative in person or by the method the regulation allows, and has it dated and acknowledged in writing. If the resident or representative declines to sign, the Administrator notes that on the copy. The Administrator sends copies to CDSS and the Ombudsman to the extent the current regulation requires.

During the notice period the Administrator offers a care conference. They help the resident and representative identify appropriate placements, send records with the resident's consent, arrange transportation, and coordinate with the physician, hospice or home health agency, and the Ombudsman if requested.

The Administrator helps arrange the move so that the resident is not moved abruptly or unsafely. If the resident's safety is at immediate risk, the Administrator follows PD-04 (Medical Emergencies, Change of Condition and Hospital Transfer) and does not wait out the notice period.

On the move-out date, staff do a joint inventory of personal belongings with the resident or representative using the admission inventory (TL-01). They return all property, funds and medications belonging to the resident, as allowed by HC-01, and get a signed receipt.
Within the time stated in the admission agreement, the Business Office completes the final accounting and returns any refund or deposit owed, with an itemized statement.

When the Department orders relocation, the Administrator gets the written order, informs residents and representatives immediately, meets with the Licensing Program Analyst, notifies the Ombudsman, and follows the Department's timelines for relocating residents. The Administrator documents each resident's relocation destination and date.
Within 7 days of move-out, the Administrator completes the discharge summary and closes the record. The record is retained under REC-01. Any required reports to the state are made under REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Approves every eviction notice and makes sure the facility follows the regulation, the admission agreement and this policy.
Verifies the ground and notice period against the current regulation, issues and documents notices, coordinates relocation, and makes required notifications.
Report changes in condition or behavior promptly and in writing. They help residents prepare for moving and handle belongings carefully.
Calculates refunds and final accounting and returns funds on time.
Is given all notices, takes part in care conferences and helps plan the move.

documentation: Signed admission agreement showing the eviction grounds and notice rights
Eviction ground worksheet and notice period verification
Copy of the dated eviction notice with signed acknowledgment or note of refusal
Care conference notes and alternatives considered
Copies sent to CDSS or the Ombudsman, as required
Relocation assistance log and discharge summary
Move-out inventory with signed receipt and refund accounting

policies.title: Sample Menu, Meal Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Cook/Dietary Staff, Resident Care Staff, residents
policies.purpose: To show that [AGENCY NAME] knows how to plan balanced, appetizing meals with appropriate portion sizes and meal times, and to set out safe food handling and therapeutic diet practices.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 item B10.0 (Sample Menu, to show the applicant is familiar with balanced meals, acceptable portion sizes and general principles of good nutrition). It includes B10.1 (planned meals and snacks for one week using the four basic food groups), B10.2 (portion sizes), and B10.3 (times meals are served). The facility serves three meals and between-meal snacks daily. Each meal includes foods from the four basic food groups: milk and dairy, meat and protein, fruits and vegetables, and breads and cereals. Therapeutic diets are served only on the written order of a physician. Menus are planned in advance, posted, and kept on file.

B10.3 MEAL TIMES: Breakfast 7:30-8:30 a.m.; mid-morning snack 10:00 a.m.; lunch 12:00 noon; afternoon snack 3:00 p.m.; dinner 5:30 p.m.; evening snack 7:30 p.m. Fluids and a nutritious snack are available at any time on request.

B10.2 PORTION SIZES: Meat, poultry or fish 3 oz cooked; eggs 1 to 2; cooked vegetables 1/2 cup; salad 1 cup; fruit 1/2 cup or 1 medium piece; potatoes, rice or pasta 1/2 cup; bread 1 slice; cereal 3/4 cup cooked or 1 cup dry; milk or dairy 1 cup (8 oz); cheese 1 oz; yogurt 6 oz; beverage 6 to 8 oz; dessert 1/2 cup or 1 small serving. Larger or smaller portions are served by request or on physician order.

B10.1 ONE-WEEK SAMPLE MENU (four basic food groups at each meal; two snacks daily):
Monday - Breakfast: scrambled eggs, whole-wheat toast, orange juice, milk, coffee/tea. Lunch: baked chicken breast, brown rice, steamed green beans, fruit cup, milk. Dinner: beef and vegetable stew, dinner roll, tossed salad, applesauce, tea. Snacks: yogurt; banana and crackers.
Tuesday - Breakfast: oatmeal with raisins, toast, milk, sliced banana. Lunch: turkey sandwich on whole wheat, lettuce and tomato, vegetable soup, pear, milk. Dinner: baked fish, mashed potatoes, steamed carrots, bread, fruit gelatin. Snacks: cheese and crackers; fresh melon.
Wednesday - Breakfast: pancakes, scrambled egg, orange wedges, milk. Lunch: spaghetti with meat sauce, green salad, garlic bread, peaches, milk. Dinner: roast pork loin, baked sweet potato, steamed broccoli, roll, pudding. Snacks: apple slices with peanut butter; milk and graham crackers.
Thursday - Breakfast: cold cereal with milk, toast with jam, grapefruit juice. Lunch: tuna salad on bread, tomato soup, cooked zucchini, fresh fruit, milk. Dinner: meatloaf, baked potato, peas, whole-wheat roll, baked apple. Snacks: cottage cheese with fruit; oatmeal cookie and milk.
