Friday - Breakfast: scrambled eggs, hash browns, toast, orange juice, milk. Lunch: baked fish, rice pilaf, spinach, fruit cocktail, milk. Dinner: cheese and vegetable casserole, tossed salad, cornbread, sliced peaches. Snacks: yogurt and berries; cheese stick and crackers.
Saturday - Breakfast: French toast, sausage, banana, milk. Lunch: chicken noodle soup, egg salad sandwich, carrot sticks, applesauce, milk. Dinner: roast beef, mashed potatoes with gravy, green beans, roll, ice cream. Snacks: fresh fruit; pudding.
Sunday - Breakfast: omelet with cheese and vegetables, toast, melon, juice, milk. Lunch: roast chicken, stuffing, cooked carrots, salad, fruit pie, milk. Dinner: tomato soup, grilled cheese sandwich, coleslaw, pear halves. Snacks: yogurt; graham crackers and milk.
Coffee, tea, water and a salt substitute or pepper are available at every meal. Substitutions of equal nutritional value are offered for any item a resident does not eat.

definitions.definition: Milk and dairy products; meat, poultry, fish, eggs and other proteins; fruits and vegetables; breads and cereals.
A modified diet prescribed by a physician for a medical condition, such as a diabetic, low-sodium, renal or mechanical soft diet.
A diet in which food is chopped, ground or pureed on physician order for chewing or swallowing difficulty.
The written plan of meals and snacks for each day of a planned period, showing what will be served.

procedures: The Administrator or Cook plans menus at least one week in advance using the four basic food groups at each meal. The plan includes two or three snacks daily and takes into account residents' preferences, cultural and religious needs, and ability to chew and swallow.
The menu is dated, posted where residents can see it, and a copy is placed in the menu file. Any change is written on the posted menu and the file copy and must be of equal nutritional value.
Staff serve meals at the times listed in this policy, in a clean, pleasant dining area. Residents who cannot come to the dining area, or who are ill, are served in their rooms.
Staff serve the standard portion sizes listed above. Residents may ask for larger or smaller portions or seconds, and staff note any consistent change in appetite.
Staff give residents requested assistance with eating and keep adaptive utensils available. They never leave a resident who is eating with swallowing difficulty alone.

When a resident has a physician-ordered therapeutic diet, the Administrator puts a copy of the written order in the resident's file. The Cook receives the diet instructions in writing and prepares the diet exactly as ordered. A therapeutic diet is never started, changed or stopped without a physician order.
The Administrator informs all kitchen and care staff of each resident's diet, allergies and food intolerances using a diet card or list kept in the kitchen, updated within 24 hours of any change.

Staff record meals refused or poorly eaten and report weight loss, poor intake, choking, or problems with swallowing to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator notifies the physician and the representative as needed (PD-04, HC-03).
The Cook washes hands before handling food and uses clean utensils, gloves where appropriate, and cutting boards kept clean. Staff with symptoms of illness do not prepare or serve food (SAF-04).

Staff keep perishable food refrigerated at 40°F or below and frozen food at 0°F or below, check these temperatures daily with a thermometer, and write them in a log. Cooked food is held hot or kept cold until served, and leftovers are dated, covered and discarded within 3 days.
Staff store food, dry goods and utensils off the floor in clean, covered containers away from chemicals and cleaning supplies. The kitchen is kept clean and free of pests.
Staff keep at least a 3-day supply of nonperishable food and drinking water for emergencies and rotate it (EDP-01).
Staff keep drinking water and juice available to residents, and offer fluids and snacks between meals. Fresh fruit is offered with every meal when possible.

Menus are kept for the period required by REC-01. The Administrator reviews menus every quarter, with resident input in resident meetings, to ensure variety and nutrition, and a consulting dietitian is used when a resident needs a complex diet.

Before adopting this policy, the Administrator pulls the current Food Services requirements in Title 22 (Chapter 8, Article 10) and verifies that the storage, sanitation and diet content in this policy matches the current text.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures menus are planned, posted and filed, therapeutic diet orders are on file, and the kitchen is run in compliance with Title 22.
Prepare and serve meals according to the menu, portion sizes and diet orders, and keep the kitchen clean and food safe.
Assist with eating, watch intake, and report changes.
Writes orders for any therapeutic diet.

documentation: Weekly menu with date, as served and with changes noted
Physician orders for therapeutic diets
Resident diet and allergy list
Refrigerator and freezer temperature log
Intake and weight concern notes
Emergency food and water supply inventory

policies.title: Control of Property, Lease and Ownership Documentation
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, Owner of the property
policies.purpose: To document that [AGENCY NAME] has legal control of the property where the facility operates and that the property may be used as a residential care facility for the elderly.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B11.1 (name and address of the owner of the facility property), B11.2 (copy of the lease or rental agreement that does not preclude use of the property as a facility or prevent compliance with regulations) and B11.3 (proof of ownership when the applicant owns the property, showing the facility street address). The facility will have legal control of the property at [ADDRESS] for as long as it is licensed. The owner of the property is [PROPERTY OWNER NAME], whose address is [OWNER ADDRESS]. Where the Licensee leases the property, the lease or rental agreement will allow use of the property as a residential care facility for the elderly and will not prevent the facility from complying with licensing regulations, including repairs, safety modifications and any changes required for fire clearance. Where the Licensee owns the property, proof of ownership showing the facility's street address will be on file. The Licensee will tell CDSS Community Care Licensing about changes in control of the property as required.

definitions.definition: The legal right, through ownership or a lease or rental agreement, to occupy and use the property as a licensed facility.
A deed, property tax bill or similar document showing the applicant as owner and the facility street address.
A written agreement between the property owner and the Licensee permitting the Licensee to occupy and operate the facility. There is no minimum length.

procedures: Before choosing a property, the Licensee confirms the building's location, size and layout are suitable for the licensed capacity and for a residential care use.

The Licensee checks local zoning with the city or county planning department. A home serving 6 or fewer residents is treated as a residential use under California law. For a home serving 7 or more, the Licensee confirms zoning or use-permit requirements in writing with the planning department and keeps the response.

If the Licensee will own the property, the Licensee obtains a copy of the recorded deed or the current property tax bill. The Licensee checks that the document shows the facility's street address and the owner's name, and places it in the licensing file (B11.3).

If the Licensee will lease or rent the property, the Licensee negotiates a written lease or rental agreement with the owner. The Licensee reviews it before signing to confirm that it does not forbid use as a residential care facility and does not prevent compliance with licensing regulations (B11.2).

The Licensee confirms the lease allows the owner's consent for repairs, installation of safety equipment such as smoke alarms, grab bars and exit modifications, and inspections by CDSS and the fire authority.

The Licensee records the full name and mailing address of the property owner on the application and on the facility's property record (B11.1). If the owner is a business, the Licensee records the entity name and a contact person.
The Licensee attaches a complete copy of the lease or rental agreement, with all pages and signatures, or the proof of ownership, to the license application.
The Administrator keeps the original lease or ownership documents in the facility's administrative file and a copy at the facility for review by the Licensing Program Analyst.
The Licensee reviews the lease at least annually, tracks the term and renewal date, and starts any renewal at least 90 days before expiration so that control of the property is not interrupted.

The Licensee notifies CDSS Community Care Licensing in writing of any change of ownership of the property, lease termination, or lease amendment that affects use of the property, and gives residents notice if the change could affect their residency.
The Administrator updates the property record and posts any updates to the file within 10 days of the change.

responsibilities.duty: Secures and maintains legal control of the property and ensures lease terms support licensed use.
Keeps lease or ownership documents on file and available, and tracks lease renewal dates.
Allows use of the property as a facility and cooperates with repairs and safety modifications required for compliance.

documentation: Name and address of property owner
Lease or rental agreement (complete copy)
Deed or property tax bill showing the facility street address
Zoning or planning department correspondence
Lease renewal tracking record

policies.title: Physical Plant, Maintenance, Housekeeping and Laundry
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, Maintenance and Housekeeping Staff, Resident Care Staff
policies.purpose: To keep the building, grounds and equipment safe, clean, comfortable and in good repair, and to meet California's physical plant requirements for bedrooms, bathrooms, temperatures, water and fire clearance.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will maintain the physical plant in a safe, sanitary and good working condition at all times. No more than 2 residents will share a bedroom. The facility will provide at least 1 toilet and washbasin for every 6 persons and at least 1 tub or shower for every 10 persons, counting live-in staff and family members who use the same fixtures (22 CCR §87307). The facility will keep indoor heat at 68°F or higher and hot water at the resident-accessible taps between 105°F and 120°F, and will maintain the plant to the standards in 22 CCR §87303. If the facility uses a private water supply and has a capacity of 7 to 15, the water will be tested at least annually. The facility will hold a fire clearance before licensure and a separate fire clearance before accepting or keeping any nonambulatory or bedridden resident (22 CCR §87202). The facility will comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) in its provision of reasonable accommodation to residents with disabilities and in any alterations it makes.

definitions.definition: A person who is unable to leave a building unassisted under emergency conditions, including a person who depends on a wheelchair or other device, or who is bedridden.
Written approval from the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal that the facility meets fire safety requirements for the licensed use and for the residents served.
A water source that is not supplied by a public water system, such as a well.
A change in rules, practices or physical features that allows a person with a disability to use and enjoy the facility equally.

procedures: The Administrator inspects the interior, exterior and grounds weekly using a written checklist. The checklist covers floors, walls, ceilings, lighting, handrails, grab bars, steps, walkways, doors, windows, screens, furniture, appliances and common areas. Hazards are corrected the same day or the area is blocked off until repaired.

Staff report any broken, unsafe or malfunctioning item to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator writes it in the maintenance log with the date, a description, who is repairing it and the date it was fixed.

The Administrator checks that bedrooms house no more than 2 residents each, that each bed is a proper bed with a clean mattress, and that each resident has storage space for clothing and belongings. No room is used for resident sleeping unless it meets the building and fire requirements.

The Administrator counts toilets, washbasins and tubs or showers against the number of persons who use them, including live-in staff and family. The facility must have at least 1 toilet and washbasin per 6 persons and 1 tub or shower per 10 persons. The count is updated whenever the census or live-in household changes, and admissions are held if the fixtures would fall below the ratio.
Staff keep bathrooms clean, stocked with toilet paper, soap and towels, and provide privacy. Grab bars, non-slip surfaces and call or help procedures are provided based on resident needs.

Maintenance staff check indoor temperature each day and keep the heat at 68°F or above whenever residents are present. They note the reading in the log when it is below 68°F and correct it immediately, moving residents to a warm area if necessary.

Maintenance staff test hot water at the resident taps weekly with a thermometer. Water must be between 105°F and 120°F. They adjust the water heater if outside that range and write down the result and the correction.

If the facility uses a private water supply and its capacity is 7 to 15, the Administrator arranges testing of the water at least annually, files the lab report, and corrects any failed result right away, using bottled water in the meantime and informing the Licensing Program Analyst as required.

Before accepting or keeping any nonambulatory or bedridden resident, the Administrator confirms the facility's fire clearance covers such residents. If not, the Administrator obtains a separate fire clearance from the local fire authority first (22 CCR §87202). The Administrator keeps the clearance on file.

Housekeeping staff clean resident rooms, bathrooms, kitchen and common areas daily and as needed using approved cleaning products. They store cleaning supplies, chemicals and toxic materials in a locked or otherwise inaccessible area away from food and medications.

Staff wash and change bed linens at least weekly and whenever soiled, and wash towels and clothing as often as needed. Soiled and clean laundry are kept separate, soiled items are handled with gloves, and laundry is washed on settings that follow infection control rules (SAF-04). Residents' clothing is marked and returned to the correct resident.
Staff dispose of garbage daily in covered containers and remove it from the premises regularly. The Administrator contracts with a pest-control service as needed and records each treatment.
The Administrator keeps exits, hallways and walkways clear and well lit, and checks fire extinguishers, smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms monthly under EDP-02.

When a resident with a disability asks for a change to the facility, such as a ramp, grab bar, or a rule exception, the Administrator considers the request promptly, discusses it with the resident, and approves it unless it would cause undue hardship or a direct safety threat. The Administrator records the request and decision. Alterations are made with the owner's consent (CP-01) and with any required permits.
The Administrator reviews the maintenance log monthly and presents recurring problems and capital repair needs to the Licensee.

responsibilities.duty: Funds necessary repairs, ensures the building meets licensing requirements, and holds the fire clearances.
Directs maintenance, inspects the building weekly, confirms fixture ratios, temperatures and water standards, and makes sure the fire clearance matches the residents served.
Perform repairs, cleaning and laundry, and record temperatures and maintenance activity.
Report hazards and resident concerns about the environment immediately.

documentation: Weekly building inspection checklist
Maintenance and repair log
Indoor temperature and hot water temperature logs
Fixture and bedroom occupancy count
Private water supply test results, if applicable
Fire clearance, including any separate clearance for nonambulatory or bedridden residents
Pest-control service records
ADA accommodation requests and decisions

policies.title: Insurance Information and Coverage
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, Business Office
policies.purpose: To state what insurance covers the operation of the facility and to make sure required coverage is in force and kept current.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B13 (Insurance Information, RCFE only): a statement of whether insurance will cover the facility operation, and if so, the type of coverage and with whom. Insurance will cover the facility operation. [AGENCY NAME] will carry general and professional liability insurance for the facility with [INSURANCE CARRIER], policy number [POLICY NUMBER], in amounts of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 in the aggregate for injury to residents and guests caused by the negligence of the licensee or its employees (HSC §1569.605). The facility will carry workers' compensation insurance as California law requires once it has employees. The facility will not require residents or their representatives to waive the facility's liability in the admission agreement. The Licensee will keep coverage in force at all times the facility is licensed.

definitions.definition: The most the insurer will pay for a single incident or event.
The most the insurer will pay for all covered claims in a policy period.
Insurance that pays medical costs and lost wages to employees injured on the job.
A document from the insurer showing the type of coverage, limits, policy period and insured.

procedures: Before applying for the license, the Licensee asks an insurance broker or carrier for a quote for liability insurance for an RCFE with the facility's licensed capacity, and confirms it meets the required limits of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 aggregate.
The Licensee buys the coverage, records the type of coverage, the carrier's name, the policy number and the policy period, and states this in the application (B13).

The Licensee asks the broker or carrier to confirm in writing that the policy covers the services provided, including assistance with self-administered medications, transportation by the facility if offered, and incidents involving staff, residents and guests.
Before the first employee starts work, the Licensee obtains workers' compensation coverage, confirms the coverage requirement with the carrier or broker, and puts the certificate on file.
The Administrator keeps a copy of the certificate of insurance and the policy declarations page in the administrative file and gives a copy to the Licensing Program Analyst on request.

If a staff or contract driver transports residents in a vehicle, the Licensee confirms that the vehicle is covered by an automobile policy that includes residents, and verifies that the driver has a valid license (PD-06).

The Business Office puts the renewal date on a calendar, requests renewal quotes at least 60 days before expiration, and confirms coverage before the old policy ends. The Administrator reviews the new certificate on receipt.

The Administrator reports any incident that could lead to a claim, such as a resident injury, a property damage event or an allegation of negligence, to the Licensee on the same day. The Licensee notifies the carrier according to policy terms and as early as possible (SAF-02).
The admission agreement will not include a clause that waives the facility's liability. The Administrator checks every admission agreement before it is used (AD-07).
The Licensee reviews coverage limits annually and after any change in capacity, services offered or number of employees, and adjusts the policy when needed.
If coverage lapses or is cancelled, the Licensee informs the Administrator right away, replaces the coverage without gap, and contacts CDSS Community Care Licensing as required.

responsibilities.duty: Buys and maintains required liability and workers' compensation coverage and reports claims to the carrier.
Keeps certificates on file, reports incidents that may lead to claims, and makes sure no liability waiver appears in agreements.
Tracks renewal dates and premium payments.

documentation: Certificate of insurance and declarations page for liability coverage
Workers' compensation certificate
Automobile coverage certificate, if the facility transports residents
Renewal calendar
Claim and incident notification records

policies.category: B14 Theft and Loss Policy (RCFE only)
policies.title: Theft and Loss Policy
policies.applies_to: Administrator, All Staff, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To protect residents' personal property and money from theft and loss, and to set out how property is inventoried, marked, stored, documented and returned.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B14 (Theft and Loss Policy, RCFE only) and includes each of the required provisions: inventory of personal property at admission; modification of the inventory; practices to safeguard personal property upon the resident's death; documentation and reporting of loss of personal property; method of marking personal property; and method for providing a secure area for safekeeping of resident personal property. [AGENCY NAME] will make every reasonable effort to protect each resident's belongings. Staff may not take, borrow, use or accept any resident's property or money. If the facility holds resident cash, it will keep receipts and accounting records and a separate account titled as the residents' money, without mixing it with facility funds, and will meet the requirements for the LIC 400 affidavit and LIC 402 surety bond (22 CCR §87217). Residents are not required to give the facility their valuables, and each resident may keep and spend their own money (22 CCR §87468.1).

definitions.definition: Items belonging to a resident, including clothing, jewelry, electronics, furniture, eyeglasses, hearing aids, dentures, mobility devices, documents and keepsakes.
A dated, written list of the resident's personal property, signed by the resident or representative and a staff member.
A locked place such as a locked drawer, cabinet or safe for items the resident chooses to store, with access limited to named staff.
Any missing, stolen or damaged property of a resident.

procedures: INVENTORY AT ADMISSION: On the day of admission, a staff member and the resident or representative list all personal property the resident brings, with a description, approximate value and condition for each item, including jewelry, electronics, hearing aids, dentures, glasses and mobility devices. Both sign and date the list, and the resident receives a copy.

MARKING PROPERTY: Staff mark clothing with the resident's name using a permanent marker or sewn-in label, and mark electronics and other valuable items with the resident's initials or name, a label, or a recorded serial number. Items that cannot be marked are described by photograph or serial number on the inventory.

MODIFYING THE INVENTORY: When a resident brings in, buys, receives, gives away or disposes of an item, staff update the inventory within 2 days and have the resident or representative initial the change. A full review with the resident or representative is done at least every 6 months and whenever the resident moves rooms.

SECURE STORAGE: The facility provides a locked drawer, cabinet or safe in [ADDRESS] for resident valuables, medications and documents the resident wants to store. Only the Administrator and a designated alternate hold the key or combination. Each resident also has a lockable space in their room when feasible. Staff advise residents not to keep large sums of cash or high-value items, and the facility will say so in writing when the resident declines safekeeping.
Items placed in secure storage are recorded on a receipt signed by the resident or representative and the staff member, and are returned only against a signed receipt.

RESIDENT FUNDS: When a resident asks the facility to hold cash, the Administrator enters it on a written receipt and in a ledger and keeps it in a separate account titled as the residents' money, not mixed with facility funds. Each deposit and withdrawal is receipted and balanced monthly, and the facility keeps the LIC 400 affidavit and LIC 402 surety bond as required (22 CCR §87217; TL-02). The resident or representative may review the account at any time.

STAFF CONDUCT: Staff may not borrow from, sell to, or accept gifts, money or property from a resident, and may not use a resident's property. Personal items belonging to staff are kept apart from resident areas. Violations lead to discipline up to termination and a report to authorities where there is suspicion of a crime (PP-06, SAF-01).

REPORTING A LOSS: A resident, family member or staff who finds that property is missing or damaged tells any staff member. That staff member notifies the Administrator the same day and writes down what is missing, when it was last seen, and where.
The Administrator searches the resident's room, laundry, common areas and any likely places within 24 hours, interviews staff on duty, and documents the search and results on a Property Loss Report.

If the item is not found within 48 hours, or if theft is suspected, the Administrator tells the resident or representative in person or by phone and in writing, and offers to file a police report. The Administrator calls law enforcement when a crime is suspected. If the loss involves suspected exploitation of an elder or dependent adult, the Administrator follows SAF-01 and reports within required deadlines.

The Administrator completes the Property Loss Report, which includes resident name, item, value, date and time, investigation steps, outcome and any report made, and gives the resident a copy. Reportable events are also recorded under SAF-02 and REC-02.

The Administrator reviews each loss to prevent a repeat, and reviews patterns of loss quarterly with the Licensee. The facility takes responsibility for losses according to the admission agreement and applicable law, and it does not ask residents to waive its liability for loss.

DEATH OF A RESIDENT: At the time of a resident's death, the Administrator secures the room and the resident's belongings, locks away valuables, medications and documents, and with a second staff member lists all items on the current inventory. The Administrator notifies the representative or next of kin and releases property only to the person legally entitled to it, such as the executor, administrator of the estate or person with a valid affidavit, against a signed receipt (HC-04).
The Administrator returns all funds held for the resident with a final accounting to the representative or estate, and keeps the signed receipts in the closed resident file (REC-01).
AT DISCHARGE: Staff review the inventory with the resident or representative on move-out, return all property and stored items against a signed receipt, and note any differences (AD-08).
All staff learn this policy during orientation (TR-01), and it is given to residents and representatives with the admission agreement.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees inventories, secure storage, resident funds, loss investigations and reports.
Follow this policy, do not take or use resident property, and report a loss immediately.
Help prepare the inventory, report missing items promptly and decide whether to use safekeeping.
Reviews loss reports and ensures proper accounting, bonding and affidavit requirements are met if the facility holds resident cash.

documentation: Admission personal property inventory signed and dated, and updates
Safekeeping receipts for stored items
Resident funds ledger, receipts and separate account records; LIC 400 and LIC 402 if funds are held
Property Loss Reports and search notes
Law enforcement report numbers
Death or discharge property inventory and signed release receipts

policies.category: B14 Theft and Loss Policy (RCFE only)
policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property Safeguards
policies.applies_to: Residential Care Facility for the Elderly (RCFE), all staff with access to resident money, valuables or personal property
policies.purpose: To protect the cash, valuables and personal property of every resident from loss, misuse and theft. To ensure that any resident money [AGENCY NAME] holds is bonded, kept apart from agency funds, and fully accounted for, as 22 CCR §87217 requires.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to keep and spend their own money and to keep their personal property. [AGENCY NAME] will not take control of a resident's cash or valuables unless the resident, or the person legally authorized to act for the resident, asks for that service in writing. If [AGENCY NAME] holds resident cash, it will first file the LIC 400 affidavit and the LIC 402 surety bond with the licensing agency. It will keep receipts and accounting records for every transaction. It will keep resident money in a separate account titled as the residents' money and will never commingle it with agency funds. Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts of money from, or use the money or property of any resident. This policy supports the Theft and Loss Policy (TL-01) and the handling-of-resident-money element of the Plan of Operation (22 CCR §87208). It follows the safeguards in 22 CCR §87217 and the title 22 provisions on commingling and bonding of resident funds.

definitions.definition: Cash, checks, benefit payments or other money belonging to a resident that [AGENCY NAME] holds or manages at the resident's request.
Mixing resident money with the money of the licensee, the facility or any staff member. This is prohibited.
The affidavit [AGENCY NAME] files with the licensing agency before it holds resident cash.
The surety bond [AGENCY NAME] files to cover resident cash it holds.
Jewelry, important papers, electronics, medications and other items of significant personal or monetary value.

procedures: The Administrator decides, and records in the Plan of Operation, whether [AGENCY NAME] will hold resident cash. If the answer is no, staff tell residents and families at admission that residents keep their own money, and no staff member may accept cash for safekeeping.

At admission the Administrator tells each resident, and the resident's representative, that the resident may keep and spend their own money. The Administrator also explains that [AGENCY NAME] will hold money only on a written request that the resident or representative signs and dates.

If [AGENCY NAME] will hold resident cash, the Administrator completes and files the LIC 400 affidavit and the LIC 402 surety bond with the licensing agency before the first dollar is accepted. Copies stay in the administrative file.
The Administrator opens a separate account titled as the residents' money. No agency operating funds, payroll, rent, or staff or owner money may be deposited in or withdrawn from this account.

Before accepting any resident money, the Administrator or designee completes the Resident Funds Authorization form. It records the amount, the purpose, who may request withdrawals, and the signatures of the resident or representative and the staff member.

The staff member who receives resident money counts it in front of the resident or representative, issues a numbered written receipt, and gives the resident the original. A copy goes to the resident's funds ledger.

The Administrator keeps an individual ledger for each resident showing the date, deposits, withdrawals, purpose, balance, and the initials of the staff member and the resident or representative for every entry.
Every withdrawal requires the resident's or representative's request and a signed receipt. Staff may not spend resident money for anything other than what the resident has requested or authorized.

The Administrator reconciles the resident funds account to the individual ledgers at least monthly. A second person who does not handle the money reviews and initials the reconciliation. Any discrepancy is investigated the same day it is found.
Staff keep resident cash that is on hand in a locked container or safe. Only the Administrator and one designated staff member have access, and the key or combination is not shared.

At admission, staff and the resident or representative complete a Personal Property Inventory listing clothing, furniture, hearing aids, eyeglasses, dentures, electronics and valuables. Both sign and date the inventory. The resident keeps a copy.
Staff update the inventory when items are added, removed or replaced. Staff review it with the resident or representative at each needs and services plan reappraisal.

Staff encourage residents to keep valuables out of the facility or in a locked space. Residents' rooms or lockable storage are available, and staff do not give out keys without the resident's permission.

Staff who learn of a missing item or money notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator follows the Theft and Loss Policy (TL-01), interviews those involved, documents findings, and notifies the resident and representative. Where the facts show a possible crime or financial exploitation, the Administrator also follows SAF-01 and REC-02.

When a resident is discharged or dies, the Administrator returns the resident's money and property to the resident or the legally authorized person within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days. This is done against a signed receipt and the final ledger and inventory, and the files are retained under REC-01.
The Administrator reviews the resident funds records and personal property inventories quarterly as part of the quality assurance review under GOV-03 and corrects any deficiency in writing.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the facility will hold resident money, funds the surety bond, and ensures agency money is never commingled with resident money.
Files the LIC 400 and LIC 402, maintains the separate resident account and ledgers, performs and documents reconciliations, and investigates any loss.
Receives and disburses resident money only with written authorization, issues receipts, and keeps cash secured.
Do not handle, borrow or use resident money or property, and immediately report missing items to the Administrator.
May keep and spend their own money, may request or end funds-holding service in writing, and may review their ledger on request.

documentation: LIC 400 affidavit and LIC 402 surety bond (if resident cash is held)
Resident Funds Authorization forms
Individual resident funds ledgers and numbered receipts
Monthly reconciliation records with reviewer initials
Personal Property Inventory for each resident, with updates
Theft/loss reports and investigation notes (see TL-01)
Discharge or death return-of-funds and property receipts

policies.category: B15 Neighborhood Complaint Policy (six or fewer, non-resident owner)
policies.title: Neighborhood Complaint Policy
policies.applies_to: RCFE serving six or fewer residents whose owner does not live in the home; administrators, licensee and designees
policies.purpose: To give neighbors a clear, reliable way to raise concerns about the facility, and to make sure [AGENCY NAME] responds to incidents and complaints immediately and keeps a record of its response.
policies.policy: This policy meets LIC 281 item B15 — Neighborhood Complaint Policy (LIC 281 (9/04) p.10 Section B table and p.20, B15). B15 applies to a non-resident-owner community care facility serving six or fewer persons. The Section B table marks it 'Required' for the RCFE column, so [AGENCY NAME] has confirmed its applicability. If the owner lives in the home, the Administrator will record in writing that the policy is not required and will keep this policy on file for voluntary use. [AGENCY NAME] will respond immediately to any incident or complaint raised by a neighbor. A set time is available each [FREQUENCY] when the owner, licensee or designee will meet with neighborhood residents (see step 5). Every complaint will be logged, reviewed and answered. No resident will be retaliated against because a neighbor complained.

definitions.definition: Any concern raised by a person living or working near the facility about noise, parking, traffic, odors, property upkeep, resident behavior, safety or any other effect of the facility on the neighborhood.
Acknowledging the complaint at the first contact and starting action to resolve it. A staff member or the Administrator must reach the complainant by phone or in person within 24 hours.
A person the owner or licensee has named in writing to act for them, such as the Administrator.
The written record of each neighborhood complaint and the response.

procedures: The Administrator confirms whether this policy is required, based on the owner's residence and the number of residents. The Administrator records the finding and date in the policy file.

The Administrator posts a notice, and gives it to adjacent neighbors in writing at opening and whenever contact details change. The notice gives [AGENCY NAME]'s name, the Administrator's name [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], a 24-hour phone number [PHONE], and the address [ADDRESS].
Any staff member who receives a complaint, in person or by phone, takes the complainant's name, contact details, date, time and concern. The staff member then tells the Administrator immediately.

The Administrator or designee contacts the complainant within 24 hours. If the matter involves an immediate hazard, such as a resident outside unattended, a fire or a medical emergency, staff respond at once and the Administrator follows PD-08, SAF-03 or EDP-02 as applicable.

The owner, licensee or designee will be available to meet with neighborhood residents at [DAY, TIME AND LOCATION, e.g., first Tuesday of each month, 6:00 p.m., at the facility]. This schedule is included in the written neighbor notice. Any change is given to neighbors in writing at least [NUMBER] days in advance.

The Administrator investigates the complaint promptly by reviewing staff schedules, incident records and the site. If the complaint concerns a resident, the Administrator protects resident privacy and shares no confidential information, following RR-02.
The Administrator takes corrective action. Examples are adjusting parking instructions, noise or smoking-area rules, landscaping and trash service, or coaching staff, and sets a target date.

The Administrator tells the complainant what was found and what was done, by phone or in writing, within [NUMBER] days. If the complainant is not satisfied, the Administrator offers a meeting with the owner or licensee.

The Administrator records every complaint in the Complaint Log. The entry includes the date and time received, complainant, nature of the complaint, staff who responded, actions taken, date resolved, and whether a meeting was held.
If a complaint alleges a licensing violation or resident harm, the Administrator also follows PD-08 and RR-01. Reports required by REC-02 and SAF-02 are made within the required deadlines.
If the licensing agency contacts [AGENCY NAME] about a neighborhood complaint, the Administrator cooperates fully, provides the Complaint Log on request, and documents the contact.
The Administrator reviews the log at least quarterly to identify recurring issues and reports trends to the licensee. The results are included in the quality assurance review under GOV-03.
Staff are told at orientation (TR-01) how to respond politely to neighbors and refer all complaints to the Administrator.

responsibilities.duty: Makes themselves or a designee available at the set neighbor meeting time and ensures resources are available to fix valid concerns.
Receives and responds to complaints, keeps the log, investigates, takes corrective action and communicates results to the complainant.
Treat neighbors courteously, record the complaint and notify the Administrator immediately.

documentation: Neighbor notice with contact details and meeting schedule
Neighborhood Complaint Log
Written responses to complainants
Meeting dates and attendance records
Applicability determination (owner residence and bed count)

policies.title: Governing Body, Licensee and Administrator Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Licensee, governing body, certified Administrator and designated substitute administrator
policies.purpose: To establish who is accountable for the operation of [AGENCY NAME], what the certified Administrator must do, and when the licensee must notify the licensing agency of changes and financial events.
policies.policy: The licensee and governing body hold final responsibility for compliance with Title 22 and the California RCFE Act. [AGENCY NAME] will employ an Administrator who meets 22 CCR §87405: at least 21 years of age, a high school diploma or equivalent, good character, and a valid administrator certificate. If the facility has 16 or more beds, the Administrator will also meet the added education and experience required. The Administrator will be on the premises a sufficient number of hours to manage the facility. When the Administrator is absent, a designated qualified substitute (identified on LIC 308) will be in charge. The licensee will make the notifications required by 22 CCR §87211 on time. This policy covers the governing body's accountability provision of Title 22 and the Plan of Operation's administrative organization element under 22 CCR §87208.

definitions.definition: The person, partnership or corporation that holds the RCFE license from CDSS.
The owner(s), board or other persons with legal authority over the licensee, who set policy and are accountable for the facility.
The certified individual responsible for day-to-day operation: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
A person who meets Administrator qualifications and is named on LIC 308 to be in charge when the Administrator is absent.
The corporate officer with principal management authority for a corporate licensee.

procedures: The governing body adopts these policies and the Plan of Operation, and approves any substantial change to either before it takes effect.

Before appointing an Administrator, the governing body verifies the person is 21 or older, holds a high school diploma or equivalent, has good character (background clearance), and holds a current administrator certificate issued by the CDSS Administrator Certification Bureau. Proof is kept in the personnel file (PP-03).
For a facility with 16 or more beds, the governing body also verifies the added education and experience required by 22 CCR §87405 before appointment.

The Administrator sets a weekly schedule showing sufficient hours on the premises to supervise operations, staff and resident care, and posts the schedule for staff. The governing body reviews it at least annually. The Administrator records time on the premises.

The governing body names a qualified substitute administrator and lists the substitute on LIC 308. The substitute's qualifications are verified and kept on file. The substitute is oriented to resident needs, emergency procedures and reporting duties.
At every absence, the Administrator tells staff who is in charge and how to reach the Administrator and substitute by phone. This information is posted at the staff station.

The Administrator maintains certification by completing 40 hours of continuing education every two years, using approved vendors, and keeps certificates and renewal records (see TR-02). The Administrator is responsible for renewal before expiration.

The Administrator directs staffing, training, admissions, resident care, medication assistance, records, finances, building safety and reporting. The Administrator is also responsible for ensuring compliance with licensing regulations.
The Administrator reports to the governing body at least quarterly on incidents, complaints, staffing, inspection results, financial status and quality assurance findings (GOV-03).

If an Administrator is replaced, the licensee notifies the licensing agency in writing within 30 days of the new Administrator's start (22 CCR §87211(g)). The notice includes the new Administrator's name and certificate number.
If the chief corporate officer changes, the licensee notifies the licensing agency within 15 working days (22 CCR §87211(h)).

The licensee gives written notice to the licensing agency and the person responsible for any resident within 2 business days of receiving any of the following: foreclosure, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy, a notice of rent default, or a utility shut-off notice (22 CCR §87211(d)–(f)). The licensee also gives notice to applicants before they sign the admission agreement. A civil penalty of $100 per day, up to $2,000, may apply for failure to notify.

The Administrator ensures that deaths, serious injuries, AED use, and incidents threatening resident welfare, safety or health are reported in writing within 7 days. Outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported within 24 hours. Fires and explosions are reported as required. Suspected abuse is reported within the 2-hour or 24-hour deadlines. See SAF-01, SAF-02 and REC-02 for the full process.
The governing body ensures annual license fees are paid (GOV-02) and that adequate funds, staff and supplies are available to meet the needs of residents.
The governing body reviews this policy at least annually and whenever rules change (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Holds final accountability for compliance, appoints a qualified Administrator and substitute, and makes the required notices to the licensing agency.
Manages daily operations, remains on the premises sufficient hours, maintains certification and reports to the governing body.
Takes charge during the Administrator's absence and carries out the same duties for resident safety.
Know who is in charge and how to reach the Administrator or substitute.

documentation: Administrator certificate and continuing education records
Proof of age, education and background clearance
LIC 308 designating substitute administrator
Administrator schedule and time-on-premises records
Notices to the licensing agency (new administrator, officer change, financial notices) with dates sent
Governing body meeting minutes and quarterly reports

policies.title: Licensure, Posting and Advertising
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator and any staff who prepare postings or marketing
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] is lawfully licensed before it operates, keeps its license current, posts required notices where residents and visitors can see them, and advertises accurately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not admit residents until it holds a valid RCFE license issued by CDSS Community Care Licensing. It will obtain the fire clearance required by 22 CCR §87202 before licensure, and a separate fire clearance before it accepts or keeps nonambulatory or bedridden residents. It will pay license fees on time under HSC §1569.185. It will operate within the Plan of Operation (22 CCR §87208) and seek approval before major changes. Required notices will be posted in a prominent place. Advertising will be truthful and will show the license number as the state requires.

definitions.definition: Approval from the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal that the facility meets fire safety requirements.
A person unable to leave a building unassisted in an emergency, including those who use wheelchairs or are bedridden, requiring a separate fire clearance.
The yearly date on which the annual license fee becomes due.
The written plan on file with licensing describing the facility's purpose, services, staffing and policies.

procedures: The Administrator submits the license application to the CDSS Centralized Applications Bureau (phone (833) 827-6084) with the required application fee ($990 for 4–6 beds; $1,486.80 for 7–15 beds) and the Plan of Operation.
Before licensure, the Administrator requests a fire clearance from the local fire authority and keeps a copy in the facility file. The facility does not admit residents until the license is issued.

If [AGENCY NAME] intends to accept or keep nonambulatory or bedridden residents, the Administrator obtains the separate fire clearance first. Without it, the facility will not admit those residents or retain a resident who becomes nonambulatory or bedridden (see AD-06).
The Administrator posts the original license in a prominent public area of the facility, where residents and visitors can see it.

The Administrator also posts, at eye level in a common area: the Personal Rights of Residents (RD-01), the California Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline 1-800-231-4024 with the local ombudsman telephone number [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE], the licensing agency's phone number, and the posted emergency exit plans (EDP-01, EDP-02).
The Administrator checks the postings monthly, confirms they are legible and current, and records the check. Staff replace damaged or outdated postings at once.

The licensee pays the annual license fee by each license anniversary: $495.60 for 4–6 beds or $742.80 for 7–15 beds. Payment is calendared 60 days ahead. If payment is late, a 50% late fee applies, so the Administrator escalates unpaid renewals immediately.
If the licensed capacity changes, the licensee notifies the licensing agency in advance, obtains approval, and pays the $25 capacity change fee.

The Administrator reviews the Plan of Operation whenever the program, bed count, services, staffing or building changes, and submits changes to the licensing agency as required before implementing them (see GOV-03).

Before publishing any advertisement, brochure, website or social media content, the Administrator reviews it for accuracy against the license, the Plan of Operation and the services actually offered. The advertisement shows the facility's license number.

Marketing materials may not promise services the facility cannot provide, may not describe care beyond what the license allows, and may not state that residents waive any rights. Rates and services listed in advertising must match the admission agreement (AD-07).
The Administrator keeps a copy of every advertisement with its publication dates for 3 years.
Staff direct all inspection and licensing visits to the Administrator or the substitute. Staff cooperate fully and give inspectors access to the facility, residents and records as the law allows.
The Administrator keeps the license, fire clearances, fee receipts and licensing correspondence in a licensure file that is available for inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Obtains and maintains the license and fire clearances and pays fees by the due date.
Posts required notices, reviews advertising, tracks renewal dates, and communicates changes to licensing.
Keep postings visible and undamaged and refer licensing visitors and media or marketing inquiries to the Administrator.

documentation: Original license and posting copy
Fire clearances (initial and nonambulatory/bedridden if applicable)
License fee receipts and calendar
Capacity-change correspondence and fee receipt
Monthly posting check log
Copies of advertisements with dates
Plan of Operation and approved revisions

policies.title: Policy Review, Document Control and Quality Assurance
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator and staff who maintain policies, records and quality checks
policies.purpose: To keep the Plan of Operation and all policies current and consistently followed, and to find and fix problems before an inspection does.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will review the Plan of Operation (22 CCR §87208) and every policy at least annually and whenever a rule, service or the building changes. It will control versions so that only current policies are used. It will run quarterly mock inspections of medication records, personnel files, appraisals and admission agreements. It will review the infection control plan (LIC 9282) at least annually, after an outbreak declaration, and at the licensing agency's request, as required by 22 CCR §87470. If [AGENCY NAME] needs relief from a regulation, it will ask the licensing agency for program flexibility in writing and will not act until it is approved.

definitions.definition: A system of version numbers, dates and approvals so staff use only the current policy.
Scheduled checks of records and practices against regulations and policy, with corrective action.
An internal review modeled on a licensing inspection.
The staff member named in the infection control plan who is trained by a qualified professional.
Written approval from the licensing agency allowing an alternative way to meet the intent of a regulation.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Policy Master List showing each policy ID, title, version, effective date, last review date, next review date and owner.

Each policy shows its version number and effective date. When a policy changes, the Administrator approves the change, updates the version, removes superseded copies from use, and archives the old version for at least 3 years.

The Administrator and governing body review every policy and the Plan of Operation at least once a year, on the calendar date [ANNUAL REVIEW MONTH]. The review also happens when a regulation, form, rate, service or building feature changes. Reviews are documented.

When a policy changes, the Administrator trains affected staff within [NUMBER] days. Staff sign an acknowledgment that they have read and understood the change, and the acknowledgment goes into the personnel file.

Every quarter, the Administrator or a designee who is not responsible for the records being checked performs a mock inspection. It covers at least: medication records and storage (HC-01, PD-05), personnel files (PP-03, PP-04), pre-admission appraisals and needs and services plans (AD-02, AD-04), and admission agreements (AD-07).
The reviewer uses a written checklist drawn from Title 22 and records each finding as compliant or not compliant, with the record or resident examined.

For each deficiency, the Administrator writes a corrective action with a responsible person and a due date. The Administrator verifies and documents completion, and rechecks the item in the next quarter.

The Administrator reviews incident and accident reports (SAF-02), resident and neighbor complaints (RR-01, NC-01), grievances, falls, medication errors and infection events each quarter to look for patterns and root causes.

The Administrator reviews the infection control plan (LIC 9282) at least annually, immediately after any outbreak declaration, and when the licensing agency requests it. The Infection Control Lead is trained by a qualified professional, and training for staff is updated as the plan changes (SAF-04).

If a regulation cannot be met as written, the Administrator submits a written program flexibility request to the licensing agency describing the rule, the reason and the alternative. The facility does not change its practice until the written approval is received. The approval is kept on file.

The Administrator presents a QA summary to the governing body at least quarterly. The summary covers findings, corrective actions, trends and the status of policy reviews. The governing body records its review in minutes.
The Administrator keeps QA checklists, corrective action records and policy review records for at least 3 years, or longer if required by REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Approves policies, reviews QA results, and provides resources for corrective action.
Maintains the master list and document control, runs reviews and mock inspections, and ensures corrective actions are completed.
Maintains the infection control plan and trains staff on it.
Use only current policies, complete training on changes and report problems they notice.

documentation: Policy Master List and version history
Annual policy and Plan of Operation review records
Staff acknowledgment of policy changes
Quarterly mock inspection checklists and corrective action logs
Infection control plan (LIC 9282) with review dates and outbreak-related reviews
Program flexibility requests and approvals
Governing body QA minutes

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Billing Integrity and Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, billing and admissions staff, and all staff who document services (if enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver)
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] bills and describes its services honestly, protects residents from misleading practices, and meets Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver (ALW) and federal home and community-based services (HCBS) requirements if it enrolls in the ALW.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prohibits false claims and misrepresentation to residents, families, payers and regulators. Charges will match the admission agreement required by 22 CCR §87507, which lists basic services, additional services and rates, requires 60 days' written notice of rate changes, and contains no liability-waiver provisions. Services will be billed only if they were actually provided and documented. This policy applies to every payer and is subject to federal Medicaid payment requirements (42 USC 1396b(l)). If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the ALW, its setting will meet the HCBS settings rule at 42 CFR 441.301(c), including a lease or agreement, privacy, resident choice, and access to food and visitors. The ALW does not pay room and board. The resident pays room and board, typically the SSI/SSP basic services rate ($1,444.07 per month in 2026). ALW providers must have licensed nursing staff on call or employed (HC-02).

definitions.definition: A bill, record or statement that misstates the services provided, the person who provided them, the dates, or the charges.

A DHCS program that pays an approved provider a daily tiered rate (Tier 1 $95.69 to Tier 5 $270.80 per day, on the 2025 rate sheet) for assisted living services to eligible Medi-Cal members. It does not pay room and board.
The federal requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c) for settings that provide home and community-based services.
The monthly amount, $1,444.07 in 2026, that residents receiving SSI/SSP typically pay for room and board. The resident keeps $182 for personal needs from the $1,626.07 grant.
The person designated to receive compliance questions and reports: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or a person named by the governing body.

procedures: The governing body designates a Compliance Contact. The name and phone [PHONE] are posted for staff. Staff may report a concern to the Compliance Contact or directly to the governing body.

At hire and annually, every staff member reviews this policy and signs an acknowledgment. Staff learn that falsifying records, billing for services not provided, or misleading residents is grounds for discipline and may be reported to authorities.

Admissions staff explain charges to the resident or representative accurately. Before signing, the resident receives the admission agreement in 12-point type and plain language, listing basic services, additional services and rates. Staff do not promise services the facility does not provide.

The Administrator ensures the admission agreement contains no liability-waiver provisions, gives 60 days' written notice of any rate change, and states refund conditions and the resident's right to contact CDSS and the ombudsman, as required by 22 CCR §87507 (see AD-07).

Billing staff prepare each invoice only from the signed agreement and the service records. A second person reviews invoices before they are issued. Charges for additional services appear only when the service was requested, agreed to in writing and delivered.

Staff who document services record them at the time or end of the shift, truthfully, with their own signature or initials. No staff member may document care for another person or alter a record after the fact. Corrections are made by a dated, initialed line-through.
The Administrator investigates any suspected billing error or overcharge within 5 business days, and refunds any overcharge to the resident or payer promptly in writing, with an explanation.

The Administrator screens new hires and current staff and contractors monthly against federal and state exclusion lists, such as the OIG exclusion list and the Medi-Cal suspended and ineligible provider list. Excluded individuals are not employed or contracted to provide care or billing for any payer.

No staff member may be retaliated against for reporting a compliance concern in good faith. The Compliance Contact documents each report, investigates it, and reports the outcome to the governing body. Reports may be anonymous.
The Administrator conducts a documented billing and documentation audit at least quarterly, as part of the quality assurance program (GOV-03), and corrects any problems found.
If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the ALW, the Administrator applies through DHCS (ProFacWAIVER@dhcs.ca.gov; WaiveProEnroll@dhcs.ca.gov) and does not bill for ALW services before enrollment is approved.

For ALW residents, the Administrator ensures the setting meets 42 CFR 441.301(c): each resident has a lease or residency agreement, privacy in their unit, choice in daily activities and services, and access to food and to visitors at any time (see RD-01, SAF-05, FD-01).

The Administrator states clearly in the ALW resident's agreement that the waiver does not pay room and board. The resident pays room and board, usually the SSI/SSP basic services rate of $1,444.07 per month (2026), with the resident keeping $182 for personal needs. The facility does not charge ALW residents for services the waiver covers.
The Administrator confirms that licensed nursing staff are on call or employed as the ALW requires, and ensures the licensed nurse oversight and delegation described in HC-02 is documented.

Staff provide ALW services only as authorized in the resident's care plan and track them in a service log that supports the tier billed. The Administrator keeps this log and supporting records for the period required by REC-01.
The Administrator reports credible evidence of fraud or overpayment to the governing body immediately, and with legal advice makes any required repayment or disclosure to DHCS or other payers.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Compliance Contact, sets the tone for honest billing and decides whether to enroll in the ALW.
Oversees billing, audits, exclusion screening and ALW requirements, and investigates reports of misconduct.
Charge only what the agreement allows, explain costs accurately and keep records.
Document truthfully, never misrepresent services, and report concerns without fear of retaliation.
Provides oversight and supports accurate documentation of nursing services.

documentation: Staff acknowledgments of this policy
Signed admission agreements and rate-change notices
Invoices, billing review records and refund records
Exclusion screening log
Compliance reports and investigation records
Quarterly billing and documentation audit results
ALW enrollment records, HCBS setting compliance records and nursing oversight documentation (if enrolled)

policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: All residents, authorized representatives, family, visitors, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident can raise a complaint freely, without fear of retaliation. It also protects residents' access to the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and to CDSS Community Care Licensing (CCL), and ensures complaints are resolved promptly and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects each resident's personal right to be told how to make a complaint to CDSS Community Care Licensing and to the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (22 CCR §87468.1). Residents may complain to the facility, CCL, the ombudsman, or anyone else, at any time and without retaliation. Ombudsmen and other advocates may visit residents privately at reasonable hours without prior notice (22 CCR §87468.1). The written grievance procedure is part of every admission agreement (22 CCR §87507), and the agreement also states the resident's right to contact CDSS and the ombudsman. Staff may not interfere with, discourage, or punish a resident or representative for making a complaint or contacting an outside agency. The facility cooperates with the ombudsman program under the federal Older Americans Act. This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction by a resident, representative, or family member about care, services, staff, other residents, charges, or the facility, whether spoken or written.
The state-designated advocate (California Department of Aging program) who receives and resolves complaints on behalf of residents of long-term care facilities. Statewide CRISISline: 1-800-231-4024.
The CDSS division that licenses and inspects RCFEs. The Adult and Senior Care Program (ASCP) can be reached at (916) 657-2592.
Any adverse action, threat, or change in treatment (e.g., room change, reduced attention, eviction threat) because a person made or considered making a complaint.

procedures: At or before admission, the Administrator gives the resident and representative the admission agreement, which contains the grievance procedure and the right to contact CDSS and the ombudsman, and explains it in plain language and the resident's preferred language.

The Administrator posts, in a common area where residents and visitors can see it, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline (1-800-231-4024), the local ombudsman telephone number ([LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE]), and the CCL contact information (ASCP (916) 657-2592 and the regional office, [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE]). The Administrator checks the posting monthly.

Staff tell any resident or representative who asks how to complain that they may complain to the Administrator, to CCL, or to the ombudsman. Staff give the numbers on request and help the resident place the call or write the letter if the resident asks.

Any staff member who receives a complaint records it the same day on the Grievance/Complaint Log form, noting date, who complained, a summary, and the resident's requested outcome, and gives it to the Administrator. Complaints may be anonymous.
If a complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member also follows SAF-01 immediately and does not wait for the grievance process.
The Administrator acknowledges the complaint to the person who made it within 2 business days.

The Administrator investigates by interviewing the resident and any staff or other witnesses, reviewing records, and examining the area of concern. Staff who are the subject of the complaint do not investigate it.

The Administrator gives the person a written response within 10 business days stating findings and any actions taken. If more time is needed, the Administrator explains why in writing and gives a date for the final response.
The Administrator tells the person in the response that they may take the matter to the ombudsman or CCL at any time, whether or not they are satisfied.

Ombudsmen and advocates who arrive without notice are welcomed, shown ID checks per the facility's visitor procedure (without delaying access), and allowed to meet with residents privately. Staff do not ask the purpose of the visit or restrict the visit to a specific resident.
Staff provide a private space for the visit and give the ombudsman access to residents who wish to see them. Staff do not monitor, listen to, or screen the visit.
The Administrator reminds all staff at orientation (TR-01) and at least annually (TR-02) that retaliation is prohibited and is grounds for discipline up to termination.
If a resident who made a complaint reports any change in treatment, the Administrator reviews it within 1 business day, corrects it, and documents the review.
The Administrator reviews the grievance log quarterly for trends and reports results to the Licensee under GOV-03.
If CCL or the ombudsman contacts the facility about a complaint, the Administrator cooperates fully, provides requested records within the time requested, and documents the contact.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the grievance procedure, postings, log and written responses; investigate complaints; prevent retaliation; cooperate with CCL and the ombudsman.
Listen to, record and forward every complaint the same day; never discourage or retaliate; give ombudsman and CCL information on request.
Review quarterly grievance trend reports and ensure corrective action.

documentation: Grievance/Complaint Log and written responses
Signed admission agreement showing the grievance procedure was provided
Photo or dated checklist of posted ombudsman and CCL information
Notes of quarterly grievance trend review
Staff orientation and in-service sign-in sheets on resident rights

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants of [AGENCY NAME] with access to resident information
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of residents' personal and health information and to preserve residents' rights to private telephone calls, mail and visits.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] safeguards resident records and discloses information only to persons authorized by the resident, by law, or by licensing requirements. Residents have personal rights to dignity, private phone calls, private mail, and private visits (22 CCR §87468.1), and the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507) explains these rights, the visiting policy and the grievance procedure. Where [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, for example if it bills Medi-Cal electronically, it also complies with the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164). [AGENCY NAME] obtains a written release before sharing records outside of required reporting. Required reports to CCL, the ombudsman, law enforcement and the local health officer are not delayed by confidentiality concerns. This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies a resident and relates to condition, care, finances, history, or placement, in any form (paper, electronic, spoken).

A health care provider, plan or clearinghouse that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, such as electronic Medi-Cal billing, and therefore must follow HIPAA.
A written, signed and dated permission from the resident or legal representative specifying who may receive what information and for what purpose.

procedures: The Administrator decides, in writing on the Privacy Determination form, whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, because it bills Medi-Cal electronically) and reviews that decision annually or when billing methods change.

If [AGENCY NAME] is a covered entity, the Administrator designates a privacy officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME]) and issues a Notice of Privacy Practices to each resident at admission, with acknowledgment documented.
All staff sign a Confidentiality Agreement before their first shift and receive privacy training at orientation (TR-01) and annually (TR-02).

Resident records (REC-01) are kept in a locked cabinet or password-protected system. Only the Administrator, designated staff and authorized professionals have keys or access. Records are never left unattended on counters, carts or screens.
Staff discuss resident information only with persons who need it to provide care, and only in locations where other residents and visitors cannot overhear.

Before any disclosure not required by law (for example to a family member who is not the representative, an attorney, insurer, or outside provider), the Administrator obtains a signed written release and files it in the resident record. Staff verify the identity of the requester before disclosing.
Staff may share information with a physician, home health or hospice agency, or emergency responders as needed for treatment in an emergency or for continuity of care, and document what was shared.
Required reports (SAF-02, REC-02) and access by CCL, the ombudsman or law enforcement are not blocked by this policy. The Administrator logs what was provided and to whom.
Residents' phone calls are private. Staff provide a phone or private space. Staff do not listen to calls.
Mail is delivered to the resident unopened. Staff do not open, read or withhold mail unless the resident asks for help.

Residents may receive visitors privately in their room or another private area at reasonable hours consistent with the visiting policy in the admission agreement. Ombudsmen and advocates may visit privately without prior notice (RR-01).

Staff do not post resident names, photographs, medical information or room numbers in public view and do not photograph or record residents without written consent. Staff do not post about residents on social media.

Staff who suspect or know of an improper disclosure report it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates within 2 business days, takes corrective action, and, where HIPAA applies, evaluates whether breach notification is required.
When records are discarded after the retention period (REC-01), they are shredded or securely deleted, and the Administrator documents the destruction.
Violations result in discipline up to termination under PP-06.

responsibilities.duty: Determine HIPAA status, secure records, approve releases, investigate improper disclosures, and train staff.
Maintain the Notice of Privacy Practices, handle access/amendment requests and breach evaluations.
Keep resident information confidential, disclose only as authorized, and report improper disclosures immediately.

documentation: Privacy Determination form
Signed Confidentiality Agreements
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments (if applicable)
Signed releases of information
Disclosure log
Breach investigation reports
Training sign-in sheets

policies.title: Medication Storage, PRN, Records and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator, trained medication-assist staff, and all staff who handle or store resident medications at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure medications are stored securely, that staff assist only within the limits of the law, and that PRN, record-keeping and destruction requirements are met.
policies.policy: Staff of [AGENCY NAME] only assist residents with self-administered medications. Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law, and never force, hide or camouflage medications (22 CCR §87465). Medications are kept in locked central storage in their original containers. PRN medications are given only under a signed, dated physician order on a prescription blank that states the symptoms, exact dose, minimum hours between doses and maximum doses in 24 hours. A medication record is kept at least 1 year. Destruction of discontinued medications is done by the Administrator and one other adult who is not a resident, and the destruction record is kept at least 3 years (22 CCR §87465). Staff who assist with medications complete the training required by HSC §1569.69. Our licensed capacity is [LICENSED CAPACITY]; this determines which training track applies. Day-to-day assistance steps are in PD-05. This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: Helping a resident who is able to direct their own medication, such as reminding, opening containers, handing the medication, and observing. It is not administering the medication for the resident.
A medication taken 'as needed' rather than on a schedule, given only under a physician order with the elements required by 22 CCR §87465.
A locked place, such as a locked cabinet or medication room, where resident medications are kept together, with residents' medications separated from one another.

procedures: Upon admission or when a new prescription arrives, trained staff verify that the label shows the resident's name, medication, dose, directions, prescriber and date, and that the container is the original pharmacy container.

Staff immediately place all medications in locked central storage. Medications are not left in common areas, in staff pockets, or in unlocked rooms. Keys are held only by the Administrator and designated trained staff.
Refrigerated medications are kept in a locked container or locked refrigerator, separate from food. Staff check the temperature daily and record it on the Refrigerator Log.
Each resident's medications are stored separately and labeled. External-use and internal-use products are kept apart. Staff do not transfer medication to another container or alter the label.

Residents who are capable and whose physician and Needs and Services Plan (AD-04) allow it may keep and take their own medications in their rooms, stored securely so other residents cannot reach them.

Staff record each medication assistance on the Medication Administration Record (MAR) at the time of assistance. Refusals, missed doses, errors and side effects are noted and reported to the Administrator and the physician the same day.
Staff may not force, hide or camouflage medications (for example, crushing into food) and may not give injections unless authorized by law. Any resident needing injections is addressed through HC-02.

For PRN medications, the Administrator confirms before first use that there is a signed, dated physician order on a prescription blank stating the symptoms, exact dose, minimum hours between doses and maximum doses per 24 hours. Staff call the physician when an order is incomplete, and do not give the medication until it is corrected.

Before giving a PRN, staff confirm the resident's stated symptoms match the order, check the time of the last dose against the minimum interval and the maximum for 24 hours, and record the symptom, time, dose and result on the MAR.

The Administrator checks the medication record monthly against physician orders and pharmacy labels and signs the review. Medication records are kept for at least 1 year and in the resident record under REC-01.

The Administrator verifies and documents training before any staff member assists with medication. For homes of 15 or fewer residents: 10 hours initial training, with 6 hands-on hours before assisting and 4 within 2 weeks, plus an exam, and 8 hours annually. For homes of 16 or more: 24 hours initial training, with 16 hands-on hours before assisting and 8 within 4 weeks, plus an exam, and 8 hours annually (HSC §1569.69).
When a medication is discontinued, expired, or a resident leaves or dies, the Administrator secures it in locked storage separate from active medications until destruction.
