Destruction is carried out by the Administrator together with one other adult who is not a resident. Both sign a Medication Destruction Record listing resident, medication, strength, amount, date and method of destruction. The record is kept at least 3 years.

If a medication is not destroyed, for example when returned to a pharmacy or released to a departing resident or representative, the Administrator documents who received it and when, and obtains a signature.

The Administrator keeps a first aid kit, posted emergency numbers and the ambulance number available. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health, including a serious medication reaction (PD-04).

Medication errors and unexplained discrepancies are reported to the physician and the person responsible, recorded on the incident form (SAF-02), and reviewed by the Administrator within 1 business day.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure locked storage, training, record review and compliant destruction; witness destruction.
Assist residents per the label and order, complete the MAR, report refusals and errors.
Verify and sign the destruction record; may not be a resident.
Issue complete orders and clarify medication questions.

documentation: Medication Administration Records (kept at least 1 year)
Physician orders, including PRN orders on prescription blanks
Refrigerator temperature log
Medication Destruction Records (kept at least 3 years)
Staff medication training certificates and exam results
Monthly medication record review
Medication error incident reports

policies.title: Nursing Services, Delegation and ALW Licensed Nurse Oversight
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, contracted licensed health professionals, and Assisted Living Waiver (ALW) participants of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define the limits of care that unlicensed staff may provide, how licensed health professionals are brought in, and the additional oversight required if the facility participates in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a residential care facility, not a nursing facility. Staff provide only incidental medical care as described in 22 CCR §87465: they may assist with self-administered medications and may not give injections unless authorized by law. Care for healing wounds and other restricted health conditions is provided only as permitted by the Title 22 regulations on restricted health conditions, which require appropriate licensed professionals, a physician's determination, and an updated Needs and Services Plan. [Confirm current regulatory text before adoption.] Conditions on the prohibited list (see AD-06) cannot be accommodated. Unlicensed staff never perform tasks reserved for licensed nurses or other licensed professionals. If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, it will have a licensed nurse available on call or employed to oversee ALW participants' care and, if it houses more than 6 ALW participants, an Individual Response System. ALW settings must also meet the HCBS settings requirements of 42 CFR §441.301(c), including a lease or agreement, privacy, resident choice, and access to food and visitors. ALW enrollment status: [ALW ENROLLMENT STATUS]. This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: Care that does not require licensed nursing, such as assistance with self-administered medication, first aid, and observing and reporting changes, within the limits of 22 CCR §87465.
A licensed professional's assignment of a task to another person. In this facility, unlicensed caregivers do not receive delegation of nursing tasks unless the task is expressly allowed by law.
A health condition that may be accommodated in an RCFE only under specific Title 22 rules, with licensed professional care and written conditions.
A Medi-Cal program administered by DHCS that pays for assisted living services (not room and board) for eligible participants in enrolled facilities.
An electronic emergency response system that allows a participant to summon help.

procedures: The Administrator reviews each pre-admission appraisal (AD-02) and each reappraisal (AD-04) to identify any health service needs beyond incidental medical care, and records the determination in the resident record.

Staff provide only the incidental care in 22 CCR §87465 and never give injections unless authorized by law. If a resident needs injections, a licensed professional, home health agency, or the resident, where allowed by law, provides them, and staff do not perform or substitute for them.

When a resident has a healing wound or other restricted health condition, the Administrator confirms before accepting or retaining the resident that it is allowed under the applicable Title 22 provisions, that the physician has described the care needed, and that a licensed professional will provide it. The Administrator then updates the Needs and Services Plan (AD-04) in writing. If it is not allowed, the Administrator follows AD-06 and AD-08.
The Administrator arranges licensed nursing or home health services through PD-07 and keeps contact information for each licensed professional in the resident record.
Licensed professionals document their own visits and orders. Staff follow written instructions from the professional, ask questions when unclear, and document observations in the resident record.
Staff do not accept verbal instructions to do tasks beyond incidental care. They tell the Administrator, who contacts the professional and, if needed, the physician.

Staff observe residents daily for changes in condition and report them to the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator contacts the physician and the person responsible and follows PD-04 as needed.
Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health or life and follow PD-04.
If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the ALW, the Administrator completes DHCS provider enrollment, keeps the ALW contact information current, and records enrollment on the ALW Status form.

Before serving ALW participants, the Administrator designates a licensed nurse ([LICENSED NURSE NAME AND LICENSE NUMBER]) on call or employed to oversee ALW participants' care, and documents the nurse's role, availability and contact information.
The nurse reviews each ALW participant's care plan and condition changes as required by the ALW program, and the Administrator keeps the nurse's notes in the resident record.
If more than 6 ALW participants will reside in the facility, the Administrator installs an Individual Response System, tests it monthly, and records test results on the Safety Equipment Log.

For ALW participants, the Administrator confirms that the admission agreement serves as a lease or agreement, and that residents have privacy, choice and access to food and visitors, as 42 CFR §441.301(c) requires. The Administrator documents any individually needed modification with the resident's consent.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and when licensing or ALW requirements change (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Decide whether a resident's needs fit incidental care; arrange licensed professionals; maintain ALW enrollment, nurse oversight and the Individual Response System, if applicable.
Oversee ALW participants' care and respond to condition changes as required by the program.
Provide only incidental care, observe and report changes, and never perform licensed tasks.
Provide orders and condition determinations.

documentation: Pre-admission appraisals and reappraisals
Updated Needs and Services Plans
Physician determinations for restricted conditions
Licensed professional visit notes and orders
ALW enrollment records and nurse designation
Individual Response System test log
Condition change reports

policies.title: Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Administrator and all direct care staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and prevent pressure injuries by identifying risk early, observing residents for changes, and acting promptly. It also ensures that residents who develop a prohibited skin condition are transferred appropriately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] observes residents for changes in physical, mental, emotional and social functioning and responds promptly, as required by the Title 22 observation requirements. [Confirm current regulatory text before adoption.] Stage 3 and stage 4 pressure injuries are prohibited health conditions, and a resident who has or develops one cannot be retained (22 CCR §87615); the facility arranges a transfer to an appropriate setting. Care of bedridden residents is allowed only as the Title 22 bedridden-resident rules permit and only with the separate fire clearance from the local fire authority. Postural supports are used only as the Title 22 postural support rules permit and only with a physician's order. [Confirm current regulatory text before adoption.] Restraints are never used for convenience or discipline (RD-02). This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: Damage to skin and underlying tissue from pressure or pressure with shear. Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable redness. Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss. Stages 3 and 4 involve full-thickness tissue loss, and these are prohibited health conditions.
A device used to achieve proper body position or balance, such as a seat belt or wedge, which is used only under a physician's order and the applicable regulation.
Any unplanned descent to the floor or ground, with or without injury, whether witnessed or not.

procedures: At pre-admission appraisal (AD-02) and every reappraisal (AD-04), the Administrator documents each resident's fall history, mobility, balance, vision, medications affecting alertness or balance, continence, and skin condition and risk factors such as immobility or incontinence.
The Needs and Services Plan (AD-04) lists individualized fall and skin-protection measures, such as assistive devices, scheduled toileting, repositioning, footwear and supervision levels.

Staff keep walkways clear, cords secured, spills cleaned immediately, lighting adequate (including night lights), and call and assistance devices within reach. Staff report hazards to the Administrator the same shift and the Administrator corrects them under CP-02.
Staff assist residents with mobility as the plan states and do not leave a resident at risk unattended in the bathroom if the plan calls for supervision.

Staff observe each resident daily, including at personal care, and report changes in walking, balance, confusion, appetite, weight, pain, or skin the same shift to the Administrator, who documents the report.
Staff check the skin of residents at risk during bathing and dressing and report new redness, blisters, breaks or sores right away. Staff do not treat open wounds themselves.

For residents who spend most of the time in bed or a chair, staff follow the written repositioning schedule, keep skin clean and dry, and use pressure-relieving cushions or mattresses as the physician or home health professional directs.
After any fall, staff check the resident without moving them if injury is suspected, call 9-1-1 for suspected serious injury (PD-04), and notify the Administrator immediately.

The Administrator notifies the physician and the person responsible the same day, completes the incident report (SAF-02), and submits the required written report within 7 days if a serious injury, as determined by the physician, or an AED use occurred (REC-02).
The Administrator reviews each fall within 2 business days to find the cause and updates the Needs and Services Plan and environment.
The Administrator reviews fall and skin data monthly for trends and records results for quality assurance (GOV-03).
If a resident develops a possible pressure injury, the Administrator arranges physician or home health assessment within 1 business day and documents the stage given by the professional.

If a stage 1 or 2 injury is diagnosed, the Administrator confirms with the physician and licensed professional that the care can be provided in the facility as Title 22 allows, and updates the Needs and Services Plan with treatment and monitoring instructions.

If a stage 3 or 4 pressure injury is diagnosed, the Administrator notifies the physician and person responsible immediately, and begins relocation planning under AD-06 and AD-08. The Administrator documents the date, the assessment and all notifications.

The facility does not admit or retain a resident who needs care in bed unless the Administrator has confirmed that the local fire authority has issued fire clearance for bedridden residents and the other Title 22 conditions are met. The Administrator keeps the clearance on file.

Staff use postural supports only with a written physician order, the Administrator's approval and the resident's informed consent, and never as a restraint (RD-02). The Administrator documents the order, the reason and ongoing review.

responsibilities.duty: Assess risk, update plans, review falls and skin changes, arrange professional assessment, and begin transfer for prohibited conditions.
Apply prevention measures, observe residents daily, and report changes and falls immediately.
Stage and treat pressure injuries and order postural supports or pressure-relief devices.

documentation: Appraisals and Needs and Services Plans listing fall and skin measures
Fall incident reports and reviews
Condition change and physician notification records
Physician and home health orders and assessments
Fire clearance for bedridden residents, if applicable
Postural support orders
Monthly trend review notes

policies.title: Advance Directives, Resuscitative Requests and Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: Administrator and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]; residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To honor residents' wishes about medical treatment and resuscitation, and to ensure a resident's death is handled with dignity, reported on time, and followed by safeguarding of the resident's property.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] honors each resident's advance directive and request regarding resuscitative measures as the Title 22 regulation on resuscitative measures requires. [Confirm current regulatory text before adoption.] Residents are informed of their right to make treatment decisions, consistent with the federal Patient Self-Determination Act, though the facility does not require an advance directive as a condition of admission. A death of a resident is reported in writing to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). If a resident is receiving hospice care, the facility notifies the hospice agency and the resident's physician, and operates under a Hospice Care Waiver approved by CDSS where required (22 CCR §87632). The facility safeguards the deceased resident's personal property. This policy has no separate official checklist items beyond the regulatory requirements cited.

definitions.definition: A written instruction naming an agent and/or stating a person's health care wishes if they cannot speak for themselves.
A resident's written request, such as a Prehospital Do Not Resuscitate form or POLST signed by the physician, that emergency personnel not perform CPR or other resuscitation.
A CDSS approval allowing the facility to care for residents receiving hospice, based on a written request stating the maximum number of hospice residents (22 CCR §87632).
The resident's legal representative, family member or other person designated in the admission agreement and emergency information.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator asks each resident whether they have an advance health care directive, a POLST or a resuscitative-measures request, and records the answer. The Administrator explains the resident's right to make or decline to make such decisions and that admission does not depend on having one.

If the resident provides a document, the Administrator places a copy in the front of the resident record and notes its location on the emergency information sheet (AD-05). The Administrator also tells all staff on duty.

A request regarding resuscitative measures is honored only if it is a valid document signed by the resident or authorized representative and, where required, the physician. The original or a visible copy is kept where emergency personnel can find it quickly, as the resident or physician directs.

Staff who find a resident unresponsive call 9-1-1 and follow PD-04. They give emergency personnel the valid resuscitative-measures form immediately, if one exists. Staff do not make decisions about resuscitation on their own.

If a resident wants to create or change a directive, the Administrator helps the resident contact the physician, an attorney or the person they choose. Staff do not give legal or medical advice, do not witness documents unless allowed by law, and do not pressure the resident.
The Administrator reviews directives at each reappraisal (AD-04) and after any hospitalization and updates the record if the resident changes their wishes.

When a death occurs, staff call 9-1-1 if the death is unexpected or the resident has no resuscitative-measures request. For an expected death of a hospice resident, staff call the hospice agency. Staff notify the Administrator immediately.

The Administrator notifies the physician, the person responsible, and, for a hospice resident, the hospice agency, as soon as possible and records the date, time and people contacted. If the death requires a coroner or medical examiner report, the Administrator cooperates and follows their instructions.

The Administrator files a written report with CCL and sends a copy to the person responsible within 7 days of the death, using the incident report form (LIC 624 or its equivalent), and keeps a copy in the resident record (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). If the death involved suspected abuse, a poisoning, an outbreak, or a catastrophe, the Administrator also follows the shorter deadlines in SAF-01, SAF-02 and REC-02.
If the death involved an AED use, the same written report within 7 days applies.

If the facility will serve residents receiving hospice, the Administrator submits a written request to CDSS for a Hospice Care Waiver before accepting hospice residents, stating the maximum number of hospice residents. CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request. The Administrator keeps the approved waiver and conditions on file, and does not exceed the approved number (PD-07).
Staff treat the deceased resident with respect. The room is kept private until the funeral home or coroner removes the body, and other residents are informed with sensitivity.

The Administrator secures the deceased resident's room, personal property, valuables, funds and medications. Two staff inventory the property, the Administrator signs the inventory, and items are kept in a secure place (TL-02). Medications are destroyed under HC-01.

Property and funds are released only to the person authorized by law, such as the executor or successor, who signs a receipt. The Administrator documents the release. The Administrator handles any refund owed under the admission agreement (AD-07).
The Administrator offers support to staff and residents after a death and records the closure of the resident record. The record is retained as REC-01 requires.

responsibilities.duty: Ask about directives, keep documents accessible, make notifications, file the 7-day death report, request and keep any Hospice Care Waiver, and safeguard property.
Know where directives are kept, call 9-1-1 or hospice as appropriate, show valid forms to emergency personnel, and notify the Administrator at once.
Sign orders and resuscitative-measures forms, pronounce death where appropriate, and coordinate end-of-life care.

documentation: Copies of advance directives, POLST and resuscitative-measures forms
Admission checklist entry on directives
Notification log for death (time, person, agency)
Written death report to CCL and person responsible (within 7 days)
Hospice Care Waiver request and CDSS approval
Property inventory and release receipts

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and consultants of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect every resident from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure that every suspected incident is reported to the right agencies within the required time. Residents have a right to be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse (22 CCR §87468.1).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, intimidation or exploitation of any resident by staff, other residents, visitors, family or anyone else. All staff are care custodians and mandated reporters under Welfare and Institutions Code §15630. Each staff member has a personal duty to report. A staff member may not hand the duty to a supervisor, and no one may stop or discourage a report. Suspected physical abuse of a resident is reported to the local long-term care ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement. The report is made by phone within 2 hours if the abuse involves serious bodily injury, and otherwise within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(b),(c)). A written report on form SOC 341 follows within the time the statute allows. Other suspected abuse, neglect or financial exploitation is reported by phone immediately or as soon as practicably possible under W&I Code §15630. Psychological abuse and any other incident that threatens a resident's welfare, safety or health is also reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1); see SAF-02). The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports in good faith.

definitions.definition: A person who is legally required to report suspected abuse of an elder or dependent adult. All [AGENCY NAME] staff are mandated reporters as care custodians.
Includes physical abuse, sexual abuse, abandonment, isolation, abduction, financial exploitation, neglect (including self-neglect) and psychological or mental suffering.

An injury involving a substantial risk of death, unconsciousness, extreme physical pain, protracted loss or impairment of the function of a body part, organ or mental faculty, or an injury needing hospitalization or surgery. When in doubt, treat the injury as serious and use the 2-hour deadline.
The state form for the written report of suspected dependent adult or elder abuse.
The resident's authorized representative, conservator, agent under a power of attorney, or family contact named in the resident's record.

procedures: Prevention at hiring: The Administrator makes sure every employee has cleared screening and background requirements before working with residents (PP-03).

Prevention at orientation: Each new employee completes training on resident rights and on recognizing and reporting abuse during orientation (TR-01). The employee signs the mandated reporter acknowledgment (SOC 341A) and the Administrator files it in the personnel record. Refresher training is given at least annually (TR-02).

Prevention in daily care: Staff treat residents with dignity, use each resident's preferred name and pronouns, and never use punishment, humiliation, threats or intimidation. The Administrator or designee observes care and resident-staff interactions on every shift and addresses concerns at once.

Warning signs: Staff watch for unexplained bruises, fractures, burns, weight loss, dehydration, pressure injuries, fearfulness, withdrawal, sudden changes in finances or property, and statements by a resident that someone hurt, threatened or took from them. Staff document what they see in the resident record.

Immediate safety: If a resident is in immediate danger or needs urgent medical care, staff call 9-1-1 first and give first aid. The staff member then separates the resident from the alleged abuser. Alleged staff abusers are removed from resident contact right away.

Phone report: The staff member who suspects or witnesses the abuse, or who is told of it, phones the local long-term care ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement. This is done within 2 hours if there is serious bodily injury, otherwise within 24 hours. The staff member makes the call personally and does not wait for the Administrator.

Ombudsman contact: The California Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline is 1-800-231-4024. The local ombudsman phone is [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE]. The licensing agency is the CDSS Community Care Licensing regional office at [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE]. Local law enforcement is [LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT PHONE]. These numbers are posted at [LOCATION OF POSTED EMERGENCY NUMBERS].

Written report: The reporting staff member completes form SOC 341 promptly and sends it to the required agencies within the statutory deadline. The reporter keeps the confirmation of transmission. The Administrator checks that the report was sent.

Licensing written report: The Administrator completes the licensing agency's incident report form (LIC 624) and sends it to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days, as described in SAF-02.

Notify the person responsible: The Administrator or designee tells the person responsible for the resident about the incident and the reports made, unless that person is the suspected abuser. In that case the Administrator takes direction from law enforcement and the ombudsman.

Preserve evidence: Staff do not clean, move or discard items that may be evidence, and do not alter records. Staff write a factual statement of what they saw or heard, with date and time, and give it to the Administrator.

Cooperate and protect: The Administrator cooperates fully with law enforcement, the ombudsman, adult protective services and the licensing agency. The agency does not conduct its own interrogation that could interfere with their work. The Administrator takes steps to protect the resident and others, such as changing assignments, increasing supervision or relocating a resident.

Resident-on-resident incidents: Staff treat physical or sexual aggression between residents as suspected abuse and report it under this policy. The Administrator reviews both residents' needs and services plans and the placement (AD-04, AD-06).
Financial exploitation: Staff report suspected misuse of a resident's money or property. Staff do not accept gifts, loans or financial control from residents (PP-06, TL-02).

Anti-retaliation: The Administrator does not discipline, threaten or retaliate against any employee, resident or family member who reports a concern in good faith. Any retaliation is itself a violation subject to discipline up to termination.

Review: Within 7 days of any report, the Administrator reviews the event for causes and corrective action. The Administrator records the outcome in the incident log and in the quality assurance review (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Act as mandated reporters. Watch for and report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation by phone within the required time, complete the SOC 341, and never delay or discourage a report.
Train staff, confirm that phone and written reports were made, send the 7-day written report to licensing and the person responsible, protect residents, prevent retaliation and review each case.
Make sure residents are safe and separated from any alleged abuser, check that the reporting staff member has made the calls, and preserve evidence.
Support a culture of reporting, make sure resources and training are provided, and receive summary reports of incidents.

documentation: Completed SOC 341 forms and proof of transmission
Log of phone reports with date, time, agency and person spoken to
LIC 624 incident reports
Signed mandated reporter acknowledgments (SOC 341A) in personnel files
Training attendance records on abuse recognition and reporting
Internal incident log entry and administrator's review notes
Record of notification to the person responsible

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, with report completion by the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident, accident, death, outbreak, fire or catastrophe is responded to, recorded and reported to the right agencies and to the person responsible within the deadlines in 22 CCR §87211.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports incidents as 22 CCR §87211 requires. (1) A written report is sent to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days of any death, any serious injury as determined by the physician, any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED), or any incident that threatens the welfare, safety or health of a resident, including unexplained absence and psychological abuse (§87211(a)(1)). (2) Outbreaks of contagious disease, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours (§87211(a)(2)). (3) Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and to the licensing agency no later than the next working day (§87211(a)(3)). Suspected abuse is also reported under SAF-01 within 2 or 24 hours. Staff report every incident to the Administrator whether or not it is reportable. The agency keeps an internal incident log of all incidents.

definitions.definition: Any event involving a resident, staff member or visitor that is unusual, harmful or potentially harmful, including falls, injuries, medication errors, elopement, behavior events, property damage and deaths.
An incident that falls within 22 CCR §87211(a)(1), (a)(2) or (a)(3) and must be reported to the licensing agency or other officials.

An injury that the resident's physician determines to be serious. If no physician has seen the resident yet, the Administrator reports when emergency or medical staff describe the injury as serious or when the resident is hospitalized for the injury.
The public health officer for [COUNTY NAME] County, phone [LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE].
The licensing agency's form for reporting an unusual incident or injury.

procedures: Respond first: Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health or safety, give first aid and keep the resident safe (PD-04). The staff member stays with the resident until help arrives.

Tell the Administrator: The staff member on duty tells the Administrator or on-call administrator by phone as soon as the resident is safe, and no later than the end of the shift. For deaths, fires, outbreaks and major accidents the call is made immediately.
Notify the person responsible: The Administrator or designee tells the resident's person responsible and, where relevant, the physician as soon as possible. Staff record the time of each call.

Complete an incident report: The staff member who saw or found out about the event writes a factual report on [AGENCY NAME]'s incident form before the end of the shift. The report includes the date, time, location, residents and staff involved, what happened, injuries, treatment given, who was notified and follow-up.

Decide if reportable: The Administrator reviews each incident report within 1 working day and decides whether it falls in the 7-day, 24-hour or fire/explosion category. The decision is noted on the report. When in doubt, the Administrator reports.

7-day written report: For any death, physician-determined serious injury, AED use, or incident threatening welfare, safety or health (including unexplained absence and psychological abuse), the Administrator completes LIC 624 and sends it to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days. The Administrator aims to send it sooner and keeps a dated copy.

24-hour report: For an outbreak, poisoning, catastrophe or major accident, the Administrator phones or faxes the licensing agency at [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE/FAX] and the local health officer at [LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE] within 24 hours. The Administrator notes the date, time and person reached, and follows with a written report.

Fire or explosion: Staff call 9-1-1 and start the fire procedures in EDP-02. The Administrator reports to the local fire authority immediately and to the licensing agency no later than the next working day. If the fire or explosion also harms a resident, the 7-day report applies in addition.

AED use: Any time the AED is used, the Administrator makes the 7-day written report to licensing and the person responsible, whatever the outcome. The AED is checked and restocked before it is returned to service.
Deaths: Staff follow HC-04. The Administrator notifies the person responsible, the physician, hospice if involved, and the coroner if required. The Administrator sends the 7-day report to licensing.
Suspected abuse: If an incident involves suspected abuse, staff and the Administrator follow SAF-01 and the 2-hour or 24-hour phone report rules. The 7-day written report is also sent.
Missing resident: An unexplained absence is a reportable incident and is handled under SAF-03.

Update the resident's record: The staff member records the incident and any change in condition in the resident record. The Administrator decides whether the needs and services plan needs a reappraisal (AD-04).

Incident log: The Administrator enters every incident, reportable or not, in the incident log within 1 working day. The log shows the date, resident, type of event, reports made and dates sent, and follow-up actions.

Follow-up: Within 7 days the Administrator reviews each incident for cause and prevention, such as environment changes, staffing, supervision or training. The Administrator documents actions taken and reviews log trends monthly in quality assurance (GOV-03).
Other notices: Other events that §87211 requires to be reported (for example foreclosure or utility shut-off notices, or a change of administrator or chief corporate officer) follow REC-02.

responsibilities.role: Employee who witnesses or discovers the incident
responsibilities.duty: Ensure resident safety, call for help, tell the Administrator and complete the incident report before end of shift.
Decide reportability, send the 7-day, 24-hour and next-working-day reports, notify the person responsible, keep the log and follow up.
Take reports after hours, make the immediate calls (fire authority, 9-1-1) and start the notification chain.
Review incident trends and make sure resources are given for corrective actions.

documentation: Staff incident reports
LIC 624 reports with dated proof of submission to licensing and the person responsible
Record of 24-hour phone or fax reports to the licensing agency and local health officer
Record of fire authority and licensing notifications for fires and explosions
Internal incident log
Resident record entries and notification log
Administrator's follow-up and corrective action notes

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All direct care and supervisory staff
policies.purpose: To prevent residents from leaving unsafely, to find any missing resident quickly, and to report unexplained absences, while respecting each resident's right to leave at any time and not to be locked in (22 CCR §87468.1).
policies.policy: Residents have the right to leave the facility at any time and may not be locked in. [AGENCY NAME] therefore does not use locks to prevent a resident from leaving. The agency manages elopement risk through the pre-admission appraisal, the needs and services plan, staff supervision and awake night staffing, not through confinement. Alerting devices such as door chimes may be used only to alert staff and only where permitted by licensing and fire authority requirements. They are never used as a lock. When a resident cannot be found, staff search immediately, then call law enforcement and notify the person responsible if the resident is not found. An unexplained absence is a reportable incident, and a written report goes to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). Because the facility has fewer than 16 beds, at least one awake night staff person is on duty whenever a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705).

definitions.definition: A resident leaving the facility or grounds without staff knowing, in a way that puts the resident at risk, such as a resident with dementia who cannot find the way back.
A resident whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not in the building or on the grounds after a first check, and who has not signed out (AD-05).
A resident's absence that staff cannot account for and that is not a planned sign-out.
At least one night staff person who stays awake and on duty throughout the night.

procedures: Appraisal: At pre-admission appraisal, reappraisal and whenever staff observe wandering or exit-seeking, the Administrator records whether the resident is at risk of elopement and whether awake night supervision is needed (AD-02, AD-04).

Care plan: For residents at risk, the needs and services plan lists the specific supervision, activities, routines and staff checks to use. Less restrictive options are used first, and no locks are used to confine the resident.

Photo and description: For each at-risk resident the Administrator keeps a current photo and description (height, build, clothing habits, usual places they go) in the emergency information file (AD-05). Staff update it every 6 months and after any change in appearance.

Awake night staff: When a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, the Administrator schedules at least one awake staff person every night and notes this on the schedule (PP-01, PD-09). If the need arises on a night when no awake staff is scheduled, the Administrator arranges it by that night or relocates the resident.
Sign-out: Residents who go out with family or on their own sign out and in as required by AD-05. Staff compare the sign-out sheet to the resident count at each shift change.
Daily checks: Staff do a head count at each shift change and at least [FREQUENCY OF CHECKS, e.g., every 2 hours] for at-risk residents. Staff record the checks on the supervision log.
Discovery: A staff member who notices a resident is missing says so aloud to other staff, tells the shift lead and starts the search at once. Staff do not wait.

Immediate search: The shift lead assigns staff to check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, closets, laundry, kitchen, basement, garage, yard, vehicles and the street in front of the building. At least one staff person stays with the other residents so that care is not left uncovered.

Check the sign-out and phone: While the search goes on, staff check the sign-out sheet, check whether the resident left with a visitor, and phone the person responsible or known contacts to ask if the resident is with them.

Call 9-1-1: If the resident is not found within 15 minutes, the shift lead calls 9-1-1 and local law enforcement. Staff call at once, without waiting for 15 minutes, if the resident has dementia, is frail, needs medication or oxygen, is not dressed for the weather, or has been missing at night or in extreme heat or cold. Staff give the photo, description, clothing, last known location and time.

Notify: The shift lead tells the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee tells the person responsible and the resident's physician and keeps in touch with law enforcement until the resident is found.
Keep searching: Staff continue searching nearby, including areas the resident favored, until law enforcement takes over. The Administrator provides all information requested.

Resident found: Staff check the resident for injuries and needs. They call 9-1-1 if needed, make the resident comfortable and tell law enforcement, the person responsible and the Administrator that the resident has been found. If injury or neglect is suspected, SAF-01 applies.

Report: The Administrator sends a written report on LIC 624 to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days of the unexplained absence, and records the event in the incident log (SAF-02). If the absence is part of a catastrophe, the 24-hour report also applies.

Review: Within 7 days the Administrator reviews how the resident left, whether supervision was as planned and whether the plan, staffing or environment must change. The Administrator reappraises the resident and decides if the placement remains appropriate (AD-04, AD-06).

Training: All direct care staff are trained on this policy during orientation and at least annually, including dementia wandering behaviors (TR-01, TR-02). A missing resident drill is done at least once a year and recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Count residents at shift change, supervise at-risk residents, start the search immediately and follow the plan.
Direct the search, call 9-1-1 when needed, keep other residents covered and notify the Administrator.
Appraise elopement risk, schedule awake night staff, notify the person responsible, report the absence within 7 days and review the event.
Provide enough staff, including awake night staff when residents need it.

documentation: Elopement risk notes in the pre-admission appraisal and reappraisals
Needs and services plan supervision measures
Photo and description file
Sign-out sheets and supervision logs
Search record with times, people and calls made
LIC 624 report and proof of sending
Incident log entry
Training and drill records

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and visitors
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents, staff and visitors, to protect staff from bloodborne pathogens, and to respond to and report outbreaks.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written infection control plan on LIC 9282. The plan names an Infection Control Lead who has been trained by a qualified professional and sets initial and ongoing staff training (22 CCR §87470). The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually, after any outbreak declaration, and whenever the licensing agency asks. An outbreak is reported by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(a)(2)). Staff follow standard precautions with every resident and follow OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) for any exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material. Employee health and TB screening are handled under PP-04.

definitions.definition: The person named in the plan, [INFECTION CONTROL LEAD NAME], who has been trained by a qualified professional and who oversees infection prevention.

Practices used with all residents: hand hygiene, gloves and other personal protective equipment (PPE) when contact with body fluids is expected, safe handling of sharps and waste, cleaning of surfaces and equipment, and respiratory etiquette.
A cluster of illness among residents or staff, or any event that the local health officer or licensing agency declares an outbreak. Staff report a suspected cluster to the Administrator at once.
Contact of eyes, mouth, mucous membranes or broken skin with blood or other potentially infectious material, or a needlestick or sharps injury.
The licensing agency's infection control plan form.

procedures: Plan: Before opening, the Administrator completes LIC 9282, names the Infection Control Lead and keeps the plan where all staff can read it. The plan is updated when the Lead changes.

Lead training: The Infection Control Lead is trained by a qualified professional, such as an infection prevention specialist, public health nurse or other qualified clinician. The Administrator keeps the certificate or proof of training.

Staff training: Each new employee is trained on infection control and bloodborne pathogens during orientation and before giving unsupervised care (TR-01). Training is repeated at least annually and whenever the plan changes or a new hazard appears (TR-02).

Hand hygiene: Staff wash hands or use alcohol-based hand rub before and after resident contact, before food handling or medication assistance, after toileting care, after glove removal and after contact with soiled items. Sinks have soap and paper towels, and hand rub is available in common areas.
PPE: The agency keeps gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection in stock at [PPE STORAGE LOCATION]. Staff wear the PPE that is appropriate for the task and discard it in the right container after use.

Sharps and waste: Staff do not recap needles. Used sharps, such as lancets for residents' glucose checks if applicable, are placed in puncture-resistant sharps containers. Contaminated waste is bagged and disposed of as required by local rules. Staff do not use sharps beyond what the law allows (HC-01, HC-02).

Cleaning: Housekeeping staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces daily and bathrooms, kitchen and resident rooms on the schedule in CP-02. Blood and body fluid spills are cleaned immediately using an EPA-registered disinfectant per label directions. Shared equipment is disinfected between residents.

Laundry and food: Soiled linen is handled with gloves, bagged at the point of use and washed separately from clean items. Food is stored, prepared and served safely (FD-01). Staff with vomiting, diarrhea or open infected sores do not prepare or serve food.

Ill staff: Staff with symptoms of a contagious illness report to the Administrator and do not work with residents until cleared under the agency's exclusion rules and PP-04. The Administrator arranges coverage.

Visitors and residents: Visitors with symptoms are asked to postpone visits, and the agency tells them how to protect residents. The agency offers residents available vaccines such as influenza as their physician recommends, and respects their right to refuse (RD-01). Resident isolation is done only as the physician or public health officer recommends, and with the least restriction needed.

Hepatitis B and exposure plan: The Administrator keeps a written bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan, reviewed at least annually. Employees with occupational exposure are offered the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost within 10 working days of assignment unless they decline in writing.

Exposure incident: After a needlestick or other exposure, the employee washes the area at once, tells the Administrator and receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost. The Administrator records the incident on the sharps injury log without the employee's name in the public log.

Suspected outbreak: If two or more residents or staff develop similar symptoms, or a physician or the health department reports a communicable disease cluster, staff tell the Administrator at once. The Administrator calls the local health officer at [LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE] for guidance. The Administrator follows the health officer's isolation, cohorting, testing and cleaning instructions.

Outbreak report: The Administrator reports the outbreak by phone or fax to the licensing agency at [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE/FAX] and to the local health officer within 24 hours. The Administrator records the date, time and person spoken to, and tells persons responsible about the outbreak and any visiting changes. Any deaths or serious injuries are reported in writing within 7 days (SAF-02).

Plan review: The Infection Control Lead and Administrator review the plan at least once a year, after each outbreak declaration, and when the licensing agency asks. They update the plan, retrain staff on changes and document the review date.
Monitoring: The Infection Control Lead tracks infections among residents and staff on a log and reports trends to the Administrator monthly for quality assurance (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Oversee the plan, train staff, monitor infections, advise on outbreaks and help review the plan.
Keep LIC 9282 and the exposure control plan current, ensure supplies and training, report outbreaks within 24 hours and arrange coverage for ill staff.
Follow standard precautions, use PPE correctly, report symptoms and exposures, and join training.
Follow cleaning, laundry and food safety routines.
Fund supplies, PPE and training.

documentation: Completed LIC 9282 and review dates
Infection Control Lead training proof
Staff training records and sign-in sheets (kept at least 3 years)
Bloodborne pathogens exposure control plan and sharps injury log
Hepatitis B vaccination offer, acceptance or declination forms
Exposure incident records and confidential medical follow-up records
Infection tracking log
Outbreak reports and phone/fax confirmations
Cleaning schedules and checklists

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: Residents, visitors, families, staff and volunteers
policies.purpose: To set clear, fair rules for smoking, visiting and animals that protect resident health, safety and rights. The visiting policy and the firearms policy are written in each resident's admission agreement, and residents keep their rights to private visits and ombudsman access.
policies.policy: Visiting: The visiting policy appears in the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507) and is given to each resident at admission. Residents have the right to private visits. Ombudsmen and other advocates may visit residents privately at reasonable hours and without prior notice (22 CCR §87468.1). [AGENCY NAME] does not deny or limit a resident's association with others based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status. Firearms: Firearms, ammunition and other weapons are not allowed on the premises, and this policy is stated in the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507). Smoking: Smoking and vaping are not allowed inside the building. They are permitted only in the designated outdoor area at [DESIGNATED OUTDOOR SMOKING AREA]. Smoking is never allowed near oxygen or in resident bedrooms. Pets: The agency sets vaccination, health and supervision rules for facility pets and resident pets, as described below.

definitions.definition: Any person other than a resident or employee who is on the premises, including family, friends, clergy, volunteers and professionals.
A representative of the California Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program who may visit residents to advocate for them. The CRISISline is 1-800-231-4024.
An outdoor location chosen by the Administrator that is away from windows, entrances, air intakes, oxygen use and combustible materials, and approved with the local fire authority where required.
A dog or other animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, as defined by law.

procedures: Visiting policy in the agreement: The Administrator makes sure each admission agreement states the visiting policy and the firearms policy in plain language and 12-point type, and that the resident or representative receives and signs it (AD-07).

Visiting hours: General visiting hours are [VISITING HOURS], and visits outside those hours may be arranged with the shift lead. The agency does not use hours to stop a resident from seeing visitors of the resident's choice. The agency accommodates visits when families work or travel.
Private visits: Staff provide a private space, such as the resident's room or a common room, for visits. Staff do not require visitors to say why they are visiting and do not listen in.

Ombudsman and advocates: Staff let ombudsmen and other advocates visit residents privately at reasonable hours without prior notice. The staff member tells the Administrator but does not delay the visit. The ombudsman contact and posters are displayed in [LOCATION OF POSTED NOTICES] (RR-01).

Safety limits: Staff may limit or stop a visit only for a real safety, health or conduct reason, for example a visitor who is violent, intoxicated, has a contagious illness (SAF-04) or has been named in an abuse report. The Administrator decides, documents the reason and tells the resident. Limits are never based on the protected characteristics in 22 CCR §87468.1(b).
Sign-in: Visitors sign in and out at the front desk or on the visitor log for safety and emergencies. Residents are never required to sign in or out to go to their own room.

Firearms: At the admission appraisal staff ask residents, families and visitors to leave firearms, ammunition and other weapons off the premises. If a firearm is found or reported, staff do not touch it. The staff member tells the Administrator, who takes it up with the owner and, if there is danger, calls 9-1-1.
Smoking indoors: Staff tell residents and visitors that smoking and vaping are not allowed inside. Staff post no-smoking signs at entrances and in common areas.

Smoking outdoors: Residents who smoke may do so only in the designated outdoor area. Staff assess whether a resident can smoke safely and independently. If the resident cannot, the needs and services plan sets supervision or other measures (AD-04). Matches and lighters are kept by staff for residents who cannot use them safely. Ashtrays are metal with lids and emptied into a metal container with water. Staff check the area each shift.
Oxygen safety: No one may smoke, vape or use open flame within the area where oxygen is in use. Signs are posted. Staff tell smokers who use oxygen about the hazard and arrange safe options.
Smoking cessation: The Administrator offers information about cessation support to residents who ask and to staff.

Facility pets: Pets owned by the agency must be approved by the Administrator, be healthy and vaccinated as required by local law and a veterinarian, and be kept clean. Pets are not allowed in the kitchen, medication area or food prep areas, and are kept away from residents who are afraid of them or allergic. Staff clean up waste promptly.

Resident pets: A resident who wishes to keep a pet must ask the Administrator. The Administrator considers the resident's ability to care for the animal, other residents' health and safety, room size and the building's rules. The resident provides proof of current vaccination and a plan for care. The Administrator documents the decision.

Pet supervision: Pets must be supervised and kept on a leash or in a carrier when in common areas. A pet that bites, threatens or harms anyone or causes a nuisance must be removed. Staff do not take on the resident's pet care unless the admission agreement says so.

Visiting animals and service animals: Visiting animals must be vaccinated and accompanied by their handler. Service animals are admitted as the law requires, and staff may ask only the questions the law allows.

Reporting: Staff report incidents involving smoking, visitors, weapons or animals to the Administrator on an incident report. Injuries and any threats to resident safety are reported under SAF-02 and SAF-01.

Policy review: The Administrator reviews this policy at least yearly with the fire authority's and the health department's current rules and updates the admission agreement when the policy changes (GOV-03).

Follow the posted rules and keep firearms and unvaccinated animals off the premises.
Approve the policies and make sure the premises meet fire and health requirements.

policies.title: Resident Records, Register and Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designated record keepers and all staff who document care
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps complete, accurate, confidential and available resident records and a register of residents, and keeps required records for the right length of time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for each resident and a current register of residents as the Community Care Licensing regulations require. Each resident record holds the signed admission agreement, the pre-admission appraisal, the medical assessment and the other documents listed in this policy. Medication records are kept for at least 1 year. Records of the destruction of medications are kept for at least 3 years (22 CCR §87465). Every advertisement that mentions dementia care is kept for 3 years (22 CCR §87706). Other resident records are kept for the period required by Title 22, and the agency does not destroy any resident record sooner than the Administrator has confirmed the correct period with the licensing agency. Records are confidential and are handled under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Part 164) and RR-02. Records are available to the licensing agency on request.

definitions.definition: The set of documents about one resident: admission agreement, appraisal, medical assessment, needs and services plan, emergency information, medication records, incident reports, notices and notes.
A current list of all residents showing each resident's name and admission and discharge information, as the licensing regulations require.
The record that shows each medication the resident is assisted with, including dose, time and who assisted, and PRN orders and use.
Individually identifiable health information about a resident, in any form, protected under 45 CFR Part 164.

procedures: Open the record: On the day of admission, the Administrator opens a record for the resident, assigns it to a locked file or secure electronic system and starts the register entry.

Required contents: The Administrator checks that the record holds the signed and dated admission agreement, the pre-admission appraisal, the physician's report and medical assessment, TB and immunization information, the needs and services plan and reappraisals, emergency contact and physician information, and the resident's personal rights acknowledgment (AD-01 to AD-07).

Ongoing entries: Staff add the medication records, PRN orders, incident and change-of-condition notes, notices, physician orders, hospice or home health records and correspondence as they occur. Each entry is dated, timed and signed or initialed with the staff member's name.

Medication records: The Administrator keeps medication records, including PRN records, for at least 1 year. When medications are destroyed, the record is signed by the administrator and one other adult who is not a resident, and kept for at least 3 years (HC-01).

Register of residents: The Administrator updates the register on each admission, discharge, transfer and death, within 1 working day. The register is kept at the facility and is available to the licensing agency.

Dementia advertisements: If the agency advertises dementia care, the Administrator keeps a copy of every advertisement for 3 years, with the date and where it appeared, along with the written dementia program (PD-09, GOV-02).
Accuracy: Staff correct errors with a single line through the entry, the date and initials. Staff never erase, white-out or backdate entries. Late entries are labeled as such.

Security: Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet in [RECORD STORAGE LOCATION] and not left in view. Electronic records require unique passwords, are backed up and are accessed only by authorized staff.

Access: Staff see only what their job requires. The licensing agency, the ombudsman, and the resident or authorized representative may see records as the law allows. The Administrator reviews other requests under RR-02 and 45 CFR Part 164, and records each disclosure that must be tracked.
Emergency access: Emergency information and medication information are kept where staff can reach them quickly, and a copy goes with a resident who is taken to the hospital (AD-05, PD-04).

Discharge: When a resident leaves, the Administrator completes the discharge or death entry, gives the resident or representative any records the law requires, updates the register, and moves the record to inactive storage within 30 days.

Retention schedule: The Administrator keeps a written retention schedule listing each record type and how long it is kept. For all resident records not given a fixed period in this policy, the Administrator confirms the required period with the licensing agency and writes it in the schedule before any record is destroyed. Until that is done, no resident record is destroyed.

Destruction of records: When the retention period ends, the Administrator destroys records by shredding or secure deletion, and logs the type of record, date and person responsible. Records that may be needed for an investigation, lawsuit or complaint are not destroyed.
Closure or sale: If the agency closes or changes ownership, the Administrator arranges for safe, confidential transfer or storage of all records and notifies the licensing agency as required.
Privacy incidents: Staff report any lost, stolen or wrongly disclosed record to the Administrator at once. The Administrator follows RR-02 and notifies affected people as the law requires.

Record audit: Every quarter the Administrator reviews a sample of resident records and the register for completeness, signatures and dates, and records the findings and corrections in quality assurance (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Open and maintain records and the register, keep medication, destruction and advertisement records for the required periods, keep the retention schedule, control access and conduct audits.
Document accurately, dated and signed, and protect residents' privacy.
Handle HIPAA requests, disclosures and breach response (RR-02), named as [PRIVACY OFFICIAL NAME].
Make sure records are stored securely and are available for licensing inspection.

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, the licensee and the governing body of [AGENCY NAME], a Residential Care Facility for the Elderly (RCFE) licensed by CDSS Community Care Licensing
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] sends every required report, notice and fee to the California Department of Social Services (CDSS) Community Care Licensing Division, the local health officer, the local fire authority, law enforcement, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and each resident's responsible person. Each must go to the right agency, by the right method, within the required time, and be documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with the reporting requirements of 22 CCR §87211 (Reporting Requirements) and the license fee requirements of HSC §1569.185 (License fees). (1) Deaths, serious injuries as determined by the physician, any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED), and any incident that threatens the welfare, safety or health of a resident (including unexplained absence and psychological abuse) are reported in writing to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days. (2) Outbreaks of contagious disease, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported within 24 hours by telephone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer. (3) Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to the licensing agency. (4) Suspected physical abuse of an elder or dependent adult is reported to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if the abuse resulted in serious bodily injury, and otherwise within 24 hours. (5) Written notice is sent to the licensing agency within 2 business days of receiving a notice of foreclosure, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy, rent default or utility shut-off. Applicants for admission are informed of any such condition before they sign an admission agreement. Failure to give this notice carries a civil penalty of $100 per day, up to $2,000. (6) A new Administrator is reported to the licensing agency within 30 days. A change of chief corporate officer is reported within 15 working days. (7) The annual license fee is paid on or before each license anniversary, and CDSS is notified before any capacity change. When in doubt, staff report. A report is never delayed to complete an investigation, gather more facts or obtain approval.

definitions.definition: The CDSS Community Care Licensing Division, Adult and Senior Care Program (ASCP), through the regional office that serves [AGENCY NAME]. Statewide ASCP telephone: (916) 657-2592. Regional office: [LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE NAME AND PHONE].
The resident's authorized representative, conservator, agent under a power of attorney, family member or other person identified in the resident's admission agreement and emergency information.
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman program serving [COUNTY]. The statewide CRISISline is 1-800-231-4024. Local office: [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE].
The public health officer for [COUNTY]. Telephone: [LOCAL HEALTH DEPARTMENT PHONE].
The fire department or fire protection district with jurisdiction over [ADDRESS]. Non-emergency telephone: [LOCAL FIRE AUTHORITY PHONE]. In an active fire, call 911.

For the 2-hour abuse reporting deadline, an injury involving extreme physical pain, substantial risk of death, protracted loss or impairment of a bodily member or function, or requiring medical intervention such as surgery, hospitalization or physical rehabilitation.
A day on which the licensing agency's offices are open, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and state holidays.
Any event listed in the policy section of this document that must be reported to the licensing agency or another agency.

procedures: Any staff member who witnesses or learns of a reportable event (death, serious injury, AED use, outbreak, poisoning, fire, explosion, catastrophe, major accident, unexplained absence, suspected abuse, or any incident threatening a resident's welfare, safety or health) immediately makes the resident safe, calls 911 if there is any emergency, and notifies the Administrator or the person in charge as soon as possible.

The Administrator, or the person in charge in the Administrator's absence, decides which report category applies, using the Reporting Timeline Chart posted in the office and kept in the Policy and Procedure Manual. If the category is unclear, the person in charge reports under the shortest applicable deadline.

Fire or explosion: staff call 911 and the local fire authority immediately. After the emergency, the Administrator notifies the licensing agency by phone or fax no later than the next working day and records the date, time and name of the person spoken to.

Outbreak, poisoning, catastrophe or major accident: the Administrator notifies the licensing agency and the local health officer by telephone or fax within 24 hours. The Administrator records the name of the person who received each report, the date and time, and keeps a fax confirmation sheet if fax is used.

Suspected physical abuse of an elder or dependent adult: the staff member who has the suspicion, or the Administrator on the staff member's behalf, reports to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if the resident has serious bodily injury, and within 24 hours in all other cases. Follow SAF-01 and PP-02 for the content of the report and each employee's personal duty to report.

Death, serious injury as determined by the physician, AED use, or any other incident threatening welfare, safety or health: the Administrator completes a written incident report on the form specified by the licensing agency (currently the Unusual Incident/Injury Report, LIC 624, or its successor) and sends it to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days of the event. Follow SAF-02 for the content and for the incident log.
Unexplained absence of a resident: staff follow SAF-03 immediately. The Administrator also completes the 7-day written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident.

Reports that fall under more than one category (for example, an injury caused by suspected abuse) are made under each applicable category and deadline. Making a report to one agency does not satisfy the duty to report to the others.

Financial and property notices: the Administrator and licensee immediately forward to each other any notice of foreclosure, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy, rent default or utility shut-off. Within 2 business days of receipt, the Administrator sends written notice to the licensing agency and keeps a copy with proof of delivery.
Before an applicant signs the admission agreement, the Administrator gives the applicant written notice of any such pending notice or condition, and documents the date given. See AD-07.

Administrator change: when a new Administrator is hired or designated, the licensee notifies the licensing agency in writing within 30 days. The licensee confirms that the new Administrator holds a current RCFE administrator certificate (see GOV-01).
Chief corporate officer change: when the chief corporate officer of a corporate licensee changes, the licensee notifies the licensing agency in writing within 15 working days.

Annual license fee: the licensee calendars the license anniversary date and pays the annual fee on or before that date ($495.60 for 4 to 6 beds, or $742.80 for 7 to 15 beds, as currently set by HSC §1569.185). A 50 percent late fee applies if the fee is late. The Administrator verifies payment and files the receipt.

Capacity change: before increasing or decreasing licensed capacity, the licensee notifies CDSS and obtains approval, and pays the $25 capacity change fee. No resident is admitted above the capacity shown on the license (see GOV-02).

After any report, the Administrator completes a Report Tracking Log entry showing the event, the agency or person notified, the method, the date and time, the staff member who made the report, and the copy retained. Follow-up requests from the licensing agency, health officer or law enforcement are answered promptly and documented.

The Administrator reviews the Report Tracking Log monthly to verify that every event in the incident log and every financial or ownership notice was reported on time, and takes corrective action for any late or missing report. Findings are included in the quality assurance review under GOV-03.

Staff are trained on this policy at orientation (TR-01) and at least annually (TR-02). The Reporting Timeline Chart and the telephone and fax numbers for the licensing agency, local health officer, ombudsman, fire authority and law enforcement are posted in the office and kept at each phone used for reporting.

responsibilities.duty: Immediately protect residents and notify the Administrator or person in charge of any reportable event. Staff who are mandated reporters also make their own report of suspected abuse as required in SAF-01 and PP-02. Staff never delay or withhold a report.

Determine the reporting category, make or supervise every report within the deadline, give written reports to the licensing agency and the responsible person, maintain the Report Tracking Log, and train staff.

responsibilities.role: Person in charge (in the Administrator's absence)
responsibilities.duty: Make time-critical reports (fire, 2-hour and 24-hour reports) and notify the Administrator as soon as possible.

Pay license fees on time, notify CDSS of capacity changes, new administrators and corporate officer changes, forward financial notices promptly to the Administrator, and provide written notices to the licensing agency within 2 business days.
File copies of all reports, fax confirmations, payment receipts and correspondence in the facility records and make them available to the licensing agency on request (see REC-01).

documentation: Unexplained/unusual incident reports and written 7-day reports, with proof of delivery to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident
Notes of telephone or fax reports for 24-hour, fire and abuse reports (date, time, agency, name of person spoken to, name of reporter)
Report Tracking Log

Notices of new Administrator and change of chief corporate officer, with proof of delivery
Annual license fee payment receipts and capacity change notices and fee receipts
Reporting Timeline Chart and posted contact list
Staff training sign-in sheets for this policy

Items are taken from the Section B table (RCFE column) and the B4-B15 narrative instructions. A14 is added from Section A because it is a required written plan. required_items.text: If the property is not currently occupied by the applicant, use of the relocation site requires authorization from the agency or person currently in possession, verified in writing.

JOB DESCRIPTIONS: a job description for each staff classification. Each must be clear, concise and relevant to the position, and must match a classification on the Personnel Report (LIC 500). Staff positions must correspond to those listed on all personnel reports.
Duties and responsibilities.
Minimum qualifications that correspond to licensing requirements, including any special licenses, certificates or special skills needed to perform the job.
Lines of supervision, including supervision given and to whom, and supervision received and from whom.
PERSONNEL POLICIES: describe the regulatory requirements commonly associated with personnel practices, such as staff coverage, staff qualifications, work schedules and conditions of employment.
Work hours/shifts, to document that positions provide coverage with competent staff. They must correspond with the staff positions and work days and hours listed on all personnel reports.
Abuse reporting procedures. Documentation must indicate that employees will be informed of their responsibility to report to the licensing agency, the police, and the child/adult protective agency.

Hiring practices, including screening of employees for necessary education and experience. Employees must be informed that conditions of employment include fingerprint clearance, statement of prior criminal convictions, TB clearance, physical examination/health questionnaire, and child abuse index check.
IN-SERVICE TRAINING FOR STAFF: a plan for in-service training, submitted to the licensing agency at the time of application as part of the plan of operation.
New employee training: a description of the training, stating who will conduct it.

Ongoing training: topics to be covered (the list should include administrator continuing education units), how often the training will be given, and how it will be documented. It must include the topics specified in regulation sections 80065 (General) and 87565 (Residential Care Facilities for the Elderly).

RCFE PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: a general overview of the program philosophies, services provided and activities in the facility. A pamphlet or brochure is acceptable only if it includes all of the following elements (B7.1-B7.11).
Brief statement of the purpose, goals and program methods (program philosophy).
Days and hours of operation (**may also appear in the Admission Policies section).
Daily schedule of activities to be provided by the facility, stating who plans, conducts and assists clients in participating.
A one-month schedule of planned social, educational and recreational activities, stating who plans, conducts and assists clients in participating.
Description of the basic services provided by the facility (** may also appear in the Admission Policies section; see Admission Guideline LIC 604/604A for the list of basic services).
Description of the optional services provided in the facility, as listed in the admission agreement (** may also appear in the Admission Policies section).
Description of how the facility will handle medical emergencies if a client becomes ill or injured.
Procedure for handling and assisting clients/residents with self-administered medications.
Transportation arrangements.
Description of community resources and consultants to be used by the facility.
A procedure, approved by the licensing agency, for immediate response to incidents and complaints.

RULES OF DISCIPLINE / PERSONAL RIGHTS. Personal rights apply to all facility categories. The detailed discipline items (types of discipline used and conditions, types not permitted, 'no corporal punishment/violation of personal rights', conferences with parents/placement representatives, grounds for dismissal/eviction/relocation/removal) are headed 'Group Homes and Foster Family Agencies only'. CDSS will evaluate the policies to ensure they do not violate personal rights and contain a clear statement that no corporal or unusual punishment will be used.

ADMISSION POLICIES: must provide information relevant to the category of clients accepted for care, including ages of clients, rates and refund policies, acceptance and retention limitations, pre-admission appraisals, needs and services plans, medical assessments, and an admission agreement containing the typical information a client or authorized representative needs before entering. A description of the following items (B9.1-B9.11) must be included.
Persons accepted for care, including age range and compatibility determination process, when necessary.
Intake procedures for placement in group homes (listed in the shared list; written for the group home category).
Criteria for assessing appropriateness of placement given an individual client's needs (i.e., interviews, procedures for obtaining and developing the necessary paperwork, etc.).
Needs and services plan.
Client's Rights/Personal Rights. At a minimum, a statement that clients/residents will be informed of their rights and that their rights will not be violated.
Medical assessment.
Pre-admission appraisal plan.
Emergency information.
Sign-in and sign-out procedures.
Immunization requirements.
Physical examination requirements (including TB testing).
SAMPLE MENU, to show the applicant is familiar with balanced meals, acceptable portion sizes and general principles of good nutrition. It will include the items B10.1-B10.3.
Planned meals and snacks for one week, using foods from the four basic food groups.
Portion sizes.
Times meals served.
CONTROL OF PROPERTY: name and address of the owner of the facility property.
Copy of the lease or rental agreement (no requirement on its length). The agreement must not preclude use of the property as a facility or prevent compliance with regulations.
Proof of ownership if the applicant owns the property (property tax bill, deed or similar). The document must show the facility street address.
INSURANCE INFORMATION (RCFE only): a statement on whether insurance will cover the facility operation. If so, state the type of coverage and with whom. If not, a statement saying so is sufficient.

THEFT AND LOSS POLICY (RCFE only). The policy shall include provisions for: inventory of personal property at admission; modification of the inventory; practices to safeguard personal property upon the resident's death; documentation and reporting of loss of personal property; method of marking personal property; and method for providing a secure area for safekeeping of resident personal property.

NEIGHBORHOOD COMPLAINT POLICY: procedures for immediate response to incidents and complaints, including a time when the owner, licensee or designee will be available to meet with neighborhood residents. Applies only to non-resident-owner community care facilities providing residential care for six or fewer persons. The Section B table marks it 'Required' in the Adult Residential/RCFE column, so confirm applicability for your facility.

official.notes: LIC 281 says to submit the Section A and B documents in the same sequence as the booklet. Organize the manual by the B-numbers above, with the A14 plan in its Section A position. The booklet says the application fee plus the Section A and B documents go to the licensing agency as one packet.
